## §90 The trainee ecosystem (PHASES A–C SHIPPED v0.10.31–33 — one world of people)

Owner: "I want the actual trainee ecosystem to make sense and be
connected. Survival shows actually draw from the active trainee pool.
Trainees exist and remember. Released trainees move throughout the
system. No just random generations popping that say they're a washout
or something. Every trainee exists within the world and comes from
somewhere."

**The law.** Every person who matters is ONE person, born once at a
door of the world, from somewhere, carried by one file for life.
Nothing stands in for a person: no counters where people should be,
no mint-from-nothing to play a part a real person could play. A
trainee who leaves a company does not leave the world; she leaves
the company. The world forgets a person only when she leaves it for
good (aged out, gone home) — and never one who has a chapter with
the player.

**A. What the audit found (read-only, 300-week census, idle house).**
227 people in the save: 140 'rival', 50 'student', 27 'prospect', 6
'released', 4 'departed'. The disconnections, in order of how badly
they break the owner's law:
1. RIVAL FLOORS ARE A NUMBER. `rival.rosterCount` is an integer
   (intake +1 at scoutIntake, −cut at evaluations, −size at debuts)
   while named 'rival' people exist beside it — Tidewater at
   "9 trainees" with 67 named people; Monarch "10" with 1. The two
   truths never meet: a seasonal cut subtracts from the counter and
   then MINTS castoffs from nothing (`KP.mintCastoff` → a new person
   with a fabricated "cut at Aurum" line) while the named floor is
   cut by a separate rule (`namedCuts`, real people → the board).
   Debut casting takes real signees first, then fills the lineup with
   freshly minted "In-house trainee" people who did not exist the
   week before.
2. THE SEASON IS INVENTED. The annual competition show (network.js
   SHOW) mints 2–3 finalists from nothing on a fixed week, gives them
   followers and a history line, and parks them on the board. No
   contestants, no eliminations, no companies sending anyone, no
   project group, no way for YOUR trainee to be on it.
3. WASHOUTS ARE INVENTED. `NETWORK.WASH.mintChance` mints a "Program
   washout" from nothing with a polish bump and a line about years of
   training nobody simulated.
4. RELEASED TRAINEES VANISH. `releaseTrainee`/`quitNow`/the trainee
   table's farewell and the scandal release all set status 'released'
   and leave the person in `state.people` — where nothing ever reads
   her again except the departed-writer royalty letter. She never
   reappears on the board, never signs elsewhere, never debuts for
   a rival, never comes back at 22 with a chapter.
5. THE WORLD FORGETS TOO EASILY. Students who age out of a class,
   prospects past prospectAgeOut, castoffs past their window are
   `delete`d from `state.people` — including people the player met,
   visited, read, or was outbid for.
6. ORIGINS ARE THIN. A person carries `source` (a label) and
   `channel` (how she reached YOUR desk) and, for school kids,
   `schoolId`; home regions are a hash (`strongholdsOf`), not a
   birthplace; the "In-house trainee" and saga trainees come from
   nowhere.
7. THREE MARKETS FOR ONE THING (§89 D7). Castoffs, free agents (a
   collapse's signing class — real people, correctly), and washouts
   are three lanes of "rival-trained person available," two of them
   minted.
What is already right and should be kept: schools hold persistent
classes of real students (§84 A); rival signings off the board turn
a prospect into a real 'rival' person with a company; the fog poach
signs a real student; a collapse mints free agents from the real
floor; departed idols persist and can return (returnRun); cross-
company friendships (society.js) and the directed ledger (§89 D3)
already give a person memory across contexts.

**B. The design.**

*B1. Rival floors are people.* `rival.rosterCount` becomes a READ:
the count of 'rival' people with `company === rival.short` not in an
act. Intake is a door, not an increment: a rival's weekly intake
signs from the world first — the open board (its interest ladder,
as now), a school class (the fog poach, as now), a castoff or a
released trainee on the market, a finalist — and only when the world
has nobody does the rival's OWN door open: an application to THEM,
born with an origin (city, a school if from one, enteredWeek) and
`company` stamped. The seasonal evaluation cuts REAL people: the
floor sorted by peak talent after tenure, the lowest N cut — and
the castoff on the board IS the person cut, file intact (what she
trained, how long, who signed her, whether she was once on your
board). Debut casting fills the lineup from the real floor only; a
floor too thin to field a debut waits (the comfort rule already
exists) — the rival's intake rate is tuned so floors stay fieldable
(measured, not assumed). The retired act's members stay people
(they already do). Save migration: an existing counter materializes
into named trainees at load, each born with an origin and a signed
week back-dated by tenure, so no save loses a debut.

*B2. The season draws from the pool.* The competition show becomes
a SEASON (≈12 weeks, one a year, the finale week as now): a casting
call goes out in the world — companies submit trainees from their
real floors (rivals pick their 1–2 most promising non-act trainees
by a hash of readiness and hype), schools submit a known student or
two, the open board's unsigned prospects enter on their own — and
the player gets ONE scene: the producers' invitation to send up to
two trainees. The decision is real: exposure (hype, followers, a
public that learns her name — the §77 public eye reads it), a
polish bump from televised training, a national-TV elimination that
costs morale and marks the file, and the project-group risk — a
finalist who makes the lineup debuts in the season's PROJECT GROUP
(a rival-style act with a fixed term, say 60 weeks, run by the
broadcaster) and is unavailable to your lineup until the term ends,
then returns famous (the §87 solo-era machinery already knows how to
hold a seat; the dual-career flag is the model). Eliminations run
weekly in the feed (the regulars have opinions); unsigned
eliminated contestants land on the board with heat and a history
line that is TRUE; signed ones return to their floors with hype.
Owner-facing names stay invented (content law). The season replaces
NETWORK.SHOW's mint entirely.

*B3. Released trainees move through the system.* A person with
status 'released' (your release, her quit, the farewell, the scandal
release) enters a RE-ENTRY clock: after a cooldown (8–16 weeks,
hashed) she resurfaces as a public prospect on the open board with
her file — "Released from HCG, week N" — unless she is past the age
wall, in which case she goes home (and the world forgets her only if
she has no chapter with you). On the board she is contested like
any public file: a rival with interest signs her (and she may debut
against you — "a face we lost" already exists for signees and now
covers releases), or the player re-signs her at a price the LEDGER
sets (`KP.ledgerRead`: a grudge over the walkout line means she will
not take the meeting; a warm standing means a discount and a line in
the file). A trainee who quit over a broken promise carries the
grudge into the next company's floor and remembers it at every
renewal. The three exits that today say "she packed" become three
chapters that continue.

*B4. No mint-from-nothing.* The world's doors, and the only places
`generatePerson` may be called after new-game: academy enrollment
(a student, with city and school), an application (to the player or
to a rival — with city), a street cast / open call (with district),
a viral kid (born on social media, with city), and the saga doors
(JV classes — born abroad, with country). Every door stamps
`origin: { city, schoolId?, channel, enteredWeek, firstCompany? }`.
Deleted outright: the WASH stream (a washout is a real cut now), the
SHOW mint (B2), the "In-house trainee" fill (B1), `mintCastoff`
(the castoff is the cut). The §89 D7 merge rides along: one market
— the open board — with `source` tags; `state.freeAgents` folds into
it (a collapse's class lands on the board with a premium and a
window, as castoffs do today).

*B5. Memory.* One file for life: history, the directed ledger, eval
history, friendships, hype and followers, the public eye's
expectations, the renewal reads — all survive a change of company
because the person object survives it. The Person tab gets a
"Chapters" strip (where she has been: the academy, the companies,
the show, the releases) read from history stamps, not a new store.
The world forgets at exits only: `KP.forget(state, p)` deletes a
person when she leaves the world (aged out, gone home) AND has no
chapter with the player (never on the roster, never visited, never
read, never a rival act member the player faced). Everyone else is
kept — and the save budget is measured (people are already the
biggest save component at ~480 KB of ~700 KB at week 620; B1 adds
~50 named floor trainees; B5's keep-rule must be checked against
the 5 MB quota by the longhaul at 620 weeks).

*B6. The headcount economy is measured.* A new tool,
`tools/audit_people.js`, runs the 40-seed soak and prints, per
org-year: births by door, exits by reason, people by status, floor
sizes per rival, board size, the mint-from-nothing count (must be
ZERO outside the doors), ghost events (a cut or a cast with no
person — must be zero), and re-entries (released → board → signed).
The harness gets bands: rival floors fieldable (every rival that
schedules a debut can cast it from its floor ≥ 90%), season ran
with ≥ 8 contestants from ≥ 3 sources, player trainee invited to the
season (≥ 40% of orgs with a roster), released trainee resurfaced
(≥ 50% of orgs that released anyone), a face we lost debuted
against us (≥ 10%).

**C. Phases.** Each is a full-ritual release; each shifts the stream.
- PHASE A — THE FLOOR (v0.10.31): B1 + B4's deletions of WASH,
  mintCastoff and the in-house fill + B3's re-entry clock + B6's
  tool and bands + the floor migration. The biggest felt change:
  the rival you watch has NAMED trainees you can read on the
  Industry page, the castoff on your board is somebody you may have
  lost to them, and the kid you released last year is on the open
  board again. Medium risk (industry.js casting and culling are
  load-bearing for every rival-side suite).
- PHASE B — THE SEASON (v0.10.32): B2 in full — the casting call,
  the player's invitation scene, weekly eliminations in the feed,
  the project group with a fixed term and the seat held, the
  returns. Highest felt value; needs §87's held-seat machinery and
  one new scene family. Medium risk.
- PHASE C — THE FILE (v0.10.33): B5's chapters strip, `origin` on
  every door, the forget-rule, the §89 D7 market merge, and the
  Industry page's named floors. Low risk, mostly surface.

**D. Rulings (owner).** (1) Rivals CAN re-sign a trainee they cut
— "Yes." (2) The season's project group is fixed-term OR permanent,
decided by a random roll per season — "Fixed-term it permanent.
Random roll." (3) "Released trainees hold grudges based on
personality": the refusal line is hers, not a constant — warmth and
professionalism forgive, dominance and competitiveness do not; the
ledger's grudge is read against HER bar. (4) "Yes, you can send
trainees to a season" — up to two.

**As built — Phase A, v0.10.31 "the floor".** Owner: the four
rulings above, then build. floor.js is the module; industry.js,
scouting.js, network.js, schools.js, sagas.js, tongue.js, founding.js,
newgame.js, sim.js, practice.js, scandal.js and save.js changed around
it. Suite_098_floor (80 checks) and tools/audit_people.js are the
eyes.

*B1 — rival floors are people.* `rival.rosterCount` is gone;
`KP.rivalFloor(state, rival)` is the read (status 'rival', the
company, not in an act). Intake is a door: a rival's weekly intake
takes a MARKET file off the open board (a castoff or a released
trainee, `FLOOR.intakeFromBoardChance` .5, hash-gated) or opens its
own door — `KP.mintRivalTrainee`: an applicant to THEM, signed at
15–18, born with a hometown (`p.born = { door, city, week }`,
`KP.stampBorn`), stamped `signedWeek`. The seasonal evaluation cuts
PEOPLE: the room graded lowest peak first, signees exempt until
ROOM.namedTenure unless the room must shrink anyway; a trainee past
FLOOR.floorAgeOut (25) leaves at the evaluation regardless. Every
cut goes through `KP.cutFromFloor`: the castoff on the open board IS
the person who was cut (file, hometown, history: "Cut at Aurum's
seasonal evaluation"); when the board is full she waits on the
market as 'released'. Lineups are cast from the floor only —
debut-aged, FLOOR.castTenureWeeks (8) on the floor — and a room that
cannot field a gender waits (ROOM.comfortRecheck) instead of minting
one. The debut-day "missed the lineup by a hair" castoff is the real
next name on the floor. A collapse releases the whole room (the
signing class stays free agents); a split walks six real trainees
out with the defectors; a company born in the world seeds its room
at its door. The opening scene and old-save backfill are doors too
(`ensureCastable`): a room that already runs an act gets the people
it must have had, back-dated. The old-save migration materializes a
counter into named trainees (deterministic rng per company).

*B3 — released trainees move through the system.* `KP.leftUs` at
every player exit (release, quit, the farewell, the scandal release)
stamps `wasOurs`, `releasedFrom`, `releasedWeek`. The re-entry rail
(order 619): after FLOOR.reentryMin–Max (8–16, hashed) weeks she is a
public prospect again (`channel: 'released'`, "Back on the open
board after N weeks"), with a desk note when she was ours; past the
market's age she goes home; with no seat on the board she waits
FLOOR.marketWaitWeeks (10) then signs elsewhere (a REAL signing —
`KP.rivalSignFromBoard`) or goes home. Rivals court her like any
public file (and can re-sign the one they cut — ruling 1). Re-signing
her is read against HER bar (ruling 3): `KP.grudgeBar(p)` = 2 +
(warmth+professionalism)/50 − (dominance+competitiveness)/60, floored
at 1; a ledger grudge at or over it is a no (the meeting happens, no
money moves, she stays on the board); under it the price remembers —
×0.8 on a warm standing, ×1.25 with a grudge. The directed ledger,
history and reads survive every exit because the person does.

*B4 — no mint-from-nothing.* Deleted: the WASH stream, `mintCastoff`,
the "In-house trainee" lineup fill. Every remaining birth goes
through a door and stamps `born`: academy (city, school),
application, referral, street, audition (open call), social,
showKid (the season — Phase B replaces its mint), rivalDoor,
auditionAbroad (the tongue's tours), abroad (the sagas' arrivals),
founding. The audit counts births by door and asserts two zeros.

*B5 — memory, and the forget rule.* `KP.hasChapter(state, p)`: on
the roster or in a lineup, ever ours, read by this desk
(`flags.readByUs`, stamped by the targeted look), lost to a rival
from our mail or a file we read, or any directed act. `KP.goHome`
is the one exit: a person with a chapter becomes 'gone' and stays;
one without is forgotten. Every deletion in the engine now goes
through it (castoff windows, aged-off leads, graduations, the
castoff who is done, the market's clock). The first chapter rule
kept 145 'gone' files per 620-week save for a chapter that was never
ours (a public lead a rival signed); tightened to our mail / our
reads.

*B6 — measured (tools/audit_people.js, 43 orgs, 116 org-years).*
Births per org-year: academy 43.8, rivalDoor 38.1, application 5.5,
auditionAbroad 3.1, showKid 3.1, referral 2.0, social 0.6, abroad
0.4. Births with no door: 0. Lineups cast with someone minted that
week: 0 (three "signed Monday, debuted Friday" cases before the
tenure floor). Floor ledger per org-year: cut 31.9, boarded 7.7,
marketed 24.3, signed off the board 31.9, re-entries 3.1, elsewhere
11.3, forgotten 12.7. People at career end per org: rival 110,
student 52, prospect 31, released 17, idol 13, trainee 4. Rival
floors at 140 weeks: median 10 (min 5, max 27). Save size: soak orgs
482–537 KB at 140 weeks (cap raised 480→600, the floor is ~55 real
people per org); longhaul 590–908 KB at 620 weeks (people 448–631
KB), down from 1.0–1.15 MB before the market clock and the chapter
rule. Harness bands: washoutReturned now reads a real cut (.50),
reentrySeen (.30), rivalDoorBorn (.90).

*Left for Phase B/C.* The season still mints finalists at its door
(B2 replaces it); `state.freeAgents` still its own lane (C merges
it); the Person tab's chapters strip; retired rival acts' members
stay 'rival' forever (82 per 620-week save — a C question).

Battery 98/98, soak 40 clean, longhaul 10x620, e2e 111, lockstep
0.10.31.


**As built — Phase B, v0.10.32 "the season".** Owner: "Phase B
approved." season.js is the module; network.js lost its finale mint
(NETWORK.SHOW → COMPETITION — the name SEASON was the year's);
industry.js grew `KP.makeRivalAct` and the broadcaster-house guards;
person.js's onBreak and group.js's lineup verb learned the away
flags. Suite_099_season (78 checks).

*The casting call* (COMPETITION.castWoy 22, one a year, one gender
per season — boyShowShare .35 by hash): each rival floor sends its
two most camera-ready (`KP.seasonReadiness`: peak × .6, charisma,
visuals, live, hype), the academies send four known students, four
unsigned names walk in off the open board, and — if this building
has a free trainee of the season's gender — the producers invite
YOU: one Desk scene, `seasonInvite`, send two, one, or none (the
coaches' eval order picks who). The body says what the owner ruled:
"Some seasons that run is a year; some seasons it is forever. Nobody
knows which until the finale." Casting closes in two weeks; the
show airs without you if you do not answer. Measured: 40/40 worlds
cast 8+ contestants from 3+ sources; 38/40 orgs invited; 23/40 sent.

*The air* (weeks 23–33): the field is cut weekly to the finale's
size (lineupSize 5 + runnersUp 3) on hash-judged scores (readiness
± COMPETITION.noise 14 — television, not the stream, so the season
never shifts a save). The eliminated go home the same week with a
record, hype and a public: rival kids to their floors (never cut
while filming; never cast into a debut mid-season), students onto
the open board as `channel: 'season'` (public, contested), yours to
the practice room with a high note and a morale dent. The timeline
watches every week (`seasonWeek`, feed-only, the regulars have
opinions). A contestant is `onSeason`: away for training, evals,
frictions, lineups ("on television until the finale").

*The finale* (woy 34): the top five form a real act via
`KP.makeRivalAct` — a debut single on the chart — under the
broadcaster's house (`projectHouse: true`, one per show title; no
floor, no scouts, no debuts of its own; not a seat in the scene's
count, never merged, split or collapsed; folds its tent when its
last act retires). The roll (permanentChance .4, hashed per season):
FIXED-TERM — `act.projectTerm.until` = finale + termWeeks (60);
rival members move to the house for the run and go home after
(`flags.seasonHome`); your finalist stays yours on paper
(`flags.onProject`, status 'trainee', on the roster, held out of
lineups — "the seat is held; the lineup waits") and comes back with
the public she earned, a polish bump, and a critical note. PERMANENT
— the house keeps the lineup: rival floors lose five trainees for
good, and YOUR finalist leaves the roster (status 'rival', the
house's contract, `wasOurs` on the file) with a critical note: "you
held the tape." Measured: 24/40 worlds saw a permanent roll; 23/40
orgs had a trainee make a lineup (held or kept).

*The edges.* Leaving this building mid-term (a release, a quit, the
founding) hands the house her contract for the run — the seat was
held for her. Nobody resigns from a television studio: the trainee
quit rail skips the away, and the debut-promise claim waits for her
to be back in the room. A contestant whose company folded mid-season
returns to the open market after the run. "Ours" at the finale means
still ours that night.

*Measured (tools/audit_people.js, 40 orgs).* Births per org-year:
academy 46.2, rivalDoor 39.1, application 5.9, auditionAbroad 3.1,
referral 2.1, social 0.5, abroad 0.4 — showKid is GONE (zero minted
finalists). Zero doorless births, zero ghost casts. Rival floors at
140 weeks: median 8 (the season takes two per floor a year and a
permanent lineup keeps them). Save sizes: longhaul 620 weeks up to
1.06–1.08 MB on the widest orgs (people 785–790 KB) — the project
acts add five 'rival' people a year who stay; the retired-act sink
is Phase C's question. Harness bands: seasonAired, seasonCastWorld,
seasonInvited (.30), seasonSent (.10), seasonOursLineup (0–.60),
seasonPermanent (.02–.90); the scene-vs-national peak tolerance
widened 5→10 (a project act debuts five half-famous names onto the
scene chart).

Battery 99/99, soak 40 clean, longhaul 10x620, e2e 111, lockstep
0.10.32.

**As built — Phase C, v0.10.33 "the file".** Owner: "Go ahead with
Phase C." floor.js grew the chapters; industry.js the retired-act
exit; risefall.js lost its second market; scouting.js prices the
lane; save.js derives the file once for old saves. Suite_100_file
(311 checks).

*The chapters* (B5, built as a store after all — a structured one).
`p.chapters` is a list of `{week, kind, …refs}` — a kind and a
reference, never prose — stamped by `KP.chapter(state, p, kind,
extra)` at every door and transition and read by ONE renderer,
`KP.chapterLine`, at render. Kinds: born (from `p.born`: the door,
the city, the school, the first house), enrolled, signed {co, how:
board | window | late | market | back}, cut {co}, released {co, how:
released | quit | silence | promise | scandal}, reentry, debut
{group}, seasonSent / seasonOut {weekNo} / seasonFinalist /
seasonLineup {act, permanent}, projectEnd {act, co}, kept, departed
{co, group, mode}, graduated, enlisted, discharged, home {why},
stayed {co}, market {co}. Capped at FLOOR.chapterCap 40. The rival
signing's `how` is a KEY now (the prose follows it inside
`rivalSignFromBoard`; an unknown key reads as 'board'), `leftUs`
takes the manner, and the opening roster and board came through
doors too ('inherited', 'opening' — 3.7 and 1.9 births per org-year
the audit never counted before). `KP.chaptersOf` returns born first;
`KP.chapterWhen` says 'before you' for a stamp older than the job.
The Person tab opens a "Where she has been" strip (the last twelve,
week-tagged); the board card's second line is `KP.fromLine`: where
she is from, and the last thing that happened to her ("From Busan —
walked into Novaline's door · Cut at Novaline's evaluation"). Idle
census at 620 weeks: 2.4–3.1 chapters per person, the longest file
21.

*The one market* (§89 D7). The collapse's signing class lands on
the open board through the castoff's door — `KP.boardMarketFile(
state, p, {channel, source, window, obs})` is the door, `boardCastoff`
a caller of it — as `channel: 'freeAgent'` with RISEFALL.
freeAgentWindow (16) on the castoff clock, three observations, and
the first house on `castoffFrom`; a full board sends her to the
market's own clock ('released'). The price is the board's price:
`KP.signCost` lifts a career to faCostBase + fame × faCostPerFame
and the heir's money (SAGA.HEIR.faInflate) reprices every MARKET
file (FLOOR.marketChannels: castoff, released, freeAgent) while the
tap is open — never the ordinary board. The verb is the board's
verb: `signProspect` on a career stamps `flags.veteran`, counts
faSigned, posts the public's verdict. Deleted: `state.freeAgents`,
`KP.signFreeAgent`, the weekly window sweep, the Industry page's
"open market" card, the app's `sign-freeagent` action.
`KP.freeAgentCost` survives as an alias of signCost. The bot buys a
career when flush. Measured (soak, 40 orgs): 1/40 orgs bought a career inside 140 weeks — collapses are rare that early, so the band's floor is 0 until a longer census says more.

*The retired-act sink.* `KP.retireAct(state, rival, act, why)` is
the only way an act concludes (prune, the seven-year wall, the
collapse — every act of the folded house, the long-retired ones too
— and the project term's end): it keeps the first retirement date
and sends every member still on the dead letterhead through
`KP.goHome` — forgotten if nobody here ever knew her, 'gone' with a
`home` chapter if somebody did; the ids stay on the act's record and
every reader of an act already filters for living people. The
collapse boards its class FIRST, then concludes the acts, then sweeps
the floor. Measured: ZERO rivals sitting in a retired act with the
old letterhead after 620 idle weeks (was ~82); people per save
260–295 (idle) and 481–634 KB of a 657–917 KB longhaul save (was
785–790 KB of 1.06–1.08 MB on the widest orgs).

*Two Phase B gaps the sink audit found.* (1) The broadcaster's house
was signing people off the market — the re-entry clock, the castoff
window and the stale exit picked from ALL rivals, and its scouts ran
the interest ladder — and whoever it signed sat on a floor that
never culls or debuts: a second sink. `KP.signingHouses(state)`
(rivals minus project houses) is now the only pool those exits draw
from, and the house has no scouts. (2) The merge gate counted project
houses as seats: two permanent project labels made three scene
rivals look like five, a merge fired, and the scene fell to ONE
(harness invariant, soak-6). The gate counts scene rivals only.

*The migration* (0.10.33) derives chapters once from the history a
person already carries (twenty-odd regexes over the stamps every
version wrote: Signed to / Cut at / Released from / Chose to leave /
Debuted with / Sent to the … season / Eliminated from … in week N /
Made the … finale / Won the … lineup / Enlisted / Discharged /
Graduated from … into solo / Contract completed|expired / Back on
the open board / Went home … / folded under), stamps `born` (door
'legacy') on a file without one, boards the old free-agent list
with the window it had left, and leaves a current save byte-for-byte
alone (no empty arrays). Harness: `careerSigned` band (measure-first,
0–100%). Suites 066/072/098/099 re-pinned to the one market and to
a home floor that may fold during a project term.

Battery 100/100, soak 40 clean, longhaul 10x620, e2e 113 (two new
checks: the strip is on the person tab and opens with where she is
from), lockstep 0.10.33.


## §91 The comeback (ALL FIVE PHASES SHIPPED v0.10.34–38 — the song made, the chart earned, the stage judged)

Owner, thinking out loud: "something that really defines kpop and
it's the comeback. The anticipation, the promotion, the stages, and
the charts. But the songs are what lead up to that. Right now, we
pick options and get the wheel in motion. What if on top of line
distribution, we essentially made the whole process player
controlled with a commercial and critical rating resulting from
your choices. We'd hire producers for our company. We'd have
writers. We'd have control over concepts and themes. We'd make
decisions on all of this based on who's most proficient at what
we're trying to do. Assigning a hip hop producer to an ethereal or
dreamy song wouldn't be likely to work well, regardless of how
skilled the producer is, for example. And the quality of the song,
the size of the fan base, and the effectiveness of marketing should
impact how the song charts. It shouldn't necessarily impact the
critical reception. Plenty of great songs never chart high.. Then,
after release, we'd have more control over promotion as well. And
each stage would be rated based on how well your performer(s) did.
Fatigue, morale, chemistry, and skill would all matter here."

**The law.** A record is MADE by named people, JUDGED twice, and
HEARD once. Made: every record names its brief, its producer, its
writer, its choreographer and the voices that sang each part — and
a person out of their lane makes a worse record no matter how good
they are. Judged twice: CRAFT is what the critics hear (the record
itself) and APPEAL is what the public wants (the hook, the moment,
the sound of the year); neither is the other, and neither is
printed as a number. Heard once: the chart is appeal × reach ×
marketing × the calendar — reach is built and bought, craft never
is. "Plenty of great songs never chart high" is a sentence the game
must be able to say about YOUR record, out loud, often.

**A. What the audit found (three read-only passes over the code).**
Much of the owner's sketch already exists in pieces, and the pieces
do not know each other:
1. THE SONG IS PICKED, NEVER MADE. Four demos a cycle (songs.js;
   two written to the brief, a stretch, a wildcard), plus the camp
   and a member's own; the player chooses one. A demo carries ONE
   quality (`hook`, normal 55/14) plus demands and a `trendFit`
   that is a random draw with no world behind it. No theme, no
   mood, no writer — the producer is the only credit.
2. PRODUCERS ARE NAMES WITH LANES, NOT SKILLS. Six persistent
   producers per world (credits.js), each with a home lane, a works
   ledger read as heat, snubs and bonds, an asking price and a
   circulating window (market.js). Nothing in the hook depends on
   WHO produced it: an out-of-lane producer pitches with no penalty
   (`laneStickiness` only biases who pitches). No writers at all;
   eight named choreographers the player cannot choose. The
   building's six seats (hires.js) include an A&R lead (hook shift)
   and a marketing lead (push momentum) — no producer, writer or
   stylist chair.
3. ONE NUMBER JUDGES EVERYTHING. `resolveDebut` folds ~20 terms into
   a single `reception`: hook ×.3, trendFit ×.13, performance ×.3,
   concept fit ×.14, chemistry, promo level (a flat ±), popularity
   lift, hype, anticipation, the MV tier, memory, season, hiatus,
   the crowd, bad blood, luck — then concept fatigue, the obscurity
   wall, the fusion roll. Chart score = (reception + pop×.2) × reach.
   Revenue, trust, reputation, awards, producer heat, the copycat,
   the sleeper, the war — every reader reads the same number. The
   only "critics" in the engine are the fusion lane's `acclaim`
   roll (caps reception at 45; `release.acclaim` is written and
   never read) and flavour strings ("reviews are kind").
4. PROMOTION IS LOCKED BEFORE THE SONG LANDS. The rollout plan (two
   slots a week, four weeks, nine activities) is billed at lock and
   plays out unchanged; after release the levers are the one-a-week
   point nudge and the content desk. Anticipation (teasers,
   campaign pushes, bookings) is real but pre-release only.
5. A STAGE IS NEVER A PERFORMANCE. `showsWeek` scores popularity ×
   fandom weight + `livePerf` × live weight + freshness + a hash
   wobble; livePerf is a group mean of talent and live reliability
   (fatigue enters at ≈ −0.03 points per fatigue point; morale only
   through the slump; chemistry, relationships and bad blood never).
   Festivals, tours, the circuit, Japan, gayo and fancons rate
   nothing. The one real performance read (`performance`, from
   demands vs skills, fatigue, benched, the choreo bill) runs ONCE,
   at release, inside reception. The encore reads vocals; the ending
   fairy reads visuals; `performance` in company reputation has no
   writer at all.
6. THE LINE CARD IS THREE BUTTONS. Recording opens trust / spread /
   center (pipeline.js); reception never reads it; `lineShare` is a
   reserved discourse kind (§89 D13: "let it become the line sheet
   the owner sketched"). No member share of any song exists.
What is right and stays: the brief (§29) and identity streak, the
producer pool with heat and the ghost story (§48), the song market
(§80.11), the making's stations (§80.5), the tracklist and the pen
(§36, §48), the rollout desk's constrained plan (§25: "never twenty
sliders"), the three shows with different natures (§27), the
release war (§26), the pressing sheet and the chodong (§80.1), the
expectation bar (§77), the point desk in words (§80.9).

**B. The design.**

*B1. Two verdicts (the release read, rebuilt — §89 D11 done
properly).* Every modifier `resolveDebut` stacks today is tagged
once, in a registry, as CRAFT, APPEAL or REACH, and the three sums
are kept on the release:
- CRAFT (the record, as the critics hear it): the composition
  (the producer's craft × the fit law, B2), the lyric (the writer's
  craft × theme fit, B2), the recording (the voices on the parts —
  the sheet, B3), concept fit (the song suits who they are), the
  room's chemistry (a tense room records cold), identity (a known
  sound, deepened), the fusion outcome (acclaim lifts craft, flop
  sinks both), luck (σ6). NEVER popularity, hype, promo spend,
  anticipation, the crowd, the season, the wall.
- APPEAL (what the public wants): the catch (a second seed from the
  commission — the producer's commercial sense), the sound of the
  year (B2: `trendFit` becomes real), the moment (the center's
  pull, the breakout, the spark), the MV tier, the lane's breadth
  (bright and performance read broad; dreamy and futuristic read
  narrow — breadth is a number on CONCEPTS), the theme's breadth,
  identity (a known sound sells), minus concept fatigue, luck (σ9).
- REACH (who hears it): fame (the wall), popularity, the fandom
  (intensity, the fanbase read), followers, momentum, anticipation,
  the promo level (the paid push × the marketing seat, the wall's
  waste), hiatus/tour/return lifts, the January dead zone, the crowd
  and the war, the house's own traffic, the overseas multipliers.
Then: `commercial = appeal × (.55 + .45 × reachIndex) + marketing
lift`, bounded as the wall bounds it today; chart score and peaks
from commercial exactly as from reception now; `release.reception`
KEEPS ITS NAME and means commercial (how it did) for every reader
that means that — popularity, trust, revenue, the chodong lift, the
war, the copycat, the expectation bar, memory's hitFactory. Readers
that mean the RECORD move to craft: producer heat (works carry
craft), the memory pedigree's vocalHouse, the reputation keys
`vocal` and `performance`, the catalog annuity's longevity (craft
keeps paying), the sleeper (craft high, commercial low → the long
tail: a late re-entry, a critics' list, the truthers), the pen's
value, the awards' new `record` category (the critics' album/song
of the year, by craft; `song` stays the public's). THE CRITICS: three
invented outlets (content law), each with a taste (a lane it
favours, a severity) and a verdict band per record from craft ±
taste ± hash — acclaimed / warm / mixed / cold / panned — printed
in WORDS on the results page and the discography, never as a
number; a split verdict is a story; the critics' expectation (the
house's last craft) settles against craft the way the public's
settles against commercial — the sophomore slump and the grower are
both sentences now. Measured-first bands: the critics' darling
(craft ≥ 68, commercial < 50) and the panned hit (commercial ≥ 64,
craft < 45) must both appear in a real share of careers.

*B2. The studio (the song, made).* The pitch stays — the world's
producers still send four demos a cycle, their themes, their
price — and the COMMISSION joins it: brief a record (a lane from
CONCEPTS; a THEME from a new small table — longing, first love,
defiance, summer, the night drive, grief, confidence, nostalgia,
escape, devotion — each with an age band, the lanes it sits in
naturally, and a breadth), choose the producer and the writer, pay
their fees, wait the writing weeks (the camp's shape: 2–3), and the
demo arrives in `g.demos` with its hidden craft and catch seeds and
the staff's words. THE FIT LAW: a producer has lanes (one home, at
most one second) and the composition's craft is CAPPED by fit —
home 1.0, neighbour .85 (a small adjacency table: bright–retro–
elegant; dark–performance–hiphop–futuristic; dreamy–elegant–retro;
fusion neighbours everything at .85), far .65. A 90 producer on a
far lane lands near 58: it works, it just isn't them — the owner's
hip-hop producer on the ethereal song. The writer's home themes cap
the lyric the same way, and a theme that fights the room (grief on
sixteen-year-olds, swagger on a warm room: the age band and the
personality read) costs craft and gets NAMED by the critics. The
members who write (the pen) are writers too, with affinities drawn
from personality. THE PEOPLE: producers and writers become persons
with a hidden craft and catch (the second fog: lanes are public
knowledge, quality is read only through the works ledger and the
critics' words on each record); the world's six producers and a new
pool of six writers are BOOKABLE per record at the market's price
by heat, and access is gated the holdout way — unproven and
workmanlike take any call, reliable wants fame ≥ .30 or a bond, in
demand wants fame ≥ .55 or the relationship; IN-HOUSE chairs join
hires.js as a seat family (`producer` ×2, `writer` ×2): hired at
theInterview, fame-gated tiers, no per-record fee, exclusive (a
rival cannot buy their ghost), bonds that form faster — and their
lane is their lane, so the in-house hip-hop chair and a dreamy
brief send you to the market anyway. That is the decision the owner
asked for: who is most proficient at what we are trying to do.
THE SOUND OF THE YEAR: `state.trend = {lane, since}` — the national
pool's releases carry lanes, the trades print the year's sound
every January, a record in the trend lane gains appeal and a far
one loses it, the trend drifts yearly on hash and a fusion
`shift` moves it for real ("changed the industry" means something);
copycat rivals read it. The fresh label's path is written into
this: unknown producers, in-lane only, no names on the phone — and
a cheap record can still be the critics' darling, because craft is
skill × fit and reach is what money buys.

*B3. The sheet (line distribution, where it finally matters).* The
recording station opens the SHEET instead of three buttons: the
song arrives with PARTS from its lane (verse, pre-chorus, chorus,
the rap, the bridge, the killing part — each with a demand: range,
rap, presence) and the producer's proposed distribution by the
voices (the ace's killing part, the lead vocal's chorus, the
rapper's rap). Options: trust the producer (the proposal, the bot's
default), every voice (flatten), front-load the ace, or the custom
sheet (the panel's steppers, bounded). The sheet feeds: craft's
recording term (the right voice on the demanding part; a weak voice
on the chorus costs the record), the stage's load (B4: who carries
the live), medical's vocal strain (singing-load weeks already roll
it), morale and the `linesCut` grievance (exists), the `lineShare`
discourse (a member under the floor share → the stopwatch posts,
the company answers), the center's hype. The three-card line card
retires; open cards migrate to sheets.

*B4. The stage, judged.* ONE rating, `KP.stageRead(state, g, stage)`
→ {score, perMember, moments}, from: the song's live demand (its
lane: a performance record lives on dance, a dreamy one on voice),
each member's live skill against HER load (the sheet's shares),
live reps and stage IQ, the choreography's difficulty against the
room, fatigue (steeper than today's −0.03 a point), morale (a low
room goes through the motions), chemistry (the relationship ledger:
tense pairs read cold in formation, close ones read as not acting),
the rehearsal (the performance director's seat — a chair that
finally multiplies something weekly), the slump, injuries and the
seated arrangement, and a hash wobble per (seed, stage, week) —
television, not the stream. Consumers: the three shows' live term
(replacing livePerf, with each show's nature kept — Prime Stage
weighs it most), the encore and fancam lotteries (keyed to the
rating and the member who carried), the ending fairy, fandom
intensity (±1), morale (±1), the discourses that are dead today
(`didntStand` and `encore` wake on bad stages; a carried stage
posts the clip), festivals (a rated set → next year's invitation),
tour nights (a bad night sells the next leg softer), gayo, the
circuit, Japan nights, the comeback stage (B5). The member's record
keeps a stage count (carried / fumbled) the dossier reads in words;
the act's rolling stage craft gives the reputation key `performance`
its first writer and the awards' `artist` a performance term. The
read posts IN WORDS, at most once a week, the point-desk way:
"Minji carried Prime Stage; the second-chorus formation came apart
behind her." Bad decisions have teeth: a punishing choreography on
a tired room is a fumbled stage on national television.

*B5. The promotion, after release.* The plan stays the plan (two
slots a week, four weeks, billed at lock — the owner's own law) and
gains four doors: THE OFFERS — each promo week the desk receives
invitations keyed to how the record is actually doing (a show
invites the chart's risers, variety invites faces with media reps,
a festival, a brand) and the player may SWAP a planned slot for one
(a cancelled booking costs a little trust with that broadcaster —
a small ledger, read at the next invitation); THE EXTENSION — at
week four a record still climbing (chart up, or the sleeper) can
run two more weeks for a fatigue price (`eraExtended` exists as an
ind and finally has a verb); THE COMEBACK STAGE — the era's first
stage is a named special: rated (B4), watched by the critics,
hype-bearing, the one everyone clips; MARKETING FIT — campaign
pushes are keyed to the record (a club record pushes through the
challenge, a ballad through radio and OST, a performance record
through the stage clip) and the marketing seat reads the fit:
effectiveness is a match, not a budget line.

*B6. The fog, kept.* Craft and appeal are never printed. Before
release the staff read the record in words through their own seats
(the A&R lead's call, the marketing lead's nerves — fogged by seat
truth, the second fog); after release the critics' words and the
chart's numbers are the truth; a stage posts a staff line. Names,
never reads (§87-adjacent law): the dossier says she carried the
stage, not what she scored.

**C. Phases.** Each a full-ritual release; each shifts the stream
(suite repairs by pattern); each a migration for open preps.
- PHASE 1 — THE TWO VERDICTS (v0.10.34): the registry, craft /
  appeal / reach / commercial on the release, the critics' three
  outlets and words, every downstream reader sorted (the table in
  B1), the awards' `record` category, the one expectation bar
  (public vs critics), the sound of the year. Subsumes §89 Phase 5
  (D11). Highest risk — every balance suite pins reception and the
  debut bands get re-measured — and the foundation everything else
  writes into. Bands: critics' darling, panned hit, trend named.
- PHASE 2 — THE STUDIO (v0.10.35): the fit law, producers and
  writers as persons with craft and catch, the themes table, the
  commission verb and its card, the in-house chairs in hires.js, the
  access gates. Medium risk (songs/credits/market surgery; suites
  033, 049, 059, 085). Bands: commissioned ≥ .60, in-house hired,
  off-lane record seen, theme named by the critics.
- PHASE 3 — THE SHEET (v0.10.36): parts per lane, the proposal,
  the panel, craft's recording term, the load, the discourse, the
  line card retired. Low-medium risk. Bands: sheet set, lineShare
  litigated [.05, .60].
- PHASE 4 — THE STAGE (v0.10.37): stageRead and its consumers, the
  per-member moments, the performance reputation, the words.
  Medium risk (suite_031 and the show bands). Bands: stage carried,
  stage fumbled, chemistry read on a stage.
- PHASE 5 — THE PROMOTION (v0.10.38): the offers, the swap ledger,
  the extension, the comeback stage, marketing fit. Medium risk
  (rollout suites, the bot's plan). Bands: offer taken, extended.
Phases 3 and 4 can swap; 2 cannot precede 1 (the seeds need the
registry). The owner reorders.

**D. Rulings (owner: "I like your recommendation on all 7" — every
recommendation below is the ruling).**
1. Producers and writers: in-house chairs AND the bookable world
   pools (recommended — the fresh label books, the established
   label hires exclusives), or one of the two?
2. Craft and appeal as words only (recommended: the fog is the
   game), or a number somewhere?
3. Themes: a separate writer axis with age and room fit
   (recommended, ten themes), or lane only for the first cut?
4. The fit law's teeth: a cap (recommended: far-lane work tops out
   near 60 whatever the skill) or a gentler slope?
5. Stages with teeth: a fumbled stage drops intensity and wakes the
   storm (recommended), or words only?
6. Promotion: offers and swaps on the locked plan (recommended),
   or a fully weekly desk?
7. The critics: three invented outlets with tastes that disagree
   (recommended — a split verdict is a story), or one voice?

**E. One truth per number, after.** `reception` = commercial (the
chart's side); `craft` = the record; `appeal`, `reach` stored for
the record. Deleted or merged: `release.acclaim` (into craft),
`COMEBACK.FOCUS` and `ROLLOUT.encoreChance` and `SEASON.festFatigue`
(dead), the random `trendFit` (into the trend), the three-card line
card (into the sheet), `livePerf` and the gig pile's `stageRead`
(into the one stageRead), the fusion roll's reception floors and
caps (into craft/appeal moves on the fusion lane), the release's
one-shot `performance` (into the recording's craft and the stage).

**As built — Phase 1, v0.10.34 "the two verdicts".** Owner: "I like
your recommendation on all 7." verdict.js is the module (loaded before
songs.js); debut.js's resolver was rebuilt around it; songs, memory,
fame, credits, tracks, awards, catalog, industry, sagas, publiceye and
newgame learned the record. Suite_101_verdicts (107 checks).

*The registry.* `KP.readLedger()` — every modifier `resolveDebut`
used to stack is tagged once, craft | appeal | reach, and the three
sums live on the report (`g.results.ledger`, rows with their names:
"the hook", "the recording", "the year's sound", "the promo buy").
CRAFT = hook ×.42 + the recording (the old `performance` read:
demands vs skills, fatigue, benched, the choreo bill) ×.30 + concept
fit ×.14 + the room (chem−50) ×.10 + pedigree (memory's vocal-house
read moved here — it is about the record) + identity (+2 on a
brief's second record) + luck σ6; the mash's outcome is a MOVE on it
(VERDICT.FUSION_MOVES: acclaim +14, shift +8, worked +3, flop −12).
APPEAL = 2 + the catch ×.55 + the performance ×.15 (the public hears
a record performed well) + the year's sound ×.13 + the lane's
breadth (CONCEPTS.breadth: bright +4 … dreamy −3) + the moment
(soloEdge + spark) + the video + the summer lift + identity −
sameness (the old concept fatigue) + luck σ9; the mash moves it too
(shift +16, acclaim −12, flop −14, worked +4). REACH is the additive
lifts the chart runs on: popularity, hype, anticipation, the promo
buy, the tour, the returns (dormancy, hiatus, the return run), the
January dead zone, the crowd, bad blood, the expectation drag (the
old "giant fanbase raises the bar"). Then `reception = appeal ×
(.8 + .2 × chartReach) + Σreach`, the wall (an industry SHIFT pierces
it: `pierce` lifts the cap three sparks' worth), the repackage
carry, clamp — and every reader that means "how it did" reads the
same `reception` it always did: popularity, trust, revenue, the
chodong, the war, the copycat, the public's bar, the seats' rep
rise, fame's hit count. The fusion lane's floors and caps
(shiftReceptionMin, acclaimReceptionCap, flopReceptionCap,
workedLift) and `release.acclaim` are gone.

*The catch.* Every demo carries `catch` beside `hook` — hash-derived
(seed, id, title; hook ×.5 + 27.5 ± 18), so the sheet can diverge
without a new draw. `trendFit` on a demo is DELETED (it was a random
number with no world behind it): `KP.trendFit(state, lane)` reads
the lane against the year at resolve — in the lane 70, next door
58, far 45 (TREND.NEIGHBOURS, the adjacency table §91 B2 named;
fusion neighbours everything). The pitch sheet says it in words
("Right sound, right year" / "Nobody is asking for this sound right
now") and shows the chip; the exec-taste stamp now reaches the
member's own demo too (latent since v0.9.17 — the stream shift found
it).

*The sound of the year.* `KP.trendLane(state, year)` is a pure read:
a hash per year chained with persistence (TREND.keepChance .55) from
the world's first year, overridden from a fusion shift's year on
(`state.trendOverrides`). The trades name it in January — and on a
career's first week — as `trendNamed` (normal priority; the Industry
page carries it permanently: "The sound of the year: Dark / Dramatic
· 2 years running"). A shift sets the lane to genre-bending: every
other sound is "next door" until the wind changes.

*The critics' circle.* Three invented outlets (VERDICT.OUTLETS: The
Needle, severe, loves elegant/dreamy/retro and resents bright;
Mixdown Monthly, even, the producers' magazine; Chorus & Co.,
generous, the pop site) read the SAME craft through a taste (±4 on
a lane they love or hate), a severity (−3 / 0 / +3) and a per-review
hash wobble (±8); the consensus is the median voice; two bands of
spread is a SPLIT. Bands at 76 / 64 / 52 / 40 (acclaimed, warm,
mixed, cold, panned) — calibrated so "acclaimed" is rare against a
craft mean of 63 on the first smoke. The words never carry a number:
`KP.criticsLine` on the results page and in the `criticsVerdict`
letter (normal; high when split, acclaimed or panned), the consensus
on the discography and as a chip, a quote in the outlet's own voice.
The letter lands AFTER the war's (the battle is the louder letter of
a release week — the first soak lost warLost's floor to arrival
order). The old "Reviews are kind; numbers are cautious" flavour now
reads the critics' word, one truth.

*The divergences — "plenty of great songs never chart high."* The
critics' darling (craft ≥ 70, reception < 50: a critical letter, +2
fandom pride) and the panned hit (reception ≥ 64, craft < 48) are
real letters with feed reactions; the critics' own bar is the
house's last craft — the sophomore slump (−12 from a warm-or-better
record) and the grower (+12). Measured, 40 orgs: darling 23/40,
panned hit 11/40, split review 35/40, the year's sound named 40/40;
debut reception median 53 (min 26, max 80), sensation 3/40, strong+
8/40, quiet/miss 16/40 — the old bands hold on the new read.

*The readers that mean the record.* Producer heat reads craft (works
carry it; old works fall back to their reception); the sleeper is
judged as a record (`tracklistResolve` takes craft; a quiet chart
week no longer hides a good b-side); the catalog keeps a well-made
record in the lottery (craft ≥ 60) and sorts revivals by it; the
awards gained `record` — Record of the Year, the critics' circle's
bonsang, by craft, while Song of the Year stays the public's (a
rival's loud, panned single wins the one; our buried record wins the
other — suite-pinned); the vocal house moves on records (craft ≥ 68
→ vocal +3); a great record is the fandom's pride whatever it sold.
Rival records carry a craft too (quality ×.9 ± a hash wobble; the
opening world's and the sagas' records included), so the circle can
judge the whole year.

*The one bar.* `KP.expectationRead(state, g, {comeback:true})` adds
the act's own standing (popularity above 40, ×.5) and
`KP.comebackExpectation` mints it at lock (a letter at loud or
above); `settleExpectations` knows debut from comeback in its words.
The old debut-only bar is the same bar now. (§89 D11's three
expectation reads: the popularity drag is a tagged reach row, the
pedigree is a craft row, the public bar settles against reception —
one registry.)

*The migration (0.10.34)* derives craft (reception ± 8 by hash),
appeal (= reception) and the critics' retroactive verdict on every
release, result, rival record and producer work that predates them;
deletes `trendFit` and stamps `catch` on every demo in a drawer;
drops `acclaim`. `KP.deriveVerdict` is the one derive — the opening
world's back-dated discographies use it at creation, so a current
save never changes under a reload. Harness bands (measure-first):
criticsDarling [.02–.90], pannedHit [0–.80], criticsSplit
[.05–1.0], trendNamed [.95–1.0]. The inbox: the executive's
directive-and-grant letter and the hiatus walk-down are critical
now (one-shot decisions and milestones the critics' letters were
crowding off a release week). Repairs by pattern (the stream shift:
one craft-luck draw per release, two trend draws fewer per demo):
twelve fixtures re-pinned (the scar door's wait, the waiting room's
rival act, the quit letter's bench, the fusion table as moves, the
season's forgotten count, the truck's cooling margin).

Battery 101/101, soak 40 clean, longhaul 10x620, e2e 113, lockstep
0.10.34.

**As built — Phase 2, v0.10.35 "the studio".** Owner: "Go ahead with
phase 2." studio.js is the module (loaded after credits.js); songs.js
pitches through it; credits.js, hires.js, debut.js, verdict.js and
save.js learned the people. Suite_102_studio (102 checks).

*Producers are people.* Every producer in the world's pool carries a
hidden `craft` and `catch` (STUDIO.craftSpread 34–86, catchSpread
30–85, by hash — backfilled on old pools, never printed) and, forty
percent of the time, a `lane2` next door to the home lane (a
versatile producer). THE FIT LAW: `KP.laneFitMult(lanes, lane)` is
home 1.0 / next door .85 / far .65 over the producer's best lane,
and the composition IS the craft through it — hook = N(craft × fit ×
.9 + 6, 9) plus the sheet's old modifiers (the brief, the bond, the
snub, the camp, the A&R chair). A 90 far from his lane lands near 58;
a 70 at home beats him (suite-pinned): the owner's hip-hop producer
on the ethereal song, as ruled — a cap, not a slope. The catch reads
the producer's commercial sense (hook × .45 + catch × .4 + 8 ± 12,
hash). The pitch stays: four demos a cycle, the producer mostly in
his lane (laneStickiness .6), and an off-lane pitch is weaker for it
and says so on the sheet ("a producer out of his lane: every part is
professional and none of it is his").

*Writers and themes.* Ten THEMES (longing, first love, defiance,
summer, the night drive, grief, swagger, nostalgia, escape,
devotion), each with the lanes it sits in naturally, an age band, a
breadth (appeal) and, for most, a trait the room must read as true.
A world pool of six writers (`KP.writersOf`: a name, two or three
themes, a hidden craft, a works ledger) and the pen: a member who
writes owns themes from who she is (`KP.penThemes`: warmth →
devotion, confidence → swagger, creativity → the night drive and
escape, low resilience → grief, under 21 → first love and summer,
past 23 → nostalgia) with a craft from her creativity. Every pitched
demo names its lyric and its theme (a writer natural to the lane,
three times in four). THE LYRIC is a craft row: the writer's craft ×
theme fit (home 1.0, off her themes .75) × VERDICT.craftLyric .08
(craftHook .42 → .38 to make room); the theme's breadth is an appeal
row; devotion feeds the fandom. A theme that fights the room — the
lineup's age outside the band, or the trait under its floor — costs
craft (−6), the sheet warns before the lock, and every critic names
the same problem in the verdict letter ("a lyric about grief sung by
a room too young to have lived it").

*The commission.* `KP.commissionRecord(state, groupId, {lane, theme,
producerId, writerId})`: the fee is the producer's by heat (unproven
6, cold streak 5, workmanlike 12, reliable 22, in demand 40 — the
house chair free) plus the writer's (a pool writer 8; the pen and
the house free), booked to production; the writing room takes two or
three weeks (hash) and the demo lands on the desk BESIDE the pitch
(`g.demos`; if the drawer is empty the pitch is written the same
week), the same shape as every demo with `commissioned`, the brief,
price 0 and the fit it was written at. One room per group at a time.
The commissioned record stays on the desk through a direction change
(the pitch re-tools around it) and is never a ghost (it is paid for).
ACCESS, the holdout way: unproven, workmanlike and cold-streak names
take any call; reliable wants fame ≥ .30; in demand wants fame ≥ .55
— or two records together with this room. The fresh label books the
unproven and writes in its lane; the names do not pick up.

*The house chairs.* Two studio seats join hires.js — `producer`
(house producer) and `writer` (house writer): hired at theInterview
like any chair (fame-gated tiers, the fee by tier, severance, the
poach call), their lanes / themes on the file as public knowledge,
their craft the hidden aptitude (STUDIO.houseCraftBase 30 + apt ×
60: a name is reliably decent, an unknown might be the gem). No fee,
bonded from day one, exclusive — and their lane is their lane: the
house hip-hop chair and a dreamy brief send you to the market anyway.
Old truths did not move: the best-seat draw runs over the six core
chairs, and a studio chair's truth is its own craft (no off-seat
damp). The building card reads eight chairs and the lanes / themes
/ records for this house. One chair each this phase (§91 B2 said
two) — the second chair when the first proves out.

*The bot and the bands.* The harness briefs a record whenever a
room's calendar is open and the account carries the fees plus 200:
the brief's lane, a theme natural to it (hash), the house chair or
the best-fitting name that takes the call (fit first, then heat),
the house writer or one who owns the theme; interviews for the
studio chairs are answered like any chair's. Bands: commissioned
[.60–1.0], offLaneRecord [.05–1.0], houseChair [0–1.0], themeNamed
[0–.90] (measure-first). Measured, 40 orgs: commissioned 39/40,
a producer out of his lane released 40/40 (next door counts), a house
chair filled 40/40, a theme named by the critics 32/40; the critics'
darling 19/40 and the panned hit 8/40 still live; debut reception
median 52 (min 25, max 79), sensation 2/40, strong+ 9/40, quiet/miss
13/40 — the old bands hold. The first soaks found the bot briefing a
record EVERY open cycle and starving its own show bookings (the
darling band went extinct at 9/40, the debut-class band at 5/40, the
end budget down a fifth); with the bot briefing like a player — on a
weak sheet, or every third cycle on principle, flush at 600 — both
bands came back (12/40, 9/40) and the budget with them. A strategy
feature is a spending change, and the bot must answer it.

*The migration (0.10.35)* backfills every demo on a desk with a
writer, a theme and the fit it was written at (by hash, natural to
the lane; the pen's own demo keeps her), mints the writers' room and
the pool's hidden numbers on first read. Stream shift: the hook's
draw changed shape and each pitch draws a writer — repairs by
pattern.

Battery 102/102, soak 40 clean, longhaul 10x620, e2e 113,
lockstep 0.10.35.

**As built — Phase 3, v0.10.36 "the sheet".** Owner: "Go ahead with
phase 3." sheet.js is the module (loaded before pipeline.js);
pipeline.js opens it at the recording station and audits it at
release; debut.js, medical.js, discourse.js, save.js, the harness,
the Studio and the Desk learned it. Suite_103_sheet (64 checks);
suite_084 re-pinned to the sheet.

*The parts.* A record reaches the booth with PARTS from its lane
(`KP.songParts(demo, laneId)`): the first verse and the second, the
pre-chorus, the chorus, the rap, the bridge, the killing part — each
with a DEMAND (range, the flow, presence), a BAR scaled from the
song's own numbers (vocal parts from vocalDemand × a part factor —
the verse .97, the pre-chorus 1.12, the chorus 1.25, the bridge 1.4,
"the high note" at/above 65; the rap from rapDemand × 1.08; the
killing part from 30 + choreoPotential × .5 against stage presence)
and a SHARE of the running time (SHEET.PARTS × the lane's SHAPE:
hip-hop doubles the rap and halves the bridge, dreamy and elegant
live on the bridge and barely rap, performance and futuristic enlarge
the killing part; the rap's share follows the song's rap demand and a
record with less than 20 of it has no rap part; no part is a
footnote — a sliver is lifted to 5% and the record gives way). Shares
sum to one and are PUBLIC (the fandom times them); the bars and what
a voice is worth on its part are not.

*The proposal and the ear.* `KP.buildSheet` assigns the parts by the
voices as the producer's ear hears them: each voice ± (100 − his
craft) × .18 by hash (a clean ear hears the truth; the unproven
mis-hears), greedy by share — the chorus first — with a second part
costing 30 fit points and the ace heard +8 on the killing part.
Measured on 160 debut fixtures, the proposal's top voice carries
~40% (a repeat penalty of 10 handed one voice 59%), one sheet in six
is heavy, and 0.4 voices a sheet sit under the floor: the producer's
sheet is top-heavy the way real sheets are, not absurd. The scene
`theSheet` (expires in two weeks; silence sends the producer's
sheet) says the song's shape and the proposal in words — "Yuna
carries the chorus and the bridge; Minji takes the first verse; Sora
has the killing part. Eunbi is not on it." — with four doors: the
producer's sheet stands (the bot's default), every voice on the
record (flat: everyone gets a part before anyone gets a second),
front-load the ace (the chorus, the killing part and the first verse
are hers; the rest by the ear among the others — she carries ≥ .45 in
every lane), or "I'll write it — in the Studio": the custom sheet,
the proposal as the starting point, a stepper per part cycling the
voices in the booth (members on a break are not in it), bounded —
one voice holds at most three parts or the even split, a preset is
not editable, nothing moves after the lock — and a Lock button;
release week locks whatever is on the desk. A booth of one (a solo)
sings every part and skips the question.

*The lock is paid for once* (`KP.lockSheet`, settle): the booth's
hours ride the share (fatigue + share × 10); every voice on the
record warms the room (+2); a voice under the floor (share < .05)
counts her seconds (morale −3) and, under professionalism 45, keeps
the count — `linesCut` on the directed ledger with a history line;
the voice of the record gains hype by her share ((share − .20) × 20,
cap 6; a solo IS the record, no lift). `pipeLedger.sheets`,
`customSheets`, `quietVoices`.

*The record and the stage.* Craft's recording row reads the SHEET:
`KP.sheetRead` sums share × min(1.15, voice ÷ bar) over the parts
(fit), and recording = fit × SHEET.recordingScale 57 + the rehearsal
bonus − the fatigue and benched penalties — through the registry as
'the recording' × craftRecording .30. Measured against the room
average it replaces, on the same 160 fixtures: the craft row p10/50/90
16.6/19.4/21.5 against 16.8/19.5/22.3 before; craft 35/47/59 against
36/47/59 — the median held, the top compressed a touch (a voice over
its bar stops paying at the cap), and the spread now belongs to the
sheet: trust fit .95, every voice .89, front-load .87 (the ace on a
chorus she cannot carry costs the record — teeth). The results carry
`recording` and `sheetLine` ("The booth: Yuna owned the chorus; Sora
reached for the rap and did not quite get there." — names, never
numbers; suite-pinned) under the critics' line on the report.
`performance` keeps the stage until the stage is judged (B4) and
still feeds appeal's 'the performance'. The release archives
`sheet` {mode, parts, shares, quiet, top} for B4.

*The strain and the stopwatch.* The medical desk's vocal roll reads
the share (`KP.sheetShareOf`: the sheet in production, the last
record's through promotion): a voice carrying ≥ .40 is a vocal lead
whatever her number says, and the nodules roll scales × (1 + share ×
2). The audit at release: each FAULT on the sheet — a voice under the
floor, one voice carrying ≥ .45 — is a lineWarChance (.30) roll on
the `lineShare` discourse, whose headline now carries the names (the
quiet voices' bars are very short / one colour is most of the video:
Minji). A flat sheet gives the stopwatch nothing (pinned).

*The bot and the bands.* The harness front-loads a real ace (hype ≥
12), flattens a sour room (morale < 50), else trusts the producer;
the custom sheet is the player's verb. Bands: sheetSet [.90–1.0]
(replacing lineCarded), lineWarSeen [.05–.70] (§91 C said .60; measured).
Measured, 40 orgs: a sheet set 40/40; the stopwatch thread 22/40
(26/40 at .30 a fault — lineWarChance .30 → .20; 72/120 on the
120-org run; band hi .60 → .70, measured); the critics' darling
17/40, the panned hit 14/40, a theme named 32/40, commissioned 40/40
— the Phase 1–2 bands hold; debut reception median 54 (min 28, max
74), strong+ 8/40, quiet/miss 15/40, end budget median 3106. The
sensation band read 0/40 on the gate run: on the same build 120 orgs
gave 5 (max 94) and a paired run of the previous build against this
one on the same 40 seeds moved the first debut −0.7 on average (the
stream re-rolled; 16 up, 22 down) — a ~4% event cannot carry a 2%
floor on 40 orgs (P(0) ≈ 18%), so the floor is 0 with the history on
the band and the 120-org run as the tail's guard. Longhaul saves
615–1001 KB (the archived sheet rides each release).

*The migration (0.10.36)* retires the three-card line card: an open
`lineCard` scene becomes `theSheet` over the producer's proposal; an
answered card (`g.prep.lineCard`) becomes its preset, locked and
already paid (no second settle); old releases keep `lineCard` as
history. No-op on a fresh save (pinned). Stream shift: the audit's
roll runs per fault, the medical roll reads the share — repairs by
pattern.

Battery 103/103, soak 40 clean, longhaul 10x620, e2e 113,
lockstep 0.10.36.

**As built — Phase 4, v0.10.37 "the stage".** Owner: "Go ahead with
stage 4." stage.js is the module (loaded after sheet.js); shows.js,
bookings.js, festivals.js, tour.js, year.js, circuit.js, awards.js,
debut.js, discourse.js, the dossier, the group page and the harness
learned the one read. Suite_104_stage (60 checks); suite_029's encore
fixture re-pinned to a room that carries; suite_042's two knock
fixtures let another member's knock pass and keep the tired one on
fumes through the knock phase (the stream moved). No migration: a release
without `liveDemand` sings the house standard (55 / 50), an act
without nights has no craft yet.

*The one read.* `KP.stageRead(state, g, {kind, id})` → {score, band,
perMember, moments, formation, pairs, present}. The era's record is
the last release: its lane picks the MIX (STAGE.MIX — a performance
record lives on the body, dreamy and elegant on the voice, hip-hop
and fusion on presence as much as either), its `liveDemand` (vocals,
dance, rap — archived at release from the demo) sets the bars, its
choreography's difficulty is the body's bar, its sheet's shares are
the LOAD. Each present voice (not on a break): her vocals against the
song's demand × (.7 + share × 1.5) — the voice carrying half the
record sings a harder night than the one with eight seconds; her
dance against the difficulty (the seated arrangement performs half
of it), each capped at 1.05 (a voice over its bar stops paying
early); stage presence against 52, capped 1.1; × 75 through the
mix, plus
(liveReliability − 50) × .25 (reps, professionalism, resilience,
the slump's damp, the veteran's stage IQ), minus fatigue over 60 at
.35 a point (steeper than the old read), minus morale under 50 at
.15 (a low room goes through the motions). The FORMATION: the room's
chemistry (chem − 50) × .12; close pairs +1 each (cap 3: not acting),
tense and conflict pairs −2 each (cap 6: cold in formation); the
choreography over the room's average dance −.2 a point (cap 12), a
room fifteen over its choreography +2 (it looks easy); every hole −3
(cap 9); the rehearsal chair (seatMult('perf') − 1) × 30 — the
performance director finally multiplies something weekly. A hash
wobble ±6 per (seed, stage, week): television, not the stream. Bands
carried ≥75 / clean ≥58 / shaky ≥44 / fumbled. The MOMENTS: the voice
≥75 and ten over the room carried it (the load law makes this hard
for the lead voice — she sings the hardest bar); the voice ≤40 and
twelve under lost it; the formation at −8 came apart, at +5 locked;
the chair; the holes. Measured on 160 fresh rooms one promo week in
(fatigue 64–71, the crunch): p10/50/90 45/55/68 against the old live
average's 45/50/54 — same centre, the spread now belongs to the
room; bands shaky 52%, clean 38%, fumbled 8%, carried 2%; a named
carrier on 16% of stages, a named loss on 18%, the formation apart
on 10%. The established legacy room: 78/83/87 rested, 73/78/82 at
fatigue 70 against the old average's 64/66/69 — carried on its good
nights, clean on the tired ones; with the caps at 1.15/1.3 every
veteran night read carried, which is why they came down. The first
cut (scale 62, fatigue from 55) read 56% of fresh stages fumbled —
too harsh for a rookie's first week; the knee moved to 60 and the
scale up.

*Paid once per rated stage* (`KP.settleStage`): every present voice
+1 played, the carrier +1 carried, the loss +1 fumbled (`m.stages`);
the act's rolling craft `g.stageCraft` (α .25); a carried stage
writes the performance house (+1 on `reputation.performance` — its
first writer; the `performanceHouse` narrative forms at 68 as it
always did), warms the fandom (+1 intensity) and the room (+1
morale); a fumbled one takes each back (ruling 5: teeth). The
lotteries, rng: the carrier's clip (fancamChance .10 — a `fancam`
discourse and a viral with provenance, "the Prime Stage fancam"),
the storm around the one who lost it (stormChance .20 — the `encore`
discourse, now headlined "losing the second chorus on a live stage"
when it came from a stage; the slump's engine reads it), the
distance watch on a fumbled stage with a tense pair in the formation
(.25 — `didntStand`, alive without a named rivalry). The booking
pile and the circuit rate LIGHT (counts and craft, no teeth).

*The words.* `KP.stageLine`: "Minji carried Prime Stage; the
formation came apart behind her." / "… while Sora lost her footing
in it — the fancams will tell two stories." / "The act played The
Countdown clean — nothing to clip, nothing to explain." / "… fumbled
Pop Wave — the sync went, the ad-libs went, and the wide shot kept
rolling." Names, never numbers (pinned). The shows post the read AT
MOST ONCE A WEEK per act (`KP.stageNote`, the week's most notable
stage, 'high' when carried or fumbled); the festival, the tour's leg
letter, the gayo note and the circuit note carry the line inside
their own letters. The dossier reads `m.stages` in words ("She has
carried a stage. The staff noticed; so did the fancams." / "There
have been nights the room covered for her. The wide shot keeps a
list."); the group page's room report reads the act's craft ("On
stage this room carries its nights" / "… keeps getting exposed").

*The consumers.* The three shows' live term IS the read (`livePerf`
retired, §91 E; the slump shield's cost rides along); the encore
moment needs a CARRIED, winning stage and a voice ≥65 — the carrier's
when she can sing it; a shaky or fumbled stage with the trophy in
hand is the shaky-encore storm on the one who lost it (the old
liveReliability thresholds gone); the ending fairy leans toward the
voice that carried the week (+20 pull). Festivals: the set is rated,
morale by band (+2/+1/0/−1), the line in the letter, and a carried
set books next year's call outright (`g.festCarried`,
`KP.festivalCertain`) the way an icon's does. The tour: each week of
the home circuit and each leg is one read, settled with teeth, the
night's words in the leg letter, and `tour.lastNight` sells the next
week's rooms (fumbled ×.9, carried ×1.05). The gayo stage is rated
(a carried December +1 intensity on top). The circuit's convention
stage warms the market ×.7 when fumbled. The awards' artist ballot
adds (stageCraft − 55) × .3. `performance` on the release report
stays the first-stage read until B5 names the comeback stage.

*The bot and the bands.* The bot books the default rollout as
before; the stage reads whatever it fields. Bands (measure-first):
stageCarried [.50–1.0], stageFumbled [.10–.90], chemistryStaged
[.05–1.0] (a formation that read a close or tense pair). Measured,
40 orgs: carried a stage 40/40, fumbled one 25/40, a pair read in the
formation 40/40; the darling narrative 19/40 (11/40 on the first
cut, 15/40 the build before — a paired run of the two builds on the
same 40 seeds put the player's trophies at 180 → 191, so the stage
made the shows friendlier to a strong room, not harder; the 11 was
the stream); the stopwatch 18/40, the critics' darling 19/40, the
panned hit 20/40, viral provenance 40/40; debut reception median 54
(min 27, max 71), strong+ 6/40, quiet/miss 14/40, end budget median
3056. Longhaul saves 615–948 KB.

Battery 104/104, soak 40 clean, longhaul 10x620, e2e 113,
lockstep 0.10.37.

**As built — Phase 5, v0.10.38 "the promotion".** Owner: "Go for
phase 5." promo.js is the module (loaded after stage.js); shows.js,
debut.js, bookings.js, the Desk's campaign card, the Studio's
rollout builder and promo view, the release report and the harness
learned it. Suite_105_promotion (59 checks). No migration: the
broadcaster ledger and the promo ledger mint lazily; an old release
without `offers` starts at zero.

*The plan stays the plan.* Two slots a week, four weeks, billed at
lock — the owner's own law (§22: "constrained choices and
opportunity costs"). Ruling 6: offers and swaps on the locked plan,
not a weekly desk.

*The offers.* `KP.registerWeekly('promotion', 585)` — after the
shows air, before the week's releases. Each promo week with a NEXT
week on the plan, a promoting act may get ONE invitation for that
week: a SHOW not already on it (its booking desk above the trust
floor) when the record is climbing, the week's stage was carried, or
the record is simply warm (reception ≥ 62 — "the numbers";
showChance .4, the show by hash); failing that, VARIETY when a face
reads varietySkill ≥ 60 with media reps ≥ 6 (varietyChance .3). At
most two invitations an era (`rel.offers`) — a choice, not a task
list. The invitation is the scene `promoOffer` on the Desk, expiring
with the week (silence is a no, the plan untouched), plus a 'high'
letter; the engine names the SWAP it would make
(`KP.offerSwapTarget`: the weakest booking of next week by pop,
never a stage while a non-stage booking stands; null when the week
has room). TAKE swaps the slot on the locked plan and bills the cost
difference (refused when the account cannot); cancelling a STAGE
writes the broadcaster ledger (`state.broadcasters[showId]` −1,
floor −3, +1 every 12 weeks) and a desk at or under −1 stops
calling — `KP.broadcasterLines` says so on the promo view ("Prime
Stage's booking desk remembers a cancellation — they are not
calling."). The bot takes an invitation that costs a lesser booking
and keeps a stage it already has.

*The extension.* `KP.extensionRead` / `KP.extendEra`: in the LAST
week of promotion, a record still climbing — `KP.recordClimbing`:
the scene entry's rank rose this week (pos < lastPos), or the
national board's, or the sleeper b-side — runs two more weeks: the
plan gains its own light weeks (popWave + radio, then a livestream),
`promoUntil` +2, the members pay fatigue 6, the bookings bill; once
an era; the `eraExtended` letter finally has a verb behind it (the
feed keeps its repackage lines for the repackage and gets the

(avg fatigue < 70).
