## §92 The b-side and the reverse run (SHIPPED v0.11.1)

Owner: "I want to add more attention to B-sides and chart reversal
chances."

The audit of what exists: the tracklist (v0.7.5) gives every b-side
a name, a producer, a hidden hook, a credit slot (a solo, a unit) and
the pen (v0.9.7); the sleeper (22% after a record people played)
blesses the best-hook b-side with a note, +2 popularity, the
extension's "still climbing" read and a +20 key in the catalog's
revival pick; the catalog (v0.9.15) reverse-charts one record per
group at 0.003 a week (0.04 while a resurfaced clip burns), the
title or the sleeper, onto the scene chart only — measured 27/40
orgs per career. Nothing else reads a b-side: it never charts
beside its title, it never climbs mid-era, the reverse run reads
neither the song's quality nor what the act is doing that month,
and the player has no verb for the catalog at all. The two asks are
one system: the record is more than its title, and the chart has a
back door.

**A. The b-sides, judged.** At landing every b-side gets a PUBLIC
heat — the streams the fans can see — from the hidden hook, the
record's craft, the credit (a solo, a unit, a member's pen) and a
hash wobble; the record keeps `bsides[]` beside the tracklist (the
hook stays hidden; heat is a number everyone can read, so the UI
reads it in words). The best b-side is the FAN PICK. The sleeper
reads heat instead of a flat roll: the pick's heat past a bar makes
the sleeper likelier, below it rarer — the truthers organize around
a song, not a coin.

**B. Double charting.** A fan pick hot enough enters the SCENE chart
beside the title the week the record lands, at a fraction of the
title's score, marked as a b-side (the chart row says so). A record
with two songs charting is the story every tracklist poster thread
wanted. The national board stays the title's and the reverse run's.

**C. The late climb.** During promotion an uncharted fan pick with
real heat can enter the chart on a small weekly roll — the in-era
reverse, the b-side the second stage keeps pushing until the public
agrees. The extension's "still climbing" read already honors it.

**D. The reverse run, re-priced.** The catalog's weekly roll reads
the song (craft and heat: a good record is a better ticket), the
act's month (a stage, a festival, a tour leg or a variety panel
inside a window doubles it — people hear old songs where they hear
the act), and the push (E). B-sides with heat are candidates in
their own right, each spent once; a strong revival enters the
NATIONAL board too, at a discount — the reverse run that reaches
the whole industry is the one the trades write up. The windfall
and the provenance stay as they are.

**E. The catalog push (the verb).** A desk verb per debuted group:
pick a catalog song (a title old enough, or a b-side with heat) and
a push — the streaming party (cheap, the fandom's own machine), the
dance challenge (needs a dancer, travels further), the live clip
(needs a stage inside the window) — each a cost, a multiplier on
the revival roll and a window of weeks; one push live per group, a
cooldown after; marketing's line on the books; the ledger counts
pushes and the ones that paid out. The bot pushes when flush and a
sleeper exists.

**F. The surfaces.** The discography names the fan pick and reads
each b-side in words (quiet · the fan pick · a sleeper · charted);
the Groups tab gets THE SECOND LIFE card: the catalog's candidates
with their words and the push buttons; the chart marks b-side rows;
the release results list the b-sides' words beside the credits.

**G. Harness.** Bands measure-first: a b-side charting beside its
title, a b-side's reverse run, the bot's push; catalogRevived keeps
its ceiling (a lottery everyone wins is a salary). Numbers unruled
— measure then rule, with history comments. Candidate slot: v0.11.1.

**As built (v0.11.1).** Everything above shipped.

A. At landing every b-side gets a PUBLIC heat (tracks.js:
hook × .62 + the record's craft × .28 + a credit lift (solo 6, unit
4) + the pen 3 + a hash wobble ±6), kept beside the tracklist as
`bsides[]` with the hook still hidden; the hottest is `fanPick`.
The sleeper reads the pick's heat: the base .22 at heat 62, ±.02
a point, floor .06, cap .60 — the same rng draw as before, so the
stream kept its shape; the sleeper is marked on her b-side. The
words (KP.heatWord: burning 70 · warm 58 · quiet 45 · skipped;
KP.bsideWord adds the sleeper, a chart peak, a reverse run) never
say the hook.

B+C. A fan pick at DOUBLE.heatAt 72 enters the scene chart the
week the record lands at .6 of the title's score, as a b-side
entry carrying `releaseWeek`; chartStamp stamps its peak and weeks
on the record's bsides and never on the title (catalog and shelf
entries are skipped for the release's peak too — the old same-week
overwrite is gone). During promotion an uncharted fan pick at
LATE.heatAt 62 enters on a weekly hash (.05) at .7 of the title's
live score — a world fact, not a draw.

D. catalog.js keeps one draw per group per week; KP.revivalChanceOf
is the one read: the base (.003, +.04 while a clip burns) × the
ticket's quality (1 + (q − 50)/50 × .4) × the act's month (×1.5 —
KP.catalogActive: a judged stage inside 8 weeks, since settleStage
stamps g.lastActivityWeek, or a tour, or a member's panel/MC seat)
× the push's multiplier. KP.catalogCandidates lists the tickets:
the title (reception 50+, the sleeper, or craft at the longevity
bar) and every b-side at heat 58+, each spent once (`revivedWeek`
on the record or the b-side); a record from before the judging
keeps the old nod (its sleeper's title rides the record's ticket).
A revival at quality 72+ enters the national board at .8 of its
scene score; the peak lands on the b-side (`nationalPeak`) or the
record (`revivalNationalPeak`); the milestone letters still speak.
KP.revivalLine says a b-side, a push, a clip, the national crossing.

E. KP.pushCatalog(state, groupId, title, kind): the streaming
party (6, ×4, 6 weeks), the dance challenge (12, ×6, 8 weeks, a
member's dance 60+), the live clip (8, ×5, 6 weeks, a stage inside
8 weeks); KP.catalogPushRead gates it (one per group, a cooldown of
20 after the window, the tickets, the kinds' reasons); marketing's
line; the ledger counts pushes, pushPaid, bsideRevivals,
nationalRevivals, lateClimbs; a push that never pays winds down at
flavor priority; an unknown title is refused with nothing spent.

F. The discography names the fan pick in words and the b-sides
that charted or ran again, and a record's reverse run with its
national peak; THE SECOND LIFE card on the group page (the tickets
as chips, the three pushes with their reasons, the running push);
the chart marks b-side, reverse-run and folded-label rows; the
release results list the b-sides' words beside the credits. The
timeline answers bsideCharts, bsideClimbs, catalogPush and the
richer catalogRevival.

G. Measured, 40 orgs, then tuned with history comments: double
charting 34/40 → 21 (heatAt 66→72), the late climb 20 → 23
(58→62), a b-side's own reverse run 16 → 8, the national back door
36 → 24 (64→72), the bot's push 40 → 38 (quarterly, not every nine
weeks), paid out 30 → 4, the lottery ticket 27/40 before the
release → 39 → 35 → 34 (activityMult 2→1.5, qualitySpan .5→.4; the
band's ceiling .85→.90 by ruling, with the salary check printed:
0.62 reverse runs per org-year, under the ~1 where the windfall
would be wages). One fixture repair (057, the old nod). Suite_111

## §93 The flavor expansion (SHIPPED v0.11.2)

Owner: "we need to big flavor text addition so we don't see so many
repeats."

The census first (tools/audit_repeats.js: the soak's 40 orgs × 140
weeks, every kept note, timeline post and spotlight line normalized
so a sentence that only swaps a name counts as the same sentence).
Measured at v0.11.0: 276 kept notes per org-year over 2,935
templates; the top template is the relationship friction note at
10.7 per org-year (4 variants carry 17 a year); the rival-signing
note is one sentence 14 times a year; the spotlight shows 113 lines
per org-year from 71 templates and its top line — the day-off piano
— 18.1 times a year, every third week; the timeline runs 28 posts
per org-year over 514 templates and its top filler 2.1. The repeats
the owner sees are a few families seen weekly, not a thin game.

The law: one mechanism, a family of sentences (the OPENERS rule) —
variants keyed by voice and trait so the same event reads
differently for different people; never the same line to the same
person inside a memory window; the content law throughout (snark at
institutions, never bodies; invented names and outlets only).

Targets, in order of weight: (1) the spotlight — three or more
lines per key, a per-person recency memory that skips what she was
last seen doing, and keys that read the situation (the era, the
season, the count) so the piano stays a surprise; (2) the
relationship notes — friction, settled, the pair that works —
keyed by the pair's dominant traits and the room they happened in;
(3) the rival-signing note — keyed by the rival's philosophy and
our relation to the lead (a file we read, a lead we never looked
at, a lineup rumor); (4) the countdown and the comeback-result
lines by band; (5) the single-variant inds (rivalHit, showcase,
masterMinted, application, gayoInvite, neverPaid) to four each;
(6) the health benching, the rival scouts, the eval-cut industry
line; (7) the timeline's top ten weekly fillers. The census prints
a REPEAT INDEX (the top template's count per org-year on each
surface); the Bible records it at every release from here, and the
number only goes down. Candidate slot: v0.11.2.

**As built (v0.11.2).** The families landed as planned, and the census
says what they did. `KP.lineFor(state, salt, lines, last)` picks a
sentence by a hash of the seed, the salt and the week — never the rng,
so a family of ten and a family of one leave the simulation identical.
Measured: the 12-seed soak with every family in place matched the
v0.11.1 soak case for case (diagnoses, chairs, pushes, chronic files,
flares), and the 40-seed bands are v0.11.1's to the org. Where the rng
was already drawn (`rng.pick` arrays) the arrays widened and the draw
count held.

The spotlight: every moment carries `lines` (quietWeek 3, afterHours
3, competitiveSting 2, leaderCarry 2, ambitionGlimpse 5 per ambition,
friendScene 6, voiceMoment 5 per voice for trainees and 5 for idols —
71 templates became 205). The pick remembers how each KEY last read
for her (`p.flags.spotMem`, one slot per key, written after the read
so both reads of the week agree) and skips it, however many other
moments came between. A draft rule that preferred a moment she was
not last seen in was withdrawn: it changed which effects and doors
fired and moved the worlds (the chronic-file band 14→5/40, flares
10→0). A flavor release must not move the simulation; the rota stays
as it was and the memory alone carries the variety.

The inbox families: the relationship notes (friction, settled, the
pair that works) keyed by the pair's traits — both competitive,
bossy, warm, quiet — 4 templates became 21; the rival signing keyed
by philosophy and our relation to the lead (a file we read, a lead we
never opened) and the rival scouts, 5 and 4 lines; the countdown 5,
the landed line 3, the benching 4, the pressure letters 3 with their
load-bearing phrases kept; rivalHit 5, the eval cut 3, showcase 5 by
the star's voice, breakthrough 4, plateau 3, masterMinted 3,
application 4, gayoInvite 3, neverPaid 3, evalTalk 3, evalSheet 3,
chodong 3, soldOutStory 3, promoOffer 3 + 3, debutClass 3,
anniversary 3 (the café banner still changes at midnight),
idolBirthday 3, diagnosisIn 3, castViral 4, gravityTrades 3,
flagshipHunt 3, rivalShowWin 4, comebackAnnounce 5. The timeline: the
two always-on pools 3→10 each, the tour posts 1→4 and 1→3, selca day
5 (every line opens with SELCA DAY), the bubble 1→3 per mood (every
line keeps the word), the pre-debut public pool 3→6, the personMoment
reactions 2→8. Every phrase the suites and the harness read survived
in every variant (flagged the quarterly books, board sees these
numbers, announced … comeback for, won … — their first, broke
containment, birthday week, debut class, after-eval talk).

The census, before → after (40 orgs × 140 weeks, the same worlds):
inbox notes 2,935 → 3,273 templates, the top template 10.7 → 2.3 per
org-year, templates seen at least yearly 31 → 19; timeline posts 514
→ 552, the top filler 2.1 → 0.5, none at yearly; spotlight lines 71
→ 205, the top line 18.1 → 3.8. *Correction (v0.11.3, §94): the
timeline numbers here were an undercount — the census read only the
feed's length delta and missed two thirds of the posts once the cap was
hit; the corrected measure is in §94.* The relationship friction note was
the loudest sentence in the game; now nothing on any surface reaches
a player four times a year. The REPEAT INDEX line and its ceilings
(notes 4 / 30, feed 1 / 6, spotlight 6) guard the number from here:
`REPEATS HOT` fails the census. Suite_112 (38): the picker, the
per-key memory, the rota, the bubble family's word, the phrase laws,
the families in play over 130 weeks, the fork.

What is left for later: the narrative, executive and company
families are already wide (76, 61 and 223 templates) and sit at

the trades' "three hits in a row", the renewal folder. If the owner
still sees repeats after this, the next pass should look at event
cadence, not add sentences.

## §94 The audit (0.11.3) — the world holds, again

Owner: *"Ok good time for a code audit."* Eight parallel read-only
review passes (determinism and the kernel; lifecycle and the estate;
the money law; releases and the charts; people and the text they
generate; the world outside the company; the UI and the PWA shell; the
test battery and the audit tools themselves) plus a scan of every
tuning constant nothing reads. Every finding was verified against the
code before it was fixed — most by a probe that reproduced it — and
every fix that can be pinned from outside is pinned in suite 113 (64
assertions). Two ritual tools grew: the longhaul's checker now runs
`KP.validateState` on the horizon and checks live rival acts, open
claims and scene groups; the lockstep checks `ENGINE_FILES` against
the page; the bump is a tool in the repo (`tools/bump_version.js`),
not a script in a scratchpad; and the test loader makes `Math.random`
throw inside the engine, so the determinism law is enforced at test
time, not remembered.

**Fixed — save-killers and determinism:**
- The prep week and the training week ran `burnout--` for every
  member on a break — soldiers, personal breaks, seasons — who never
  had a bench: `undefined--` wrote NaN into the save, the reload
  turned it into `null` and counted down from there, and the two
  careers diverged. Guarded both; the validator now reads every
  numeric flag; the 0.11.3 migration deletes the NaN.
- Three scene resolves (the diagnosis, its expiry, the JV pact) drew
  on a second `rngFor` that the kernel's own save then overwrote, so
  the rest length replayed as next week's first roll. Resolves use
  the stream the kernel hands them; expiries get the phase's.
- Reads that wrote: `socialOf` minted a castoff's, a student's and the
  next chapter's public numbers at first render (a viewed save
  diverged from its unviewed twin); `regionsOf`, the content, fame,
  discourse and outside ledgers were created by whichever render
  touched them first. Every door mints at the door; every ledger
  exists from `newGame` (`KP.ensureLedgers`) and the migration gives
  old saves theirs; reads go through `regionsRead`.
- `undefined` keys written into national entries and bookings (JSON
  dropped them; a reload had a different key order); the seed chart
  entry's `weeksOn` written to the wrong row after a cap sort.

**Fixed — the money law:**
- The revenue-share toll read every positive stream, the fund's own
  wire included: the fund took 12% of its raise back in the quarter
  it landed. The toll reads revenue; financing, the distributor's
  advance and the shelf sale are capital.
- The fair settlement debited backpay from nothing, the lavish
  greetings edition billed an empty account, a thin overseas leg paid
  the interpreter below zero, protecting her with nothing in the
  account was free. The clamp law everywhere: take what exists, owe
  the rest, or do not offer the door.
- "Match it" was offered with no money and fell through to the walk.
  Options the account cannot pay are not on the table.
- `KP.resolveScene` ignored a resolve's `{ok:false}`: the walkout's
  "negotiate" at an empty account dismissed the walkout for free, the
  festival "accept" consumed the invitation. A refused resolve keeps
  the question on the desk.
- The directive's grant paid out after a MISSED deadline, off the
  books (the soak's unexplained residual); the theater rental billed
  off the books; the settlement letter was returned to callers that
  dropped it. Ruled: a miss earns no reinvestment, every movement is
  booked, the letter rides the bus from inside `settleShare`.
- The pitch button was disabled whenever the account was short, so the
  §86 "deck prints on credit" door was unreachable by the player.

**Fixed — lifecycle, the estate, the founding:**
- Neither the dissolution nor the next chapter reset the books: the
  new label's first statement netted the dead label's streams and
  booked the chest as payroll. The founding never reset the red: the
  war chest paid the company you left. Both reset; the first
  statement nets from the chest.
- The founding's three letters were pushed by hand to the tail of a
  full inbox and fell off on the next tick; the derived short was not
  checked against the old company's (one letterhead, two houses); every
  prospect file was deleted, chapters and all; the people who stayed
  never got `wasOurs`. The letters ride the bus, the short is checked
  against rivals and the folded, chaptered files go home the floor's
  way, the stayed are remembered.
- A released idol kept her personal break and her bench, re-signed as
  a trainee who was on break forever. `leftUs` clears them.
- The salaried door's "three signings on a short leash" never bound
  (the inherited act counted as the debut). The leash binds until a
  debut of THIS chapter. The next building's chairs re-minted with the
  dead building's ids (same hidden truths on strangers): the seat ids
  carry the chapter. The chapter's trophies and daesang were the dead
  label's; the inherited act's past read as "undefined · Wk 0 · Y-5".
- A departed member's voice stayed on the line sheet (the record was
  sung by someone who had left); the pointer sweep clears her parts
  and re-cuts the preset.
- `disbandGroup` left the gravity watch, the open doors about the
  lineup and the promotion on the retired act; a sting's door outlived
  its group and crashed the Desk on every render. The disband sweeps
  every pointer and every open question.

**Fixed — the world:**
- The broadcaster's project house was read as a prestige-sorted
  letterhead: the fog poach signed academy students to a house that
  runs no floor, no evaluation and no age-out, and the house could
  never fold its tent; it filled the power ranking, stamped interest
  that raised the player's sign cost and took the flagship catch-up.
  Every prestige-sorted pick reads `signingHouses`.
- An act paused for service announced comebacks it could not make
  (and ambushed with them). The calendar skips the paused; the pause
  clears the announcement.
- A collapsed, merged or folded company's short went back into the
  name pool and a reborn short inherited the dead company's
  narratives. `deadShorts` keeps them retired; `forgetCompany` sweeps
  the stories.
- Debuts and records in the year's last four weeks were never
  award-eligible (two seasons, no window). The field runs from the
  week after last year's nominations closed.
- A disbanded act was invited to the gayo, "fumbled" a stage with no
  members, and could win Song of the Year; an emptied lineup stayed a
  show contender through its window. Closed chapters do not compete.

**Fixed — the record:**
- A commission landing while the calendar was closed blocked the pitch
  meeting for the whole cycle; a repackage locked during a hiatus left
  the hiatus running through the era; the winter festival sat at week
  49 of a 48-week year (biennial, and it ate a January slot); the
  tight-belt discount was spent by a refused lock; an act in Japan
  booked and "played" festivals in Korea; a reverse run restamped the
  era's b-side peak; the Studio read its own copy of the b-sides while
  the group page read the release's (one truth now: the release); the
  late-climb b-side never counted as "still climbing" for the second
  wind — and the suite line that would have caught it carried
  `|| true`; the award-night question expired a week after the
  trophies, so the speech never ran.
- Ruled: a rollout activity's popularity paid PER MEMBER (a quintet
  promoted five times harder than a soloist on the same stage, against
  the fandom lines' explicit "once per activity"). It now pays once
  per activity, scaled by who showed up, times a lineup norm of five —
  the typical lineup's trajectory the soaks were tuned on is unchanged;
  soloists and septets now promote like acts.

**Fixed — the text:**
- A benched trainee trained "light" at +5 fatigue a week with the wall
  roll still running: pinned at 100, she hit the same wall every ten
  weeks for years, each time an `urgent` letter with no decision in
  it, and her chosen intensity was overwritten for good. The bench
  rests (the idol week's law), counts down, and leaves her intensity
  alone. The spotlight no longer reads a benched person as "logged out
  of the building at 1am".
- The one door re-derived its line after the memory had moved, so the
  card and the door showed different sentences; the door reads the
  recorded line.
- Thirty-odd lines hard-coded "her" and "she" in option labels,
  toasts, histories and feed reactions while the boys' hall runs
  (option labels are rendered raw): every one is filled for the
  person. The gaffe's headline names nobody's gender. The weathered
  story's formation letter was raw tokens and, like the stood-by-her
  letter, was never sent.
- Letters sent from the desk (`KP.note`) never reached the feed pass,
  so nine registered reactions (the seated notice, the opened channel,
  the snub answered, the chronic file…) could never fire; the feed now
  reads the week's action letters too. The biased regular's post was
  attributed to a random handle; faded rivalries were never pruned.

**Fixed — the UI and the shell:** the release-confirm modal rendered a
player-typed stage name unescaped (the one injection sink); the free
fan meeting's toast read `undefined`; unit-era and solo-disc reception
printed digits (the reveal law — now words); a corrupt save meta threw
before the splash timer and the splash never left; a corrupt or
broken save loaded with no message (now a toast and a validator
warning); the desk's drafts crossed careers (one `resetDrafts` on
every career boundary); the service worker cached 404s and served
`index.html` for failed script fetches.

**Fixed — the tools' honesty:** the repeat census counted only the
feed's length delta and so missed two thirds of the timeline once the
cap was hit — the §93 ledger's "timeline 2.1→0.5" was an artifact; the
corrected census reads ~400 posts per org-year with the top filler at
14 (a comeback-announcement reaction with two variants; now seven, the
fancam two → seven). The census also counted the long-clock pass
(every per-org-year rate 12% high), keyed every spotlight line as
family "?", and ate "Choreography" for Cho. The soak's first-trophy
band read the legacy door's old win as truthy (40/40 forever), two
bands tallied one fact, and thirty bands at 0–100% could never alarm
(twenty-five now ruled from the measured counts). Six unfailable
assertions became claims; four suites that only ever passed through
their fallback branch (the critics' darling, the tour's nights, the
over-delivery, the extension's read) now run the path they name.
Thirteen tuning constants nothing read were deleted, and the season's
"two trainees" is read from its constant.

**Measured, ruled, watched:**
- The dead-in-soak bands stay at 0–100% with their reasons on record:
  `doctrineDeniedSeen`, `careerSigned`, `callHeld`, `holdoutMet` (the
  bot never takes those doors; the suites hold the mechanisms) and
  `quietWeekCaught` (0/40 — morale never falls to 38 under the bot;
  watch in human play).
- The Japan lane now refuses when a booked festival falls inside the
  trip (the audit made the missed-slot path honest and the bot flew
  over its own bookings: 32/40 misses).
- The default door's signing leash is unchanged (the legacy act counts
  as the first debut, as the constant's comment says); only a later
  chapter's leash binds until its own debut. If the owner wants the
  tutorial rail on the default door too, it is one line.
- What is left for later: the narrative/executive/company letters
  recur because the events recur (§93); the Japan calendar and the
  tour desk do not consult festival bookings symmetrically (tours were
  tuned around it); `state.host` is written and never read (the
  protégé host has no mechanics yet).
- The numbers at the ship: battery 113/113; soak 40 clean, every band
  alive (the flare chain: 133 cases, 75 chairs, 25 pushes, 33 rests,
  11 chronic files, 7 flares across 40 orgs); longhaul 11 × 620 clean
  with the validator on the horizon; e2e 134; the corrected census —
  inbox top template 2.0 per org-year (13 at yearly), timeline 6.9
  (73 at yearly) from 14.6 before the two families widened, spotlight
  3.3 (25 at yearly); the census ceilings re-ruled from these (notes
  4 / 30, feed 10 / 90, spotlight 6); lockstep 0.11.3 with the sixth
  place.

## §95 The season, televised (SHIPPED v0.11.4)

Owner: *"How deep is the survival show setup? I'd like that to feel
like an event when it runs."*

**How deep it is (v0.10.32–v0.11.3).** The season is real but quiet.
Once a year (castWoy 22) a show with a rotating title casts from the
world — two camera-ready trainees per rival floor, four known
academy students, four unsigned names off the board — and invites
this building through one Desk scene (send two, one or none). Twelve
weeks air: every week the field is cut on a hidden score (readiness
± noise 14, hash-judged so the save never moves), the eliminated go
home famous (hype, followers, a chapter on the file), the rest get
tired and seen. The finale forms a five-member project act under the
broadcaster's house, fixed-term or permanent on a roll; your finalist
is held out of your lineups for the term and comes back with a public
(or, on a permanent roll, the show keeps her). The soak: 40/40 worlds
air a season, 35/40 orgs are invited, 20/40 send somebody.

What the player sees of those twelve weeks: the casting letter, the
invitation, one timeline post a week (three templates), one letter
when her kid is cut and one at the finale, and a status line on the
Industry tab. No rankings, no episodes, no missions, no named
moments, nothing to decide once she is sent, no world reacting to who
is winning, no ceremony. The mechanism is sound; the EVENT is
missing. (One audit leftover found on the way in: the v0.11.3 bench
rest reached contestants and project members — `onBreak` covers
them — so a trainee on television was resting; scoped to the bench
and the personal break.)

**The plan — one mechanism per beat, every beat a letter or a door:**
1. *Rankings and the line.* Every week on air the whole field is
   ranked on the score the cut already uses; the ranks are kept per
   contestant (`c.ranks`), and the cut line is a number the player can
   read. The Industry tab becomes a leaderboard: the top eight and
   yours, with movement arrows, companies, the line drawn, the
   mission of the week, the public's pick.
2. *Episodes.* A fixed twelve-week mission schedule (the signal song,
   the position evaluation, the team battle, the concept evaluation,
   the cover mission, the final mission…) and one letter a week —
   `seasonEpisode` — that says the mission, her rank and movement (or
   the leader's, when nobody of yours is in), one named moment (the
   center that held the camera, the climber, the one on the line, the
   fancam that crossed a million by morning), and who went home. The
   letter is critical on the weeks she sits on the line or goes home;
   the timeline's weekly post reads the pick and the leader.
3. *Doors during the run.* The vote push (budget, three a season with
   diminishing effect, and a hash chance the edit calls it "company
   money"); the coach visit (the vocal or dance chair flies out: a
   score bump this week, the room at home trains thinner); the edit —
   once a season the producers cut her a villain or an underdog edit,
   and the desk answers with a statement or lets it ride (a statement
   defuses a villain edit at a price; a statement spoils an underdog);
   withdraw (pull her out: morale, hype and a public that noticed).
4. *The public's pick.* A fan favourite from the cast on (the highest
   hype, flipping to the leader by hash), named in the timeline, paid
   in followers; a pick that misses the lineup is the finale's
   "robbed" story.
5. *Her arc.* Nerves on the line (morale), a lift at the top; a
   friendship made on the set (the industry-friends system) at the
   finale; rival interest stamped on an eliminated finalist (the
   scouts have her number); the file reads the whole run.
6. *The finale as a ceremony.* The ranks read in reverse, eighth to
   first, with companies; the lineup and its act; the roll; her place
   in it. Critical when she was in the finale.
7. *The Desk.* The finale on the upcoming strip; a Today card during
   the run when she is in ("episode 7 of 12 — she is 4th; the line is
   9th").
Bands measure-first (pushes, edits, coaches); the soak bot pushes
when she sits near the line and the account can pay. Suite_114.
Candidate slot: v0.11.4.

**As built (v0.11.4).** season.js grew the event on the mechanism it
had; nothing about who is cast, who is cut or who wins moved, and
every new number is hashed off the seed, the person and the week —
the suite's fork across a whole season is byte-identical.

*The ranking reveal.* Every week on air the field is scored once
(`weekScore`: readiness ± noise 14, plus the week's push, the coach,
the edit) and ranked first to last; the rank is kept per contestant
(`c.ranks`, one number a week). `KP.seasonBoard` is the board the
Industry tab reads (rank, movement, company, ours), `KP.seasonLine`
the last safe rank next week as the field stands, `KP.seasonMission`
the week's mission from a twelve-week schedule (COMPETITION.MISSIONS:
the signal song, the position evaluation, the first ranking reveal,
the team battle, the concept evaluation, the cover mission, the second
ranking reveal, the unit stage, the fan-vote mission, the rehearsal,
the final mission, the finale).

*The episode.* One letter a week, `seasonEpisode`: the mission; her
place and movement (or the leader's and the public's pick when nobody
of ours is in); where the line falls next week; one named moment; who
went home, with companies. Priority: critical when she sits within two
of the line or goes home, high while she is in, normal for a season
without us (the inbox law trims it in a loud week; the timeline's
post carries the night). The moment is a family picked by hash among
what the week offers — the center, the mentors' line, the climber,
the faller, the one on the line, the pick's fancam (paid in followers),
ours at the top — never the same kind two weeks running
(`s.lastMomentKind`). The elimination letter for ours is critical now
and names the mission and her rank at the reveal.

*The doors.* `KP.seasonPush` (pushCost 8; pushScores 6/4/2 — three a
season, thinner each time; a hash chance .25 the recap calls it
"company money": hype −6 and a letter the timeline answers).
`KP.seasonCoach` (coachCost 3; coachScore 4; the vocal or dance chair
flies out — `state.coachAway` — and `KP.seatMult` reads .7 for that
seat that week: the room at home trains thinner). `KP.seasonWithdraw`
(morale −8, hype halved, the record says withdrawn, a critical letter,
the thread). The edit: once a season, at a hashed week 3–5 with chance
.5, the producers cut her a villain or an underdog edit (`seasonEdit`,
a scene with a one-week fuse): ride (default — a villain costs 5 a
week for three weeks; an underdog earns 4) or a statement
(editStatementCost 4, hype −3: it ends a villain edit, it spoils an
underdog). The verbs live on the Industry board beside her row; the
Desk shows a gold "On the air" card while she is in (episode, her
place, the line, the mission, the pick) and the finale sits on the
upcoming strip, hot while ours is in.

*Her arc.* Top three: morale +2 a week; within two of the line: −2. A
finalist of ours makes a friend on the set (`industryFriends`, how
'season', hash-picked among the other finalists); an eliminated
finalist's number goes to the two biggest signing houses (interest 2).
The public's pick: the highest hype from the cast on, flipping to the
week's leader with chance .3, paid in followers when the fancam
moment lands; the finale names whether the pick made it ("robbed").

*The ceremony.* The finale letter reads the eight in reverse with
companies, names the lineup and its act, the roll, her place, and the
pick's fate; critical when she was in the finale. The show's name
carries its own article now ("THE FINAL LINEUP finale", "the
STARFORGE finale").

*The audit leftover.* `onBreak` covers the season and the project run,
so the v0.11.3 bench rest reached contestants; the rest is scoped to
the bench and the personal break — a trainee on television works.

Suite_114 (41). Measured in the first soak (40 orgs): vote pushes
16, coach visits 19, edits cut 13, episode letters with ours in 20 —
every org that sent — and the bands ruled from these. Battery
114/114, soak 40 clean, longhaul 11 × 620, e2e 134, lockstep 0.11.4.

## §96 Where we stand — the depth survey (post-0.11.4; recommendations 1–4 SHIPPED v0.11.5, v0.11.7, v0.11.9, and 4 in three parts v0.11.10–v0.11.12; 5 in seven parts v0.11.13–v0.11.20; 6 in parts from v0.11.22)

Owner, after the televised season shipped: *"Where does this leave
us? Can you take a look at what needs more depth and give me a
report?"* This section is the report. It is a map, not a contract:
the owner reorders it with a feel report, as always. No code moved
for it.

**The bar.** The season is the measuring stick, because it is the
freshest example of the house sentence from §55.6 — an event the
game narrates should instead ARRIVE (a scene with a decision), CLAIM
something real, and LEAVE a mark. Before v0.11.4 a season was cast →
twelve silent judged weeks → a cut letter → a finale letter. After,
it has a board the player reads every week with the line drawn, a
letter a week naming her place and a moment, doors during the run,
an arc for the contestant, and a ceremony. The survey asks of every
other loop: which of those does it have, and which does it only
narrate?

**The method.** Four read-only passes over the engine and the UI,
one per slice (the record and the stage; the people; the company;
the world), 49 loops in all, each scored 0–3 on six axes — READS
(what the player sees and where), DECISIONS (verbs, scenes, doors;
proactive or reactive), ARC (does it change a person, a group or the
company durably and legibly), EVENT (a moment the player waits for,
or plan → wait → result), FLAVOR (a family or a lone string), TEETH
(what a bad call costs, what a good one earns, whether it can be
ignored free). The season after v0.11.4 is the 3 on Reads, Decisions
and Event. Every grade below is cited to file and line in the slice
reports (the four slice reports and the texture
probe’s output are kept under `docs/surveys/0.11.4-depth/`) and the claims the ranking leans on were re-read in
the code before this section was written. Alongside the grades, two
measurements: the inventory (what exists) and the texture (what
reaches the desk in bot play, `depth/texture_probe.js` wrapping the
40-seed soak).

**The inventory (v0.11.4).** 87 engine modules + 7 UI modules; 3,078
lines of constants; 557 exported verbs; 153 UI actions; 53
registered scene kinds; 387 registered letter inds; 114 suites; 98
Bible sections.

**The texture (bot play, 43 orgs, 130 org-years).** A scene is
waiting on the desk at the end of 71% of weeks. 68.6 scenes open per
org-year — 65.2 reactive, 3.4 proactive (the bot's only proactive
scene is the solo direction meeting). 11.3 letters a week are
written before the inbox law trims to five; 10.7 critical letters a
year; by priority per year: normal 257, flavor 183, high 137,
critical 11. The desk's decisions are dominated by five small asks:
festival invites 11.5 a year, the extra hour 9.7, promo offers 5.6,
the sheet 5.3, the interview 5.2 — more than half of everything the
player is asked. The big arcs are rare by design: the renewal table
1.7, the diagnosis 1.2, award night 0.6, the story 0.6, red ink 0.4,
the offer 0.13, the new chair 0.02, the JV 0.02. Nine registered
scenes never opened in 130 bot-years: distributorCall (structurally
dead on the inheritance door — fame seeds tier 2, so there is no
next tier to court), enlistPapers and servicePlan (no boy reaches
notice age inside 140 weeks), frictionQuietNo, lastStatement (the
bot makes the honest moves), quietEra and returnRun (the slump,
bot-dormant since v0.9.18 — and returnRun is unreachable for anyone,
below), traineeQuit and walkOut (bot-dormant since v0.9.20). All are
suite-held; §18 watches them for human play. One hygiene line: 160
letters a year carry no `ind` — a long tail of ~100 small legacy
templates (the feed chain the §39 debt rider names) the census
cannot see by name.
