## §101 The long goodbye, part one (SHIPPED v0.11.10 — §96 recommendation 4, a member leaves)

Owner: *"Approved to tackle as much of the remaining queue as you see
fit"* and *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. Recommendation
4 ships in two. This is the half where a member goes; the half where a
group ends, and what happens to a departed artist afterwards, is §102.

**The finding** (§96): "How a group ends is a status flip with a good
sentence on it: the farewell lap is announced… and nothing reads
`contract.leaving` for two years; the last contract's expiry is one
`high` letter; the archive card reads "0 members"… a departed idol's
file "stays open forever" and is reachable from no list." The renewal
table told the player "the seventh year becomes a farewell lap — her
stages, her goodbyes, on her terms", and then the engine did nothing
with it until the week she left.

One new module, `farewell.js`. It makes no draw: every pick is a hash
or a voice.

**The lap.** A chosen ending is an object with a date. `KP.beginLap`
is the one write path at the renewal table's three endings (the
ending written right, the plea that fails, the line held on someone
who leaves): it sets the two old fields and stamps the week
(`contract.leavingSince`). `KP.lapOf(state, p)` reads it: the last
week, the weeks left, the mode, how the fans were told, her last era
and her last stage. The last week is the clock's own (the seventh
year from a start that service pauses), so it is derived and never
stored.

**The member desk: one question.** A warm lap in a living group of
two or more puts one question on the one queue (`farewellNews`, a
priority candidate: an event that waits its turn, three weeks on the
desk): how are the fans told? It is not asked of a cold ending, a
solo act, a member on a break or in service, or with fewer than
eight weeks left. How she raises it is a line by voice. Both answers
cost. TELL THE FANS NOW: she says it herself; the fandom runs 5
hotter, the act gives up 2 popularity as the casual audience starts
counting down, her morale rises 2, it is on her ledger
(`saidItHerself`), and from then on every record before her last
era is a countdown record. KEEP IT IN THE HOUSE UNTIL THE LAST ERA
(the first option, and today's behaviour): nothing moves this week,
and everything rides on that last era happening. Silence keeps the
secret by default, and she noticed who decided (`leftWaiting`, a
high letter).

**The release reads the lap.** A record that lands inside her last 24
weeks (`FAREWELL.lastEraWeeks`) is her last era, and a lap has one.
(1) The lock tells: `KP.farewellLockTells`, called by `planDebut` and
by `planRepackage`, writes a second announcement naming her, the
landing and the date the paper ends; an in-house lap becomes known
there, and a question still on the desk is answered by it. A lap she
announced herself is still named, and the telling stays hers.
(2) The landing reads it (`KP.farewellReadsRelease`, in
`hiatusReadsRelease`'s shape, beside it in `resolveDebut`): reach
row "the farewell", +3 and up to +4 more at a tenth of a point per
week the fans have known; the fandom +3; the report says whose last
era it is; the release archives `farewellFor`. A record nobody
announced tells the fans the week it lands. (3) The countdown: on a
lap she announced, a record that lands before the window carries
reach row "the countdown", −2, and the report says every question at
the press day was about her. That is what telling early costs, and
it is why a long lap and a short one want different answers. A
reissue can be the last era. The Studio's date picker marks the
dates that fall inside her last weeks and says when the window
opens if none reaches it (`KP.farewellWould`, a pure read).

**Her last stage.** At the close of her last era (order 597, behind
the era's own close at 596) a critical letter, `lastStage`: the show
and the week, how it went (carried by her, carried by another who
"handed her the ending pose", clean, wobbled, fumbled), and a closing
line by voice, seven of them. It is read at the close because an
extension can add a stage in the last promotion week: only the close
knows which stage was last. An era with no music-show stage writes
none.

**The promise.** "Write the ending right" opens a claim
(`farewellEra`, held by her, due the week she goes): a last era
before she leaves. Kept by her last era landing; settled at the exit,
on any door she leaves through, before `departIdol` voids her other
claims, so it reads kept or broken on the promises page and never
merely void (a member bought out after the promise was promised a
last era and did not get one). Broken, it is on her ledger with what
a broken promise does to a person; on a warm exit everyone left in
the room loses 3 morale and the letter says the promised era never
came. The plea that fails makes no promise.

**The exit reads the lap back.** `KP.farewellAtExit` runs before the
lineup forgets her. THE BOW, when she had her last era: a critical
letter read the way the finale is read, last thing first: her last
stage; her eras from the last back to the first (the ones in between
counted, not listed, past four); her time at the center in the
calendar's units; the trophies on the shelf; the close friend she
leaves, by name; the chair she keeps (the songs she wrote here, whose
checks follow the person, or her credits in the booklet); and the
handwritten letter, dated. The room gets 2 of its grief back. A
PLAIN warm goodbye, when the fans knew and no last era came: the
letter and the cost it always had. A SUDDEN one, when the company
had the time and the fans were never told: 3 more popularity, a
fandom grudge, and a letter that says today is when they found out.
A lap too short to plan in, one begun before laps were dated, or one
whose last era was announced and then slipped past her last week is
never charged as sudden. A member RELEASED at her own request (the
walkout's third answer) gets her own words: the old path called it
"contract completed today" with a handwritten letter, and her file
now says released. A cold ending is the letter it always was.

**Every ending leaves a list and a lineup.** `KP.lineupPointerSweep`,
the one sweep every door out of a lineup runs last, writes
`g.alumni` (who, and the week); a disband sweeps members still in
the lineup, who are the final lineup and not alumni. The last
contract out writes `g.finalLineup` (only the disband verb did, so
an act that ended by expiry read "0 members" in the archive). An act
concludes in one place now (`KP.concludeAct`): a release over a
story that emptied a lineup left the act standing with nobody in it,
and it concludes like any other, with a sentence on the letter. A
concluded act no longer gets the anniversary letter: it had "the
members streaming from the practice room" for an act with nobody in
it. Its fandom keeps the date for three years in a quiet letter of
its own (`anniversaryKept`, normal), and nobody's morale moves.

**The screens.** "The last year" on Today, one card per lap: the
date, how the fans are told, where her last era stands (still ahead,
locked, landed, or out of time), the promise as a chip that turns
red when no record can land in time. The lap on her file's contract
line and on the roster row. Former members on the act's page, each a
door to her file. An Alumni list on the Talent tab, and a departed
artist's file is named an alumni file (it said "Trainee file"). The
concluded act's page is a record: the final lineup with where each
is now, read off her own file (it said "still with the company" of
members whose contracts had ended), the former members, the
discography, which marks whose last era a record was. The archive
card counts who was there at the end and who went before, and it
opens that page: the page existed and nothing opened it.

**Old saves.** Migration 0.11.10 (ensureLedgers: farewellLedger).
Alumni are read back off the files that already name the group (the
departed and graduated chapters), and an act the old build ended
with its last contract gets the final lineup it never had: whoever
left last. A lap in flight keeps its date and gains no week it
began: the question is still asked, and its goodbye is never charged
as sudden.

**The bot and the census.** The bot answers the question: she tells
the fans when the lap is short enough that the next record is the
last one anyway, and a long one stays in the house. The first soak
measured every row of the lap at 0/40. Inside 140 weeks only the
inherited act reaches its renewal tables, and a boss who answers
them keeps everyone. So the census holds three ceilings (a lap began
0/40 under .30, an alumna on a list 0/40 under .30, a cold ending
0/40 under .10), and the lap is measured where people do choose to
go: the long-horizon pass, three careers of 380 weeks, whose slim
clock bot learned one verb (a single that lands inside a leaving
member's window). It prints its own line and holds its own guards:
11 laps, 11 asked and 11 kept in the house, 11 told by the era, 4
last eras shared between them, 11 last stages, 11 bows, 11 promises
kept, none broken; every departed artist on an act's list, every
concluded act with a final lineup. The countdown, the sudden
goodbye and the broken promise are suite-held: a competent bot does
not produce them.

*Left for §102.* The disband as a scene with doors (the last
concert, the quiet statement, the farewell record) and the final
statement naming what each member does next. *(Shipped v0.11.11; a
departed artist signed across the street moved to §103.)*

Suite_120 (382): the engine, and Today, the file, the act's page,
the Talent tab, the Studio and the archive rendered through the DOM
stub. Mutation-checked against ten broken engine lines, each caught
by a named assertion. A real-browser pass over the new screens (30
checks, no page errors). Battery 120/120, soak 40 clean, longhaul
11 × 620 clean, e2e 134, lockstep 0.11.10. Migration 0.11.10.

## §102 The last bow (SHIPPED v0.11.11 — §96 recommendation 4, a group ends)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The group's half
of the long goodbye ships on its own. What happens to a departed
artist afterwards (the signing across the street, the letter when she
debuts there) is §103.

**The finding** (§96): "How a group ends is a status flip with a good
sentence on it." The disband was one quiet button at the bottom of
the act's page, one confirmation, and one statement that said the
same thing of every act: "the members remain with the company — their
own calendars, their own rooms, the same building".

One new module, `ending.js`. It makes no draw.

**Three doors.** The quiet button now opens a sheet, and the sheet is
a read (`KP.endingDoors`, pure): three doors, the kindest first, each
with what it does, what it costs the room, what the board reads and
what it leaves on the shelf, in the numbers the verb will use. A door
that is shut says why in place of its button, and the verb
(`KP.endGroup`) refuses on the same words. A project that has not
debuted is still dissolved from its old one-line confirmation.

THE QUIET STATEMENT is the door the game always had, at the price it
always had: today, free, 10 morale from every member, `disbandedUs`
on every ledger, and the board's 8 trust if the act still sells.
Nothing is left on the shelf but the records.

ONE LAST CONCERT is the fancon machinery at a bigger room. The room
costs twice a fancon's (20), the till is two and a half times a
fancon's off the same fanbase read, and the act concludes when the
house lights come up. It needs what a fancon needs: an organized
fandom (intensity 30), a group that is here, the bill up front. It
costs the room 4 morale where the statement costs 10, and the ledger
word is `lastNight`, which weighs for the company: a night that was
given, not a group that was taken. The board prices it like the
statement: it is still an act that sells, ended today. A small
fandom does not cover the room, so the door is not free money: it is
a softer ending bought at a loss.

A FAREWELL RECORD is an arc. The announcement is a critical letter
with two dates on it: the week it was said, and the week the record
must be locked by (30 weeks out). The fandom rallies (+6). The board
reads a planned ending and prices it lighter (3, not 8). Nobody's
morale moves. From there the act owes a record, and three readers
know it. (1) The lock tells: the record an ending act locks is
announced as its last (`KP.endingLockTells`, from `planDebut` and
`planRepackage`). A record already in production when the door is
taken becomes the last one, and the announcement names its date.
(2) The landing reads it (`KP.endingReadsRelease`, in
`hiatusReadsRelease`'s shape, beside the member's read in
`resolveDebut`): reach row "the last record", +4 and up to +3 more
for an organized fandom; the report says what the record was; the
release is archived as the act's last. A leaving member's own row
("the farewell", §101) is absorbed by it: the act's last record is
everyone's last era, so her lift is inside it and not on top, and it
still counts as her last era for the promise made at her table.
(3) The close concludes: a rail at order 598, behind the era's own
close (596) and a member's last stage (597), concludes the act the
week its last promotion ends. That week's wire reads the era back
first and the act second. It waits for a tour to come home and for a
member's solo record to land: an act does not end under a record.
This door costs the room 2 morale, the least of the three, and the
ledger word is `lastRecord`, which weighs most.

Announced and never made is a broken promise. Six weeks before the
date one high letter says so. The week after it, with no record
locked, the quiet statement goes out by itself: the statement's
morale and 6 more, `disbandedUs` and `promiseBroken` on every
ledger, 8 trust whether or not the act still sold ("not unstable,
upstairs said; unserious"), and nothing on the shelf. A record
locked inside the date is not a lapse however late it lands. While
the record is owed the act cannot take another door, cannot be ended
by the old verb, cannot go on an ordinary hiatus, and gets no
reissue door at its close (the last record has no second act). A
service hiatus slides the date: a full window from the discharge.
If the lineup empties by contract first, the act closes that way and
owes nothing.

**The final statement names what each member does next.** One
composer (`KP.finalStatement`) for every door, and the middle of it
is a roll call read off the lineup before the lineup empties
(`KP.endingRollCall`, pure). A fact with a date goes first, each in
her own sentence, in lineup order: in service, until when; on a lap
the fans know about, the date she named; her solo career, below; on
a personal break, she stays on it; a second job, by its name. Those
with nothing special on file share one sentence. A lap that was kept
in the house is not announced by the company's statement. The head
of the letter is the door's: the statement's old two sentences; the
last night's seats, till and set, first record to last; the last
record's title, the count of the discography and the years it took.
The tail is the door's too, and so is the timeline's reply (one
draw, as before; four families).

**A member whose solo career was open keeps it.** Found while
reading: the in-group solo (`dualCareer`, §87 F) needs a group around
it, so ending the group silently closed a career the company had
opened. Now it becomes an act of its own: the same object a
graduation opens, through one shared helper (`KP.openSoloAct`), under
her name, out of the act that ended. The statement says so, her file
says so, and the sheet says so before any door is taken, with what
it holds up: the new act takes the development slot until her solo
debut.

**A member's solo record on the calendar shuts every door.** Also
found: the old verb ended the act under her record, the record
shelved the next week, and the bill had been paid. The verb refuses
now, on any door, and names whose record it is.

**What the door leaves on the shelf.** A fandom that was given a
goodbye keeps the catalog warm: the act's share of the catalog
annuity pays a quarter more for three years after a last concert and
half more after a farewell record (`g.afterglow`, read by the
annuity's own loop). The statement leaves nothing. It is a modest
number on an old shelf and a real one on a young one, which is the
right way round: it rewards ending an act at the right time, not
late.

**Every conclusion says how it came.** `g.ending` keeps the door and
the week (statement, concert, record, lapsed), and the two endings
nobody chose are written the same way: the last contract, and a
release over a story. A concluded act's page says how it ended and,
while it lasts, what that left on the shelf.

**The screens.** The sheet. "The last record" on the act's page
(when it was said, the date, what follows), with the quiet button
gone: the door is taken. The same card on Today, with the weeks left
to lock it, turning hot inside six. A line in the Studio's date
picker that the record on the desk is the last one. On the record
page: how it ended, the warm shelf, and the last record marked in
the discography.

**Old saves.** Migration 0.11.11 (ensureLedgers: endingLedger). An
act the old verb concluded is known by the line it wrote on every
member's file that week, and its page says it ended with a
statement. An act that ended any other way under an older build
keeps no word for it: none is invented.

**The bot and the census.** The bot never ends an act: ending one is
a decision, not a policy, and no competent boss does it inside 140
weeks. So the doors are suite-held, and the harness gained a short
pass that rides each of them through a real career instead (three
seeds, 90 weeks, the inherited act takes one door in week 10, every
week validated). The record career announced in week 10, landed its
last record in week 14 and concluded in week 19. The concert career
played its last night in week 10 to a till of 105 on a room of 20.
The lapse career announced in week 10 and lapsed in week 41. Inside
the census nobody ends an act, and every band stands exactly where
v0.11.10 left it: the stream is unmoved.

## §103 Across the street (SHIPPED v0.11.12 — §96 recommendation 4, what comes after)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The last piece
of the long goodbye, on its own. With it §96's fourth recommendation
is complete: a member leaves (§101), a group ends (§102), and the one
who left has somewhere to go.

**The finding** (§96): "a departed idol's file 'stays open forever'
and is reachable from no list." §101 made it reachable. Nothing was
ever written in it again: the last line of every alumna's file was
the week she left.

One new module, `across.js`. The main stream is never drawn from:
every pick is a hash, and the one record this module makes is made
on an rng of its own, keyed by her file.

**The clock.** A departed artist's next chapter has a date: 12 to 40
weeks after she left, hers by hash, stamped the first week the rail
sees her (order 621, behind the open board's own re-entries at 619).
Nothing is written before it.

**The chapter is one of two.** On her date another house signs her
as a soloist, or she builds a life outside the industry. The odds
are read off her file (`KP.acrossChance`, pure): a base of 0.4; 0.12
for each step of her own name, the renewal table's fame, up to four;
0.15 more when leaving was not her idea (a cold exit: she did not
choose to stop); 0.06 less for every birthday past twenty-seven, the
market's clock. A name of two steps or more signs with the top half
of the street. An empty street leaves only the second chapter.

**The signing is a letter in the tone of how she left.** How she
left is stamped on her file at the exit from this build on
(`flags.departShape`, the five shapes §101 gave an exit) and read
back off her chapters and her paper for anyone who left before it
(`KP.exitShape`; a sudden goodbye cannot be told from a plain one
there, and is not guessed). The letter says who, formerly of which
act, to which house, how many weeks after, and how the paper ended.
Then the tone, and each tone has one small consequence. After THE
BOW she thanks the company by name, twice, and the board reads it:
trust +1 ("the cheapest advertising it will ever get"). A PLAIN
goodbye is cordial and nothing moves. A RELEASE is "a fresh start"
and nothing moves. After a SUDDEN goodbye she says what she was not
given, and the fandom of the act she left remembers it (a grudge
point, if that act is still standing). After a COLD exit the
announcement does not mention the company; the comment section
does, and the board reads that too: trust −2. A promise broken on
her file speaks whatever the exit looked like: she "learned to get
dates in writing", and the old fandom hears it.

**She stays departed until the record lands.** A rival's floor is
cast into rookie groups and culled by age, and she is neither. So
the signing changes nothing but her file: a chapter ("Signed to X as
a soloist"), a date for her first record there (6 to 16 weeks out),
and where she is now, in words. No house can cast her.

**The debut is a rival act of one.** On its date she belongs to
that house, in a solo act under her own name, made by the same
function that makes any rival act from named people
(`KP.makeRivalAct`), marked as an artist who was ours. Its concept
is the last one she recorded here; its generation is her old
group's; it does not debut as an unknown (a seeded popularity from
her own name). Her record goes on the chart this company releases
against, and from there the machinery that carries every rival act
carries her: the release cycle, the chart, the head-to-head ledger,
the crowded week. The letter says what the record did, what it
means for the act she left, and who posted: after a warm exit a
close friend still in the building posts the cover an hour after
midnight and her morale rises 2; with no such friend the company's
own account does; after a cold exit nobody does, and "the fandom
keeps a list of who did not". If the house that signed her folded or
merged before the record, the contract moves to another, and the
letter says so; with no house left at all the deal falls through
and her chapter becomes a life outside.

**A veteran is nobody's rookie.** Found while building: a
seven-year artist's first solo record would have stood in the
year's rookie field, been written up as a monster rookie at the
numbers her talents land, and carried a generation's torch. An act
marked as an alumna's stands in none of the three.

**A life outside is words on a file.** What she does is read off
what she was best at (a dancer's studio, a vocalist's academy, a
writer's borrowed name, an agency, a radio slot), by hash inside
that, and one in four simply goes home. A quiet letter, a chapter,
nothing else: no number moves. She stays an alumna on the books.

**An alumna is never forgotten.** Found by the suite: the world's
exit (`KP.goHome`) forgets a stranger with no file, and "no file"
was read off the ledger and the scouting flags. An artist who
completed a contract here with nothing ever written on her ledger
was a stranger by that test, so when her act across the street
ended she was deleted from the save. Completing a contract here is
a chapter here, by itself (`KP.hasChapter`). She goes home, with
the last line of her file as where she is now, and stays on the
list.

**The list is who was ours.** `KP.alumniOf`: every artist who left
this building, whatever her status is now, most recent first. The
Talent tab's Alumni list reads it, and its line is where she is now
(`KP.whereNow`): signed with a house, a soloist there since a week,
what she does outside, or how she left when there is no later
chapter yet. Her file stays an alumni file under any status and
says "now:" when there is something to say. The act's page reads
its former members through the same word. On the Industry tab an
act that is hers reads "solo, formerly ours" on the house's card;
on its page her cell says "was ours" and opens her file, with a
note from the file room in place of the scout's "moved faster"
(which was about a face lost off the board, and she was not that).

**Old saves.** Migration 0.11.12 (ensureLedgers: acrossLedger). An
artist who left long before her next chapter had a clock would have
every chapter written in the week the file is opened: the ones
already overdue are spread over the next 2 to 31 weeks by hash. One
whose date is still to come keeps it.

**The bot and the census.** No bot verb: the chapter is the world's.
Inside the census an attentive boss loses almost nobody, so it holds
two ceilings (an alumna signed across the street 0/40 under .20, a
life outside 0/40 under .20; every older band stands exactly where
v0.11.11 left it), and the chapter is measured where people do
leave, in the long-horizon pass. Three careers of 380 weeks set 20
clocks: 9 signings (6 after a bow, 3 after a cold exit), 4 of them
debuted by the end with all 4 acts still running, 5 lives outside,
and 6 chapters still to come. The seven-year clock's own line is
unmoved (11 laps, 11 bows, 11 promises kept). The pass guards
that the ledger is the wire, that every alumna whose date has passed
has a chapter, and that one who debuted is in an act of the house
she belongs to or has gone home with her file intact.

Suite_122 (153): the engine, and the Talent tab, her file, the
act's page and the Industry tab rendered through the DOM stub.
Mutation-checked against eighteen broken engine lines, each caught
by a named assertion. A real-browser pass over the new screens (19
checks, no page errors). Battery 122/122, soak 40 clean, longhaul
11 × 620 clean, e2e 134, lockstep 0.11.12. Migration 0.11.12.

*Not built.* The door back: an alumna who could be re-signed. "The
door stays open" is still only a sentence, and it would want its own
release.

## §104 The mission (SHIPPED v0.11.13 — §96 recommendation 5, the trainee years, part one)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The practice
room ships in pieces. This is the first: the month gets a room, and
the sheet says more than who is first. The door a month (the talk as
a scene, the showcase slot as a pick), the year-end sheet and the
posting, and the absences are each their own release.

**The finding** (§96): "The trainee years: two dials, four silent
weeks, an evaluation sheet." v0.11.5 gave the sheet its priority
ladder, put the trajectory on the board and rendered the trainee
paper. The two dials still had no reason to move from one month to
the next.

Nothing new is drawn. The rotation, the moment and the notice are
hashes; the showcase keeps the one draw per trainee it always made.

**The month has a room.** Each showcase is held in one of five rooms,
one for each talent: the ballad round, the formation round, the
cypher, the solo stage, the camera test. The coaches run a rotation
(`KP.evalMissionAt`, pure): every room once in five months, in an
order of the save's own, never the same room twice running. A lap
whose order would open on the room the last lap closed on swaps its
first two; the swap never reaches a lap's last room, so the rule
needs no look further back than one lap. The room is known a month
ahead: the next one is posted the day the sheet goes up, as a quiet
notice with its date.

**Drilling it is the dial's reason.** A trainee whose focus is on the
month's room, first or second, and who is training at all, has
drilled it a week (`p.missionWeeks`, capped at the month). Not at
rest, not on a break, not in a lineup in rehearsal: the debut
schedule owns that week. On the day a drilled room is carried in:
+4 on the showcase for the whole month, pro rata for less
(`KP.missionPrepOf`). The showcase closes the month and every
counter starts again; a showcase too small to be held closes it all
the same.

The number is an edge and not a ladder. The sheet is still a read of
what the coaches can see, plus the day's nerves; a drilled room
moves a trainee past a neighbour, not past the room. And the sheet
is a ranking, so the edge is only worth having when not everybody
takes it. That is the decision: the month can go to the room for the
one at the bottom who is two sheets from the talk, or for the ace
whose streak is a month short, and it costs that trainee a month of
what she actually needs.

**The sheet says what the room was.** After the story it always
carried, the sheet names the room and what it asks; then, if a
trainee drilled it since the day it was posted and climbed, it names
her ("and it showed"); if nobody drilled it at all, it says the room
was read on what it already had.

**The line.** With a project open the room reads the sheet at the
lineup's edge (the seats the practice room's own speculation counts,
never past the size of the room), and the sheet now says where that
is: "the top 3 have a case". A trainee who crossed into it this
month is named, and one who fell out of it, and a month with a
crossing posts high. §96 asked for critical; v0.11.5 measured what a
churning room does to a monthly critical (seven in ninety weeks) and
ruled against it, and that ruling stands.

**One thing from the room.** One sentence a month about one trainee,
or two, that is not about rank: a first showcase, the piece drilled
"in her sleep", two years in front of the long table, the youngest
who would not look at it, the last on the sheet stacking the chairs,
two friends a place apart, the stairwell at seven in the morning.
Each of the seven kinds finds its own subject off the files or
stands down (the youngest must be the only one that young; the last
on the sheet is not the room's anecdote the month she gets the talk;
a new signing who has already stood a showcase is not having her
first). The week's hash picks among the kinds that have a subject,
and never the kind told last month (`state.lastEvalMomentKind`, the
season's shape). If that was the only one open, the room says
nothing rather than repeat itself. Words only.

**The screen.** The Training tab opens on the month's room: its
name, the talent, what it asks, the date, what drilling does, and
who is drilling it this week with the weeks each has in. The room is
marked on every trainee's dial. A building with too few trainees for
a showcase shows neither.

**Old saves.** Nothing to migrate. A file from before has no
counters and no room on record; its next showcase has a room, the
first sheet on this build names it, and the ledger's new counts
start beside the old ones.

**The bot and the census.** The bot trains each trainee's two best
reads, so it drills a room whenever the room is one of them and it
does not rest her. Measured over 40 careers: 1249 showcases; 154
trainee-months drilled whole, in 38/40 careers (floor .60); 40
sheets named a climb for it; 688 sheets told one thing from the room
(55%), in 40/40 careers (floor .60); 15 months the line was crossed.
This is a real mechanic and the stream moved with it: 87 of the
census's 340 rows shifted, most by one or two careers, and every
band holds. The seven-year clock's lines (§101, §103) are unmoved:
that pass's bot sets no focus, so nobody there drills anything.

Suite_123 (108): the engine, and the Training tab rendered through
the DOM stub. Mutation-checked against seventeen broken lines, each
caught by a named assertion. A real-browser pass over the Training
tab (12 checks, no page errors). Battery 123/123, soak 40 clean,
longhaul 11 × 620 clean, e2e 134, lockstep 0.11.13.

*Left for the next pieces.* The after-eval talk as a scene and the
showcase slot as a pick; the year-end sheet read in reverse and the
posting as a letter for the room with a door for the ace left off;
the absences' cadence.

## §105 The talk and the slot (SHIPPED v0.11.14 — §96 recommendation 5, the trainee years, part two)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The second
piece of the practice room. §96 asked for "one door a month through
the one queue (the after-eval talk as a scene; the showcase slot as
a pick)".

**The finding.** Two sheets at the bottom of the board was ten
minutes with the coaches, two points of morale and a letter: the
most serious thing that happens to a trainee short of leaving, and
nothing for the desk to decide. The showcase had no seat the desk
could give to anybody.

Nothing new is drawn.

**The talk is called on the day and held when the desk says how.**
The sheet still calls it at the second sheet in the bottom third,
and that month's sheet still posts critical; it now says the talk is
due, not held. On the day nothing is said and nothing lands
(`p.flags.talkDue`: the week, her place). The question comes through
the one queue (`afterEvalTalk`, a priority candidate: an event, not
a roll): one person scene at a time, two weeks on the desk. A talk
the door never gets to is held by the coaches after three weeks; a
talk due with somebody who has stopped being a trainee is dropped.

**Three answers.** LEFT WITH THE COACHES is the first answer and is
exactly what the talk was: two morale, the line on her file, the
letter in one of the three ways it was always told. Nothing on her
ledger. SAID STRAIGHT, by the one who signed her: it lands harder
(four, not two), it goes on her ledger as told straight (which
weighs for the desk, and counts where the building reads whether its
boss has the hard conversation), and her file remembers it: the
month she comes off the bottom of the sheet she knows who told her,
and that is four morale back, once. While she is still at the bottom
it pays nothing. NO TALK, A MONTH ONE ON ONE: the head coach takes
her until the next showcase. It costs 6, it gives her a point of
morale now (given something, not told something), and it is worth 3
on the day on top of whatever she drilled. Then the sheet answers
for it: off the bottom, two morale and a line on her file; still
there, three morale gone and a line that says the hours did not move
the sheet. It is help and not truth, and it can fail in front of
her. The answer is not offered to a till that cannot cover the
hours.

**Silence leaves it with the coaches.** The question was the head
coach's, not hers, so an unanswered one writes nothing against the
desk on her ledger: the coaches hold the talk, and that is the cost
it always had.

**The closing slot.** The last one up has the long table's whole
attention. By the coaches' custom it goes to last month's first, and
nothing comes of it: the census's old behaviour, unchanged
(`KP.showcaseSlotRead`, pure). The desk can give it to somebody else,
once a month (`KP.setShowcaseSlot`): she is read 2 higher on the
day, gains 2 morale for being given it, and it is on her file; the
one who had it by custom loses 1, and the sheet says who had the
slot and who did not. Giving it to the custom's holder is the custom.
The pick is for one showcase: a pick who is off the floor that day
has no slot, and next month it is back with the coaches. Like the
drilled room it is an edge past a neighbour and not a ladder, and
unlike the room it is taken from somebody.

**The screens.** The question is on the Desk through the one card,
its three answers stacked one a row. The closing slot is on the
Training tab under the month's room: who has it by custom, a chip
for the custom and one for each of the others on the floor.

**Old saves.** Nothing to migrate. An old build held its talks on
the day, so no file carries one in flight; the next one called is a
question.

**Two older suites re-pinned, with the reason on each.** Suite_087
read the talk onto her file the day the sheet went up; it now reads
the call on the day and the line when the talk is held. Suite_114's
season fixture sent "the two we send" and then relied on that seed's
pair staying on the show for ten weeks: the stream moved, the invite
picked a different pair, and that pair was cut in its first month.
The fixture now forces its own gate (the two are made strong enough
to stay), and passes on this build and on v0.11.13 alike.

**The bot and the census.** The bot leaves the talk with the coaches
unless the trainee is already low and the books allow the month one
on one; it never says it straight (suite-held). It gives the closing
slot to a trainee who is one sheet from the talk. Measured over 40
careers: 220 talks called and 220 asked, in 40/40 careers (floor
.60); 195 left with the coaches, 22 a month one on one (off the
bottom of the next sheet 8, still there 13), none said straight,
none unanswered, none left unasked. 550 closing slots given, 523 of
them past a custom holder, in 40/40 careers (floor .30). This is a
real mechanic and the stream moved with it: 150 of the census's 340
older rows shifted, and every band holds but one, which has its own
paragraph below.

**What the long check caught, and it was not this release.** The
first soak on this build failed twice. Neither failure was the talk
or the slot.

*A lineup of one.* The soak's weekly invariant "every rival act is
made of real people" kept its own rule from v0.4.3: at least four.
v0.11.12 gave the street its first soloists (an alumna debuts under
her own name, an act of one), and the rule never met one. In a
140-week census career an artist has to leave, wait, be signed and
debut, and that happened in 0 of 40 careers on v0.11.12 and on
v0.11.13. On this build's stream it happened in one, and the
invariant called her act no lineup at all, thirty-three weeks
running. The engine was right and the check was wrong: v0.11.13 as
shipped fails the same check over 200 careers (3 soloist signings,
91 violations). The rule is the engine's now (`KP.actLineupOk`: a
group fields at least four, a soloist's act is her and nobody
else). The census reads it, and so does the seven-year pass, where
soloists debut on every run (67 acts still running at the end of
the long careers, 4 of them soloists), with a guard that the rule
met at least one. Suite_122 holds it (159; six broken rules, each
caught by name), and with the old rule put back the soak now fails
on every run, not on one career in 200.

*The flare.* "Orgs whose veteran worked around the file" read 0/40
against a floor of one career. The flare is the last link of a thin
chain: a diagnosis pushed through opens a chronic file 35% of the
time, and the file flares on 5% of its heavy weeks. Before ruling it
noise the chain was measured. The push roll was read raw over 200
careers: 35 of 116 opened a file and the draws are uniform (the
first 80 careers had run cold at 8 of 47, which is what prompted the
look). The census was then run at 200 careers on this build and on
v0.11.13 side by side. Careers with a flare: 12/200 here, 21/200
there (z 1.6). Of the 340 rows the two builds share, none moved past
z 2.6 and six past 2, where chance alone gives about fifteen: the
two builds are the same world. At six careers in a hundred, none in
forty happens one time in twelve, so the floor goes to zero with its
history written on the band, as the sensation floor did at v0.10.36.
The chain is held where it can be: suite_084 forces a chronic knee
through heavy weeks, the throughput line prints every link, and a
run with twenty chronic files and no flare is a violation (silent at
40 careers, where there are three to six).

*Found on the way, and left for its own release.* The same v0.11.12
gap is in the words: when a soloist's act across the street ends,
the letter announces "the conclusion of team activities", her file
says she "disbanded", and the alumni line lowercases her name. The
rival service letters are written for a group too. Reproduced, not
fixed here: it is the next piece (v0.11.15; SHIPPED, §106).

Suite_124 (119): the engine, and the Desk and the Training tab
rendered through the DOM stub. Mutation-checked against twenty-two
broken lines, each caught by a named assertion. A real-browser pass
(14 checks, no page errors). Battery 124/124, soak 40 clean, census
200 clean, longhaul 11 × 620 clean, e2e 135, lockstep 0.11.14.

*Left for the next pieces.* The soloist, read as one (above). The
year-end sheet read in reverse and
the posting as a letter for the room with a door for the ace left
off; the absences' cadence.

## §106 The soloist, read as one (SHIPPED v0.11.15 — a repair of v0.11.12, §103)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. This piece was
not on the queue. The long check on v0.11.14 (§105) found that the
soak's own lineup rule had never met a soloist; tracing it turned up
the same gap in the words the player reads, and it ships on its own.

**The finding.** v0.11.12 let a departed artist debut solo at
another house: the street's first acts of one. Everything that reads
a rival act was written when every act was a group. Reproduced on
v0.11.14 before anything was changed: when her act there ends, the
letter announces "the conclusion of team activities" for her, her
own file says "<her name> disbanded", and the alumni list, which
lowercases the first letter of her last chapter, prints her name in
lower case ("jung Da-min disbanded"). At the seven-year wall "the
members could not land on the same next chapter". A warm male
soloist at the service wall was given the stagger, so "the group
held the line short-handed" and his act went on releasing while its
only member served. A friend made in a waiting room was "Name of
Name".

Nothing new is drawn, and one number moves (the service wall, below).

**The two endings, in her words.** An act of one ends the two ways
any act does: the records stop landing and the house lets it go, or
the paper runs out after seven years. Both are told as hers now
(`soloEnded`: one letter, her name on it): what she made there and,
when she was ours, one sentence that says so. Her file says her solo
run ended, or that the contract ran its term; the house's move says
the same. A twin holds it: the same act with the solo flag off ends
the same week in a group's words, leaves the stream in the same
place and costs the house the same prestige.

**Her file is stamped, and the alumni line reads off it.** When it
ended, under which name the house then had, and how
(`p.flags.across.endedWeek`, `endedCo`, `endedHow`; `KP.acrossEnded`);
the ledger counts it. `KP.whereNow` reads "home since <date>, after
a solo run at <house>" off the file, never off the wording of a
chapter. The act's page says "solo run ended", heads her strip "The
artist", and the file room's note goes into the past tense.

**The letter is one the week will not cut.** Read in a browser, the
new letter was not in the inbox: at normal priority the week's
budget of five had cut it. So the letters about a former artist were
counted after the trim for the first time. Over the soak's long
careers the signing and the debut (both high) reached the inbox
fifteen times in fifteen; the life outside (normal since v0.11.12)
three times in five. Both the ending and the life outside are high
now: each is the one letter that closes an artist's file. The long
pass counts every one of these letters on the wire and again after
the trim (18 of 18), with a guard.

**The service wall.** A soloist does not rotate: he enlists, the run
pauses, and the letter is one man's ("the photo at the gate has one
person in it"). The timeline's posts say nothing of kings or boy
groups. This is the number that moves: a warm male soloist's act
stops releasing while he serves.

**The sentences that name another house's artist.** A soloist is
named alone (`KP.ofAct`). The friendship, the coffee truck and the
senior's shout-out are reads now (`KP.societyLines`) and the rail
writes exactly those; so are the world's story
(`KP.rivalStoryLine`), a rival's first trophy
(`KP.rivalFirstWinLine`) and the timeline on a hit
(`KP.rivalHitPosts`). One who was ours once is "who used to work out
of this building", not a stranger. A story about a soloist is about
her; her first trophy is "her first as a soloist"; a hit of hers is
"a win for soloists".

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.15). A file on which a solo run
already ended has its last chapter and the line on her history
rewritten in her words, is stamped from the chapter's date, and is
counted. A chapter in any other words is left as written. A soloist
an old file left mid-"rotation" is moved to a pause that ends the
week his own service does. Loaded through the app in a real browser,
the old save's alumni row reads the same as a new one.

**Two older checks re-pinned in suite_122, and a third, with the
reason on each.** The ledger's shape gained a count. "Where she is
now" was pinned to the last line of her file; it is read off the
file now, and that chapter still carries the words it was given. The
life outside was pinned as a normal letter.

**The soak.** No solo run ends inside the long clock (0 of 4 in
seven years), and the suite forces the roll. A new pass rides both
endings through a real career at the shipped odds (5% and 3% a
week), validated every week: the letter once on the wire, in a
soloist's words, in the inbox after the trim, her file stamped, the
alumni line read off it. The long pass gained an accounting guard:
every solo debut is still running or ended in a soloist's words.
With the solo branch removed, the letter demoted, or the stamp
dropped, the soak fails by name. The census did not move: against
v0.11.14, 0 of its 342 rows changed over 40 careers, and 0 over 200.

Suite_125 (95); suite_122 160. Fifty-nine broken lines, each caught
by a named assertion, and three more caught by the soak. A
real-browser pass (17 checks, no page errors). Battery 125/125,
soak 40 clean, census 200 clean, longhaul 11 × 620 clean, e2e 135,
lockstep 0.11.15.

*Left for the next pieces.* The year-end sheet read in reverse and
the posting as a letter for the room with a door for the ace left
off; the absences' cadence. *Seen and not changed here, because they
are mechanics and not words:* a soloist counts as an act when a
house is judged overextended, and a friendship with a former
colleague is still made in a waiting room.

## §107 The year's sheet (SHIPPED v0.11.16 — §96 recommendation 5, the trainee years, part three)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The third piece
of the practice room, and half of what was planned as one: the
posting (the lineup list as a letter for the room, with a door for
the ace left off) is its own release.

**The finding** (§96): "the year-end sheet read in reverse as the
loop's ceremony". Twelve showcases make a year, and the twelfth sheet
was the same letter as the other eleven. Nothing in the building
knew a year had passed.

Nothing new is drawn, and nothing new is kept on a trainee but a
flag: the year is read off the twelve sheets every file already
carries (`evalHistory`).

**The year so far is a read** (`KP.evalYearRead`, pure). A trainee
has a place on the year's sheet once she has stood four showcases
this year and half of the ones held. The first career it was read
in gave the year to a trainee who had stood four of ten, all at the
top: four months at the top is a strong winter, not a year. The
order is her average standing in the room she stood in (a 2nd of 4
and a 4th of 8 are not the same month), then her months at the top,
then her best month, then how many she stood. This calendar year
only; trainees on the roster only. The Training tab shows it under
the month's board all year: every trainee with a place, her months
at the top, how many showcases are left, and what a place takes.

**Once a year it is a ceremony** (`KP.evalYearDue`,
`KP.evalYearSheet`). On the year's last showcase, after the month's
own sheet and the next room are posted, the head coach reads the
year from the bottom up: one critical letter. Fourth and below are
read as names; third, second and first each get a clause (months at
the top, or her best month, in how many showcases); the last name
in the letter is the year's first. The one who climbed furthest
from her first sheet of the year to her last (two places or more,
and not the year's first, whose clause already says it) is named as
the year's climb, with the month she started in. Trainees who did
not stand enough of the year are named as that. The letter closes
one of three ways, turned by the year, never the same two years
running.

**What it does is small and is hers.** The year's first gains 3
morale, is marked on her file (`p.flags.yearTop`), and has a line
on it; the board carries "first of Y1" beside her name. The year's
climb gains 2 and has a line. The first name read has a line and
nothing else: her months already moved her. A year with fewer than
three places has no sheet. Measured, the 342 older census rows do
not move at all: the morale is small and lands on the two trainees
who need it least. The ceremony is the point, and so is the flag:
the posting will read it.

**The wall keeps three years** (`state.evalYears`): each sheet as it
was read, names and all, so a trainee who has since debuted or left
is still on last year's. The Training tab shows the sheet as read
until the new year, and last year's sheet in January until this
year has places of its own.

**Found in a screenshot: the board showed two firsts.** The real
career used for the browser pass had put the year's first on a
break for the year's last showcase. The evaluation board listed
every trainee by her last rank, whenever that was, so it showed her
old "1" above the new first, under the date of a sheet a month old.
That is from v0.9.16, not from this release. The board is the
latest sheet now: those who stood it, in order, under its own date,
and under it who did not, with where she last stood.

**Old saves.** Nothing to migrate. An old file's year so far reads
off the sheets it already carries, and its year is read on the
year's last showcase like any other.

**The bot and the census.** The bot does nothing with it. Measured
over 40 careers: the year was read 47 times of a possible 80, in
36/40 careers (floor .60); the year's climb was named 31 times, in
25/40 (floor .30); 180 places on 47 sheets, the longest 6. A new
building's first year often has fewer than three trainees who stood
half of it. The soak guards the wall against the ledger, and that
no career reads a year whose last showcase has not been held. The
first cut of that guard said "at most two", and the 200-career
census caught it: in the saves whose showcases fall on week 141 a
career reaches the third year's (one career in 200 had the room for
it). The guard was wrong, not the game. The 342 older rows did not
move: 0 of 342 against v0.11.15, at 40 careers and at 200 (where
the year was read 228 times, in 175/200 careers).

Suite_126 (95): the engine, and the Training tab rendered through
the DOM stub. Mutation-checked against fifty-seven broken lines,
each caught by a named assertion. A real-browser pass over a real
first year (18 checks, no page errors). Battery 126/126, soak 40
clean, census 200 clean, longhaul 11 × 620 clean, e2e 135, lockstep
0.11.16.

*Left for the next pieces.* The posting as a letter for the room
with a door for the ace left off; the absences' cadence.

## §108 The posting (SHIPPED v0.11.17 — §96 recommendation 5, the trainee years, part four)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The fourth
piece of the practice room, and the one the year's sheet (§107) was
waiting for.

**The finding** (§96): "The list on the wall, the most repeated
ceremony of a career, is a modal of the exec's sentences with no
letter for the room and no door for the ace left off."

What a lineup did to the room was already in the engine: the ones
on it had a line on their files, the one locked into the project
and left out was docked 8, and the month's first left off was
docked 6 with "first on the board, not on the list" on her ledger.
None of it was told, and none of it could be seen before the list
went up.

Nothing is drawn.

**Who the room will look for and not find is a read**
(`KP.postingRead`, pure). The floor is every free trainee. Off the
list, the room looks for the month's first (the board's), the
year's first (the last sheet on the wall, if she is still on the
floor), and anybody locked into the project. It reads the same
before the list is posted and after. The lineup builder shows it
while the list is still a draft: who is first on this month's sheet
and not on it, who was first on the year's sheet and not on it, who
is locked in and not on it, and that the one slighted most will
come to the desk about it.

**The list is one critical letter**, in the inbox the moment it is
posted (a player action: `KP.note`, never the week's trim). The
list, with the leader and the center marked; the one on it who
waited longest, if that is two years or more ("the first list with
her name on it"); who is not on it, in the room's order of
attention; how many others read it twice; a closer, one of three,
the act's own. A solo is a notice, read the same way. The
executive's review is still the modal, and it now says the list is
on the door and who will come about it.

**The year's first left off is a slight now.** Until this release
only the month's first was docked. The year's first who is not the
month's first is docked 4 and has it on her ledger. One who is
first on both is docked the month's 6 and 2 more, and it is on her
ledger once, not twice. What group.js did to the month's first and
to the dropped is as it was, to the number.

**The door** (`offTheList`). The one the list slighted most (the
month's first; the year's first when the month's is on the list)
comes to the desk once, through the one queue, as a priority
candidate, any week of the six after the list. She is not asking to
be put on it: "I am asking what the sheet is for." Three answers.
TELL HER WHY: 3 morale back, and told straight on her ledger: a
reason is worth half the dock. PROMISE HER THE NEXT LINEUP: 6
morale, on credit: it opens the practice room's own promise
(`debutByPromise`), kept the day she debuts and broken the day
another act debuts without her or two years pass, and when it
breaks she packs the same night and the room watches. It is not
offered to a trainee who already holds one. THE LIST IS THE LIST: 2
more morale gone, and nothing new on her ledger: being passed over
already stands. Silence, when she has come and stood in the
doorway three weeks, is left waiting on her ledger, as for anyone
who knocked.

**A promise of the next lineup is about the lineup after this
one.** The practice room's promise breaks "the day a debut goes out
without her". The list that just left her off is about to debut
without her, by design, so a promise made at this door would have
broken on that debut. The claim carries the act it was made about
(`exceptGroupId`) and the check steps over it. A twin holds it: the
same promise without the exception is broken by that debut.

**The answers stack.** Read in a browser, three short answers were
laid three to a row and "Promise the next lineup" wrapped to three
lines. It is worded "Promise her the next lineup", past the length
at which the Desk gives each answer a row of its own.

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.17). Nothing on an old file changes.
Its ledger arrives, all zeros, and its next list is a letter.

**The bot and the census.** The bot tells her why. It never
promises: a promise of the next lineup is a commitment and a
boss's to make, so that answer is suite-held, with the breaking and
the keeping of it. Two floors: a posted list is a letter (40/40
careers, 200/200), and the one a list left off came to the desk
(11/40, 61/200). Over 200 careers: 413 lists; the month's first
left off 75 times and the year's first 19; 73 locked in and
dropped; 67 came to the desk, and all 67 were told why.

**What moved, and why.** The door takes a week on the one queue and
its answer moves morale, so careers part ways after it: 69 of 344
older rows moved at 40 careers, the largest by three careers; 117
of 344 at 200, the largest by nine of 200. None left its band. Two
more runs name the cause. With the posting switched off, all 344
older rows read as v0.11.16's. With the letter and the slight
standing and the door shut, the same. The door is the whole of it.

**The walkthrough.** It ran 134 checks where v0.11.16 ran 135. The
one that did not run is conditional: it reads the staff's note when
a comeback lock draws one, and this career's second lock drew none,
because the walkthrough's own list left the month's first off, she
came to the desk, and the weeks after went differently. Three
checks were added where the walkthrough posts its list (the
builder's read, the review's line, the letter), each shown to fail
by name when its line is broken: 137.

## §109 The return (SHIPPED v0.11.18 — §96 recommendation 5, the absences, part one)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The absences
are the last part of the fifth entry, and they are three pieces: the
return (this one), the wait, and the quiet.

**The finding** (§96): "The absences are the purest plan → wait →
result loops left: a two-year service chapter is a chip and a
date."

This piece is the result end. When the last man came home the desk
got one `high` letter with one sentence in it for every act ("every
member home, every clock running… The window is open."). The window
was 24 weeks, stored as the week it opened, and no screen read it.
Nothing said when it was closing and nothing said when it closed.

The weekly draws nothing. The timeline reacts to the ceremony and
to the lapse, one pick each, as it does to every letter it has a
reaction for.

**The chapter** (`g.wait`). The stretch an act is short is a
record: the week the first one left, who that was, how many went.
The service opens it as each man leaves and the ceremony closes it.
Two men away at once are one chapter. A man who leaves after the
act was whole again opens a new one.

**The ceremony** (`KP.wholeAgain`, critical: the window opens
whether or not the letter survives the week, so it must). It reads
the chapter. One man of a stagger: he came through the gate this
week, so many weeks after he went in. Together: all four, the same
week, so many weeks after they went in together (two is "both").
Two away at once: the last one home, counted from the first one
out. Then the window's last week by name, and what a record locked
inside it is worth.

**In the release sheet's points, not the engine's.** The first
wording said the return's "countdown opens at 26". Read in a
browser, that number means nothing: no screen shows the build-up.
What the 26 comes to where the player can see it is the release
sheet's anticipation row, and there it is about a point
(`KP.returnWorth`: the banked build-up over the sheet's rate). The
letters, the card and the Studio say that.

**The window is one read** (`KP.returnRead`, pure): its last week,
the weeks left, whether it is open, whether it is closing. The
group page shows a card and a chip from it. The Studio's button
reads "Lock the return" while it is open, with a note that the lock
is what counts and not the date. The lock itself reads the same
read, and a window spent is counted.

**Closing, and closed.** Four weeks out, a `high` letter. The week
after its last week, the window is cleared and a critical letter
says so: it stood open 24 weeks, no record was locked inside it,
and the next record's build-up starts from nothing. An act that
ended takes its window with it, quietly.

**A soloist's service is the act's service chapter** (a repair,
found by probe before anything was built). A group that enlists
together goes on a service hiatus and the hiatus clock does not
cool it. A soloist's act had none. So the desk could declare an
ordinary hiatus over a man in service, and the forgetting ran for
the whole of it: 40 popularity to 0 over the service, where the
same act left alone came home at 19.5. The whole act away is now a
service chapter once the calendar is clear, at the enlistment or
the first clear week after it; a declared hiatus already running
becomes the chapter from its own first week; and the desk is told
why it cannot declare one. Pinned to the number: ten weeks of the
chapter cost 3.5, the fade between records, where the declared
hiatus cost 9.5.

His letters are one person's. The ceremony said "is whole again —
every member home" of a one-man act, and the gate letter had him
met by "managers, members, and a coffee truck". He is home, the
solo desk is open again, and his managers met him.

**Three things the page said that the engine did not do.**
The service card said "Nothing cools while the reason is the law".
The hiatus clock stops; the fade between records does not, and it
halves an act over a service. The card says which is which. The
hiatus card counted the fandom's patience from the announcement, so
the week everybody came home it read "Past the grace window" while
the engine had restarted the clock at the gate; it counts from the
gate. And the return's teaser was "four silhouettes" for every act;
it is the act's own count.

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.18). A window an old file carries
gets its last week. One that closed before this version is cleared
with no letter: the engine already read it as spent. An act that is
short today gets its chapter. A soloist in service under a declared
hiatus is read as a service chapter on the first week, and the
forgetting stops there.

**The long haul.** The soak cannot see any of this: no boy reaches
notice age in 140 weeks, and the census rows say so. The 40-career
soak is the same output as v0.11.17's, line for line, and at 200
careers all 346 rows read as they did, line for line. The long
haul's service scenario is where it is measured, and it gained a
man who debuts alone. Seeded beside the boy group in week one, his
debut emptied the till, the label dissolved in week 26, and the
scenario measured nothing for 594 weeks while the audit printed
CLEAN. He arrives in year four now, and a service scenario that
goes quiet is a flag. Over its 620 weeks: 5 enlisted and 5 home, 2
acts whole again, 2 windows spent, 0 lapsed, and 1 soloist's
chapter. Across all eleven scenarios: 4 whole again, 4 spent, 0
lapsed: the lean bot always locks in time, so the closing letter
and the lapse are suite-held. Held every tenth week: a soloist in
service with a clear calendar is in a service chapter; no window
outlives its last week. Held at the end: every act that came home
whole had a ceremony; windows spent, lapsed and open never
outnumber the acts that came home; no window lapsed without a
closing letter before it.

## §110 The wait (SHIPPED v0.11.19 — §96 recommendation 5, the absences, part two)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The second of
the absences' three pieces. The return (§109) was the result end of
a service. This is the eighteen months before it.

**The finding** (§96): "a two-year service chapter is a chip and a
date, 'the desk has no verbs here; nobody does'". The desk still has
no verbs. The recommendation was a cadence from the fandom's side,
and that is what this is: three marks between the gates, each a
letter composed from the state, and a map on the page.

The weekly draws nothing. The timeline reacts to day 100 and to the
turn, one pick each.

**One man's wait is a read** (`KP.waitRead`, pure): how far in, how
long to go, how he went, the marks and the next one. A full service
has three: day 100 (week 14 of it, the week that day falls in), the
half (week 36), and D-100 (14 weeks before the gate). A service too
short to hold them in order has only its gate, so a fixture's
three-week service says nothing.

**One letter an act, a mark.** Four men who went together cross a
mark in the same week and get one letter, for the four of them. Two
of a stagger who left the same week are named together. The ledger
counts letters, not men.

**Day 100: the fandom's project gets a name and a count**
(`waitHundred`, normal). The game has always said the fandom "runs
the wait like a project". The project is one of four, by hash of
the seed, the act and the week the chapter opened: the letter
drive, the paper cranes, the forest, the rice. Its count is real
state: the weeks waited, at the project's rate, times how big and
how warm the fandom is. It carries the fandom's own name and color
when it has them. A count a letter gave is never said smaller
afterwards: a pile of letters does not shrink because the act had a
bad month, so the chapter keeps the last count said and the next
one starts from it. The letter ends with how the act works until he
is home ("works as three"), or that it waits with him.

**The half: he writes from the base** (`baseLetter`, high). The
leader writes if he is among them, else the eldest. It is composed
from his file. What the act did without him: a record out since he
left, by its title, and where it peaked if it reached the top
twenty ("somebody on a base always knows"); with none, he asks
about the work; with nobody at home, the letter is about the base.
How he went, which the service now records (`how`): at the wall, or
early; together needs no sentence. Whether his papers sat on the
desk unanswered. How he signs it, by how he carries the company:
the company's name before his own, his name and the date, or his
name alone, polite the way a form is polite. If there is a room at
home it reads the letter standing up, and each of them is lifted 2.

**The papers are the service's own stamp.** The first cut read "left
waiting" off his ledger between the papers and the bus. The suite's
fixture had a man left waiting at some other door in those weeks,
and the letter blamed the papers for it. Every door that expires
leaves that act. The papers' own expiry stamps the man now
(`papersUnanswered`), the letter reads the stamp, and the gate
clears it with the papers.

**D-100: the countdown turns** (`waitTurn`). It says when he is
home, what the project stands at, and the return's rule ahead of
time: that week the act is whole, a window opens for 24 weeks, and
a record locked before he is home is a comeback like any other.
That last sentence is the one a player needs before the gate and
could not have had. An act that is wholly away is told instead that
nothing can be locked before then. If another man is still away
after him, the letter names him and the week the act is whole, and
promises no window; it is `high` only when the act is whole once he
is home.

**The gate.** The ceremony (§109) closes the project: its last
count, never less than the last one said, and the project's own
closing line. A chapter that never reached day 100 has no project
to close.

**The service map** (the group page). The plan scene says the
scheduling office "pinned a two-year map of who-is-away-when to the
wall", and nothing showed it. Each man of a boy group, in order:
the ones away (how far in, when home, the next mark), the ones
still to go (the papers' age and the wall's, or that the papers are
held, or that the wall is close), the ones served. The plan. From
day 100, the project and its count. It goes up two years before
the first papers. His file says the same of him where it said a
date.

**Read in a browser.** The map's first cut put everything about a
man away on one row, and his name broke across two lines. His row
says when he is home, and a line under it says how far in he is and
what is next. The turn said "the paper cranes stands at"; the verb
agrees with the project now.

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.19). Nothing changes. A man already
away keeps the marks still ahead of him and never hears a late one.
How he went was not recorded, so his letter does not say.

**Measured.** The soak cannot reach a service. The 40-career soak
and the 200-career census are the same output as v0.11.18's, line
for line. The long haul measures it. Its service scenario: 5 men
went and 5 came home, with 5 day-100 letters, 5 letters from the
base and 5 turns. Across all eleven scenarios: 11 went, 11 day-100
letters, 11 from the base, 10 turns. Held at the end: a house whose
men came home heard from the wait, and no mark was said more often
than men went.

*Corrected by §112.* These are letters written, not letters landed.
The week's budget cut nine of the eleven day-100 letters, six of
the eleven from the base and eight of the ten turns before the
Desk. They are critical since v0.11.21, and all of them land.

## §111 The quiet (SHIPPED v0.11.20 — §96 recommendation 5, the absences, part three)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The last of
the absences' three pieces: the two absences the desk chooses, the
declared hiatus and the personal break. With it §96's
recommendation 5 is closed.

**The finding** (§96): "the absences are the purest plan → wait →
result loops left". A declared hiatus is a bet with two halves. The
members rest, and the wait banks anticipation the return converts.
The card said how many weeks and whether the patience held, and
gave no number. The bank's arithmetic was read once, by the release
sheet, after the bet was over. Nothing said when the rest was in.
Nothing said when the bank was full, the week from which every
further week only costs. A personal break was ended by hand from
her file, and the file had to be opened to learn whether she was
rested.

The weekly draws nothing.

**The bank is one formula** (`KP.hiatusBank`). It is the release
sheet's own arithmetic, lifted out so the card and the letters read
the number the release will: nothing through the six weeks of
patience, three quarters of a point a week after, the cap of 10 in
week 19. No value changed.

**The bet is a read** (`KP.hiatusRead`, pure): how long, how much
patience is left, what a return announced this week would read, the
week the bank is full, how tired the members are, and what the
cooling has cost. The cost is measured, not estimated: the week the
patience runs out stamps the act's popularity, before that week's
cooling, and the read is the difference. A service chapter is not a
bet and has no read; its card and its letters are §109 and §110.

**The card carries it.** Under the hiatus card, twelve weeks in: "A
return announced this week would read +5 of a possible +10 on the
release sheet's return row. The bank is full May · Wk 4 · Y1, in 7
weeks. Popularity is down 5.4 since the patience ran out. The rest
has done its work." Past the patience the card used to say "the
rest is still working, and so is the forgetting", which the read
beside it could contradict. It says the forgetting is working. The
walk-down letter (`hiatusCooling`) said the same sentence the week
after the rest was in; it reads the bet now.

**Each half says when it is done.** The rest (`hiatusRested`): the
week the members' average fatigue reaches 10. It says where the
patience stands and that what the hiatus buys from here is the wait
alone. The bank (`hiatusFull`): the week the bank fills. "No week
after this one adds to it. From here every week only costs." A
hiatus a service chapter left behind gets neither: its weeks were
counted from the chapter, and the gate's ceremony (§109) spoke for
that wait.

**A personal break rests** (a repair, measured before building). A
member on a break recovered 2.5 fatigue a week. Her idle groupmates
recovered about 5. The idol week stops for her, so the break's own
relief was all she got, and the rest the statement promised was
slower than doing nothing. From 80 she needed 24 weeks to reach 20.
The break now takes off an idle week's recovery, scaled by her age
like anyone's, and its own relief on top: 10.5 a week. From 80 she
is at 17 in six weeks.

**She says when she is rested** (`breakRested`): the week her
fatigue reaches 20. How long, that the act went on as three without
her (unless the act is parked too), that the seat is kept, and
where the break ends. Her file's button says "rested" or "still
resting", and stands out when she is.

**The story's break is twelve weeks** (a second repair, found
writing that last sentence). A severity-three story forces a break,
and the response desk says of it: "Twelve weeks, minimum. The story
chose the calendar." The file's button ended that break the same
week, "back after 0 weeks", so the third severity cost one tap more
than the second. The date an early return left on the file then
ended whatever break the desk granted next. The break knows the
story forced it now (`forced`). The desk's verb refuses it and
gives the date (`KP.breakLock`). The file shows a line that cannot
be pressed: how long, how rested, the week she is back. The clock
ends that break and no other. Her rested letter names the date and
offers the desk nothing. Every break the census sees is of this
kind, because the bot grants none and never ended one, so no
simulated career could move from the lock.

**The letters come the week the screen says so** (a third repair,
found by a probe after the suite was green). The first cut sent the
letters from the absence rail, which runs before the two rails that
do the resting. So the card and the file said rested a week before
the letter did, and the bank's letter gave a cost one week short of
the card's (11.4 against 12.0). The suite's check was "the read
says rested when the letter comes", which was true a week late. The
letters have their own rail now (`quiet`, after the member desk and
the hiatus); the cost's stamp stays where it was, before the
cooling. The suite pins all three: the card never says rested
before the letter, the file never does, and the letter's cost is
the card's.

**The letters land** (a fourth repair, found by counting what
reached the Desk). The rest's letter and the break's were `high`.
The week keeps five letters below critical, in the order they were
pushed, and these are pushed late. Over 40 careers the budget cut
17 of the rest's 87 letters and 3 of the break's 8. Each one's
stamp had already burned, so it was never said. All three of this
piece's letters are critical now, the standing law for a one-shot
(§89 B), and the same 40 careers cut none. The ledger had counted
what the engine composed. *The same count on the wait's letters
(§110)*, across the long haul's eleven scenarios: 9 of 11 day-100
letters cut, 6 of 11 letters from the base, 8 of 10 turns. §110's
"Measured" paragraph counted compositions, not deliveries. That
repair is the next piece.

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.20). A hiatus whose rest is already
in, or whose bank is already full, is stamped, so neither letter
arrives as late news; the card shows the read either way. A break
already rested is stamped the same way. A forced break in flight is
marked as one, by the week it began against the story's clock.

**Read in a browser.** The locked line's return week broke after
the month ("back Apr ·", then "Wk 2 · Y1"). A span around it kept
it whole and split the button into two columns. Its own spaces do
not break now, and the line is one run of text.

**Measured.** Over 200 careers the rest was said 507 times, in 190
of them; 62 members on a break were told they were rested; 54 acts
were still parked at the end. No bank filled: the bot announces its
return from week 12 and the bank fills in week 19, so that band's
floor is zero by measurement. The long haul's eleven scenarios
filled 14.

The rows moved, and by one cause. At 40 careers 18 of 346 older
rows moved, 17 by one career and one by two. At 200, 102 moved: 70
by one career, 23 by two, 7 by three, 2 by four. None left its
band, and two rows are new. Under the same 200 careers with the
break's old rate and everything else in, none of the 346 moved. The
break's rate is the whole cause: members came back rested where
they came back tired. The lock, the letters' rail and their
priority moved one number between them, the rest's count at 40
careers (87 where it was 86).
