## §112 The letters that land (SHIPPED v0.11.21 — a repair of §103, §109, §110 and the §96 wiring, found by counting the Desk)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. A repair, not
a piece of §96. Found while finishing §111, where the same fault
was caught in that piece's own letters before it shipped.

**The finding.** §110's "Measured" paragraph said the wait's
letters were said. They were written. The week keeps five letters
below critical, by priority, then arrival (the inbox law, §89 B),
and these arrive late in the week. The same count on the Desk,
across the long haul's eleven scenarios:

| letter | shipped as | written | cut |
|---|---|---|---|
| day 100 | normal | 11 | 9 |
| the letter from the base | high | 11 | 6 |
| the turn | high or normal | 10 | 8 |
| her signing across the street | high | 31 | 4 |
| her debut there | high | 37 | 2 |
| her life outside | high | 15 | 1 |

And over 200 careers of the census: the met mandate (§96 wiring),
high, written 168 times and cut 157. It is said in a debut week,
the loudest there is. The window's closing letter (§109) was never
written in either run, because the bot spends its windows; it is
the same letter in the same place.

**How it passed.** A suite reads the week's wire before the trim
(§99), so that a missing letter fails by name. The census lines
read ledgers that the composer increments. Nothing read the Desk.
It had happened twice before inside this program and was half
seen both times. The wiring (v0.11.5) ruled the met mandate's band
from "greenlight 4" of 40: that was the letter landing, and the
mandate was being met in more than four careers in five. The
soloist's repair (v0.11.15) found her life outside landing three
times in five, raised it from normal to high, and stopped one rung
short.

**Eight letters are critical.** Each is said once: its stamp
burns, or the week it belongs to never comes again. The law's own
remedy is the one used ("a note that wants to survive a loud week
must be critical"). Day 100, the letter from the base, the turn
(for every man, not only the last one home), the window's closing
letter, her signing, her debut, her life outside, the met mandate.
The met mandate's band is re-ruled from the letter landing: 168 of
200, where it read 11.

**The Desk is counted** (`tools/desk_count.js`). It wraps the
kernel's one trim and counts, by kind, what each week wrote and
what landed. The census and the long haul both print two lines
from it: the totals, and the rare letters the budget cuts (a year
of play writes the kind about once or less, and a quarter or more
never land). A list names the letters said once, eighteen of them.
Suite_131 holds each to critical at its source. The tools hold
each to it at the Desk: one written and cut is a hard violation in
the census and a flag in the long haul. The long haul's service
line says what landed beside what was written.

**A law, added to §99's.** The suite reads the wire. The census
counts the Desk. A count of letters in a "Measured" paragraph is a
count of letters landed, or it says that it is not.

**What the count shows beyond this repair** (measured, not
changed: the rule is the owner's law). Over 200 careers the week
wrote 302,706 letters and 153,561 landed.

| priority | written | landed | cut |
|---|---|---|---|
| critical | 13,104 | 13,104 | none |
| high | 121,783 | 94,273 | 23% |
| normal | 118,561 | 39,891 | 66% |
| flavor | 49,258 | 6,293 | 87% |

The budget holds: no week lands more than five below critical. In
27% of weeks more than five letters arrive at high or critical, so
"then arrival" decides, and arrival is the order the systems run
in. Of the high letters from systems that run before order 300,
two were cut in 11,158. From order 800 on, half were.

| high letters, by the order their system runs at | written | cut |
|---|---|---|
| before 300 | 11,158 | 2 letters |
| 300 to 599 | 37,601 | 2% |
| 600 to 699 (the release week) | 28,897 | 39% |
| 700 to 759 | 11,548 | 28% |
| 760 to 799 | 21,323 | 32% |
| 800 and later | 11,256 | 49% |

So some kinds almost never land, whatever they say: three eras in
the red (4 in 100; its scene still opens), a member's first
songwriting credit (3), the sophomore slump (15), a hit the critics
panned (16), a lost head-to-head week (18). Fourteen of the 93 high
kinds land less than half the time, and five of them less than one
time in ten.

**Three rules, replayed.** The trim decides nothing in the
simulation, so the same 200 careers were replayed under each rule.
Every rule lands the same 153,561 letters.

| | today | shuffled | least seen first |
|---|---|---|---|
| high kinds landing under half the time | 14 | 17 | 2 |
| high kinds landing under one in ten | 5 | none | none |
| three eras in the red | 4% | 43% | 95% |
| a member's first songwriting credit | 3% | 43% | 78% |
| the sophomore slump | 15% | 48% | 95% |
| a story breaks | 68% | 86% | 98% |
| the monthly sheet | 69% | 72% | 62% |
| narrative letters (63 a career) | 75% | 67% | 41% |
| outside offers | 100% | 88% | 78% |
| health letters | 99% | 81% | 87% |

"Shuffled" breaks ties by a hash of the week, so no system is
first every week. "Least seen first" breaks them by how often this
career has already been shown the kind. It nearly ends the
starving, and the letters it costs are the ones a career sees most.
Health letters would have to be critical under either: they land
today only because their system runs early.

*The owner's to call:* the tie-break. Recommended: least seen
first, with health letters made critical. Until it is called, the
rule stands, every new letter said once goes in as critical, and
the census names what is cut.

**Measured.** Priorities move no career: at 40 careers and at 200
the output is the same as v0.11.20's line for line, but for the

12,913 over the 200 careers before, 13,104 after, one more a
career. Weeks with four or more went from 283 to 307 of 29,440. The
loudest week has nine, as it had: three records landing, two fusion
verdicts and a season finale among them. After the repair no letter
on the list was written and cut, in the census or the long haul.
Across the long haul's eleven scenarios the wait wrote 11 day-100
letters, 11 from the base and 10 turns, and the same numbers
landed.

## §113 The head (SHIPPED v0.11.22 — §96 recommendation 6, the other side of the wall, part one)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The first of
recommendation 6's pieces. The plan for the rest: the ledger each
house keeps on us, the call a head makes, the seat in play, the
titans' weeks, the press.

**The finding** (§96): "the rivals have a philosophy word and a
scoreboard, no head, no voice, no door, and no memory of what you
did to them". This piece is the head and the voice. The door and
the memory read what it stamps.

The weekly draws nothing, and nothing here draws from the main
stream.

**Every signing house has a head** (`wall.js`, `r.head`): a name,
and a temper. The name comes from a private stream keyed by the
seed and the house, so it is the house's own and the same in every
fork of a save. A name another head carries, or our own
executive's, is drawn again. The temper is a hash in the schools'
pattern (§84). The stamp is made once: at a new game, the week
after a house is founded, and on an old file when it is opened.
The broadcaster's project house is a show, not a house, and has
none.

**Four tempers**, each a sentence on the card:

- *duelist*: takes a shared release week as a personal remark
- *broker*: believes every problem is a trade nobody has priced yet
- *steward*: runs the house like a trust and returns calls on
  Thursdays
- *showman*: has never met a microphone that was not meant for her

They are words in this piece. They were chosen for what comes
next: who ambushes, who trades, who offers a truce, who wants the
joint stage.

**The read is pure** (`KP.rivalHead`): the stamped head, or the one
the stamp will give a house founded since the last tick. It writes
nothing, so a screen can ask. A house a day old is on the Industry
tab with the head it will have.

**The card says who runs the house**: "Kang So-seo runs it: a
duelist, who takes a shared release week as a personal remark."

**The January issue quotes one head.** The trades' yearly ranking
was a list and a sentence about the top seat. It ends now with one
head speaking: the one whose year it was (`KP.rankingStory`). A
house that took the seat. The house that lost it, when we took it.
The house in second, when we hold it. Otherwise the house one rung
above us, which holds the top if that rung is the first. What the
head says comes from a family for the temper and the seat: four
tempers, five seats, two lines each, forty lines, and the pronouns
are the head's own. The same head in the same seat the next year
is given the family's other line.

**The January issue is critical.** It is said once a year, in a
week that does not come again, so by §112's law it cannot be cut.
It joins the list of letters said once (nineteen now).

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.22). Each house gets the head a new
game would have given it. Nothing else on the file moves.

**Found by the mutation run.** Two guards guarded nothing and were
deleted: a house's own name excluded from the names taken, when a
house being named has none; and our own row excluded from the
houses a ranking can quote, when it is never among the signing
houses. Four broken lines crashed the suite where they should have
failed by name, and each crash got a guard.

**Measured.** Over 200 careers 1,146 heads were stamped and 893
houses stood at the end: 251 duelists, 212 brokers, 219 stewards,
211 showmen. The January issue came out 400 times and quoted a head
400 times. Across the long haul's eleven scenarios: 146 heads, and
132 quotes in 132 rankings. No career moved. Nothing draws from the
main stream, and the census output is v0.11.21's line for line but
for its own new lines, a kilobyte of save, and what reaches the
Desk. The January issue no longer takes one of the week's five
places, so 364 more letters landed over the 200 careers, and two
rows that count a letter landing moved with them: a passed
candidate in a rival's chair (169 careers, from 167) and the
protest truck (143, from 142).

Suite_132 (395): the stamp, the private stream, the read, the
story, every line of every family filled for a woman and for a man,
the ranking through the real weekly, the card through the DOM stub,
an old file. Mutation-checked against 55 broken lines, each caught
by a named assertion. On the first run 49 of 56 were: three
survived and four crashed the suite. Two of the survivors were the
guards above, the third got a check, and each crash got a guard. A
real-browser pass: each house's card, an old save opened through
the title screen, and the January issue brought to the Desk through
the real weekly (19 checks, no page errors). Battery 132/132, soak
40 clean, census 200 clean, longhaul 11 × 620 clean, e2e 137,
lockstep 0.11.22.

*Left for the next piece.* The ledger: what each house remembers
of us, in words on its card (§114), and what that weighs. *Not built:* a
head who leaves. A house keeps its head for as long as it stands.
*Still the owner's to call*: the Desk's tie-break (§112); and from

## §114 The ledger (SHIPPED v0.11.23 — §96 recommendation 6, the other side of the wall, part two)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The second of
recommendation 6's pieces. The plan for the rest: what the ledger
weighs, the call a head makes, the seat in play, the titans' weeks,
the press.

**The finding** (§96): the rivals had "no memory of what you did to
them". The card had two sentences about one thing, the offer letter
(v0.11.5). Everything else the game decides between the houses was
a counter on the rival or a feud on our group, and none of it was a
sentence a player could read.

Nothing here draws, and nothing rolls on the ledger in this piece.

**Each signing house keeps books on us** (`r.directed`,
`KP.recordHouse`). An act is a week and a kind. It is recorded
where the game already decides it, and the call site names the kind
and nothing else. One table (`KP.C.WALL.KINDS`) holds each kind's
weight on their regard for us and the words the card uses. An
unknown kind throws. A house that does not stand records nothing,
and the broadcaster's project house keeps no books.

Eleven kinds. What we did:

- we took a head-to-head week from their act (−2)
- we signed a trainee they had cut (−1)
- we put their offer letter on our board's table (−3)
- we declined their offer (−1)
- we walked out of the house to found our own (−6, the old house
  only)

What they did:

- they took a head-to-head week from us (+1)
- they parked a comeback on our date (0)
- they signed a lead this desk had read, off our board (0)
- they signed an artist who was once ours (+1)
- they signed someone who had left this building (0)
- they took the co-build we passed on (+1)

A lead counts only if this desk had read the file and the house
signed it off our board: by its own scouts, or by its intake taking
a public file. One this desk never opened was never ours to lose,
and one whose window we let close was not taken. Someone who had
left this building counts by any road, once, and is not also a
lead.

**The caps.** A house keeps the latest five acts of a kind and
twenty-four in all; the oldest goes first. The walkout is the one
act the table keeps for good.

**The read is pure** (`KP.houseRead`). Their regard for us is the
sum of the weights, each halved every 104 weeks: a house forgets
more slowly than a person does (48). What they hold against us is
the sum of what we did, never halved; the next piece reads it. Five
words for the regard: warm toward us (3 and up), cordial with us
(1), even with us (−1), cool toward us (−3), holding a grudge
(below). An empty book has no word.

**The card says it**: "Kang So-seo is cool toward us. On the books:
lost a head-to-head week to us (Mar · Wk 2 · Y2); parked a comeback
on our date (Feb · Wk 4 · Y2); and 2 more." The head's name, the
word, the three latest acts with their weeks, and a count of the
rest. A house with nothing on its books says nothing. The offer's
two old sentences are gone: its two answers are acts among the
rest.

**The founding.** The house we walk out of becomes a house across
the street, and it opens its books with the walkout. It weighs six:
a grudge for two years, cool for five, and a week it takes from us
the same month does not thaw it. What the other houses hold is
kept: they kept books on the architect, as their offer flags and
the rivalry stories already did.

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.23). What an old file records with a
week goes on the books with that week: an offer leveraged or
declined, the last date they parked on, the walkout, an artist of
ours they signed, and whoever is on their floor today that had left
this building or was a lead this desk had read (her file says by
which road she came, and when). Head-to-head weeks were recorded
on our groups without the house's week, and stay off.

**Found while finishing it.** The first build recorded nine kinds
and was through its mutation run when three gaps showed. The old
house had empty books, so one week taken from us would have read
"cordial with us" on the card of the house the game itself marks
as holding a grudge. A read lead was recorded only when a house's
scouts signed it, and not when its intake took the same file off
the open board. Someone who had left us and signed across the
street was a letter and not an act. All three were closed before
the piece shipped, and the check chain was stopped and run again.
One more thing on the same card: a floor of one read "1 trainees".

**Found by the check chain.** The long haul's new flag for the
walkout fired on its first run, in four scenarios founded through
other doors: a fresh start after a dissolution, and a blank start.
Those leave no house behind. The flag was wrong and was corrected,
then proven to fire by breaking the record in a scratch copy.

**Found by the mutation run.** On the first build, 51 of 55 broken
lines were caught. One crashed the suite where it should have
failed by name. The half-life was not pinned. The order of an old
file's seeds was not tested. And the record of an artist they
signed survived its own removal, because until the version was
bumped every reload ran the new migration and seeded the act back
from her flag. The version is bumped before the mutation run and
the browser pass. After the three gaps were closed, 78 of 79: every
file in the old-save fixture had one signing, so the last signing
and the first could not be told apart.

**Measured.** Over 200 careers 2,901 acts went on the books: 1,081
head-to-head weeks they took and 814 we took, 833 dates parked on,
79 castoffs of theirs signed here, 73 offers declined, 17 people
who had left us signed there, two pacts taken, one offer put on the
board's table and one artist of ours signed across the street.
Every career had something on the books with a house (200 of 200).
Of the 893 houses standing at the end, 612 kept a book: 8 warm
toward us, 96 cordial, 253 even, 184 cool, 71 holding a grudge.
Across the long haul's eleven scenarios, 374 acts; the founder's
old house holds the walkout, dated the week of the founding. No
career moved: nothing draws and nothing rolls on the ledger, and
the soak, the census and the long haul are v0.11.22's line for line
but for the ledger's own lines and a kilobyte or two of save. The
census bot never reads a lead, puts an offer on the board's table
once in 200 careers, and does not found a house; those three are
held by the suite, which forces each through the game, and by the
browser pass, which taps the real Look button, the real answer and
the real papers.

Suite_133 (115): the table, the record, the read and its five
words at their lines, the caps, the card's sentence, each act
through the game where the game decides it, the roads onto a
floor, the founding, an old file, the card through the DOM stub.
Suites 115 and 122 hold the offer's two answers and the signing
across the street to the books. Mutation-checked against 82 broken
lines, each caught by a named assertion in every suite that owns
the line. A real-browser pass (29 checks, no page errors): the
card, an old save opened through the title screen, the offer
answered on the Desk, the founding signed with its button, and a
file read with the Look button and signed off the open board a week
later. Battery 133/133, soak 40 clean, census 200 clean, longhaul
11 × 620 clean, e2e 137, lockstep 0.11.23.

*Left for the next piece.* What the ledger weighs: one roll at a
time (the date a house parks on first), each measured on its own.
*Not recorded yet:* the call a house makes to one of our chairs,
and what we do about it; it belongs with who makes the call
(recorded in §116). *Not
built:* a head who leaves. *Still the owner's to call*: the Desk's
tie-break (§112); and from §109, the fade between records through

## §115 The weight (SHIPPED v0.11.24 — §96 recommendation 6, the other side of the wall, part three)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The third of
recommendation 6's pieces, and the first in which the books weigh
something. One roll only: which house parks a comeback on our date.

**The finding** (§96): the ledger was to weigh "what the physics
already roll". The first of those is the ambush. A house in
shifting distance of our date parked on it at 12% a week, and the
house was always the most prestigious one in reach. The head had no
part in it, and neither had anything we had done.

Nothing here draws. Whether a date is parked on is not changed.

**Who parks** (`KP.houseMotive`, pure). Each house in reach has a
motive: what it holds against us today, point for point, and its
head's temper leaning on that.

- what it holds: the regard on its books when that is below zero
  (§114), so it fades as the regard does. A house that is warm
  toward us has no spite, and is not held back for being warm.
- the temper: a duelist +2, a showman +1, a broker 0, a steward −2.

The house with the greatest motive parks. With nothing between the
houses, the most prestigious does, as it always did. A house inside
its cooldown is not in reach, whatever it holds.

**The broadcaster's show** has no head to take offence and keeps
no books. It parks only when no house is in reach. It was weighed
by prestige like a house before; left that way it would have parked
whenever the houses in reach were stewards.

**The letter says why**, and so does the Studio's clash card
(`KP.parkWhy`, kept on the clash). When the house holds something:
"Nam Yeon-sung has not forgotten: Aurum lost a head-to-head week
to us (Jan · Wk 1 · Y1)." It names the act that weighs most today,
the newest of equals. When it is the temper: "Baek Joo-eun is a
duelist, who takes a shared release week as a personal remark."
When it is only the calendar, nothing is added.

**The letter is critical.** It opens a decision, and it says its
reason once. As a high letter 3 in 264 were cut by the week's
budget.

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.24): the wall's ledger counts parked
dates from zero. A clash open on an old file has no reason on it
and reads as it always did.

**Measured, before and after**, over the same 200 careers:

| over the same 200 careers | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| dates parked on | 852 | 864 |
| by the most prestigious house standing | 521 | 283 |
| by a house with something against us | 360 | 452 |
| by a duelist’s house | 216 | 358 |
| by a showman’s | 197 | 224 |
| by a broker’s | 194 | 168 |
| by a steward’s | 227 | 101 |
| by the broadcaster’s show | 18 | 13 |
| the date held | 732 | 734 |
| the date slipped | 94 | 96 |
| that week taken by us | 316 of 718 | 335 of 725 |

In the census's own count, 849 dates were parked on by a house over
the 200 careers: 452 for something on the books, 264 on the head's
temper, 133 for the calendar alone. 382 were not the most
prestigious house in reach, and in 165 of the 200 careers that
happened at least once (a band, 40% to 100%). Across the long
haul's eleven scenarios, 72 dates: 27 for the books, 35 on temper.

**Told from noise at 1,000 careers.** Who parks decides which act
lands on our week, so careers move. At 200 careers 169 of the
census's 350 rows moved, nine of them by ten careers or more, and
the largest was the first group reaching number one on the scene
chart: 188 careers to 173. A second 200 careers on both builds did
not repeat it (173 and 176); of the 37 rows that had moved by five
or more, 15 moved the same way again and 19 the other way. At 1,000
careers on both builds the first group reaches number one in 888
careers and 887, the daesang goes home in 76 and 74, a head-to-head
week is lost in 665 and 666, and 13 and 12 careers dissolve. One
row of the 350 differs by more than two standard deviations and
none by three. A date is parked on 4.2 times a career before and
4.3 after. A change to who a roll falls on moves rows at 200
careers by chance alone; a row that moves is a question, and 1,000
careers on both builds answer it.

Suite_134 (72): the table, the motive, why in words, who parks

against each other, a steward passed over and a steward alone, the

## §116 The letterhead (SHIPPED v0.11.25 — §96 recommendation 6, the other side of the wall, part four)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The fourth of
recommendation 6's pieces: two more places where a house chooses
us. The second roll the books weigh, and a signature on both.

**The finding** (§96, and §114's "not recorded yet"). When a house
called one of our staff away, the house was drawn at random and
only its name was used. The scene had no head in it, said nothing
of why this house, and what we answered went nowhere. The offer
letter came from a letterhead and nobody.

**Who calls** (`KP.callingHouse`). Every house is in reach of a
phone, so there is nothing to sort: it is a weighted draw on the
one number that was always drawn there. A house's weight is 1, plus
half a point for each point of motive, never under a quarter. The
motive is §115's, with its own lean: what the house holds against
us today, and its head's temper.

- a broker +2 (a broker trades in people)
- a duelist +1
- a showman 0
- a steward −2 (a steward promotes from within)

So a broker's house is called from twice as often as a showman's,
a steward's a quarter as often, and a house with a lost week on its
books as often as a broker's. With every weight equal the draw
picks the house it always picked. A house that is warm toward us
is neither more nor less likely.

**The scene is signed, and says why.** "Heo Si-seo of Whitecliff
Company wants Nam Byung-chul". When the house holds something, the
scene ends with it: "Heo Si-seo has not forgotten: Whitecliff lost
a head-to-head week to us (Feb · Wk 1 · Y1)." When it is the
temper: "… is a broker, who believes every problem is a trade
nobody has priced yet." A showman or a steward with nothing on the
books gives no reason. The letter about a road manager names the
head too.

**The answer goes on the books** (§114's table, thirteen kinds
now):

- matched: the house "called one of our staff and was outbid" (−1)
- wished well, or left unanswered: the house "hired one of our
  staff away" (+1)

So the two answers cost different things. The raise keeps the
person and cools the house, which then parks on our dates and
calls again a little more readily. Letting them go loses the
person and warms it.

**The offer is signed.** The letter: "Novaline Entertainment's
letterhead, Park In-beom's signature: they want YOU." The scene
carries one line in the head's own hand, by temper:

- duelist: "I would rather have you inside this building than
  across the street from it."
- broker: "Everything has a price. I have worked out yours, and I
  think you will find it fair."
- steward: "This house will outlast both of us. I am choosing who
  looks after it next."
- showman: "Picture the announcement. I already have."

**Not weighed: who writes the offer.** §96 listed "the offer's
suitor" among the rolls. Measured first: in 78 offers over 200
careers exactly one house could have written, every time. There is
no choice to weigh. The pact we pass on is taken once or twice in
200 careers, and is left as it is.

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.25): the wall's ledger counts calls
from zero. A call open on an old file has no short and no reason on
it: its head is found by the name it carries, and its answer still
goes on the books.

**Measured, before and after**, over the same 200 careers:

| over the same 200 careers | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| staff calls | 538 | 538 |
| from a broker’s house | 107 | 175 |
| from a duelist’s | 145 | 175 |
| from a showman’s | 141 | 123 |
| from a steward’s | 145 | 65 |
| from a house with something against us | 171 | 248 |
| matched | 425 | 424 |
| wished well | 111 | 111 |

The table counts every call the run made, the tool's side worlds
included; the census's own line counts the 200 careers. There, 528
calls: 246 from a house with something against us, 179 on its
head's temper; 414 were matched and went on the house's books as
outbid, 111 as a hire. In 189 of the 200 careers a house that
called had a reason the scene could give (a band, 40% to 100%).
Across the long haul's eleven scenarios, 79 calls: 31 for the
books, 36 on temper.

**At 1,000 careers on both builds** (§115's law). How often a call
comes is not changed: the roll is the one it was, and the draw
takes the one number it took. What moves careers is the books: an
answer is an act now, and what a house holds weighs on the dates it
parks on (§115). Over 1,000 careers 2,617 calls, 2,012 matched and
587 hired away. Dates parked on for something on the books: 2,103
before, 2,344 after. No outcome moved: the daesang goes home in 74
careers and 74, the first group reaches number one in 887 and 880,
a head-to-head week is lost in 666 and 681, 12 and 12 careers
dissolve. Of 351 rows, 152 differ and none by two standard
deviations.

**Found by the mutation run.** 41 of 45 broken lines were caught on
the first run. Two survived. The check that a house with something
against us calls accepted whichever house the draw gave it, so the
old unweighed draw passed it; it now runs the hires week on a
stream that always says the same number, where the draw says the
first house and the books say the last. And the check that who
calls takes one number from the stream compared two worlds built by
the same code, so a second draw passed it; it now reads what the
week asks of the stream. Two more crashed the suite where they
should have failed by name, and each got a guard.

Suite_135 (70): the tables, the weighted draw at its shares, the
one draw, who calls through the hires week, the reason on the
scene, each answer on the books for a road manager and for a chair
(matched, wished well, unanswered, a chair already empty), a scene

two new acts to the table. Mutation-checked against 45 broken

the line. A real-browser pass (22 checks, no page errors): the
house with something against us calls, the Desk's scene is signed

house's card says it was outbid, the manager is wished well in a

## §117 The truce (SHIPPED v0.11.26 — §96 recommendation 6, the other side of the wall, part five)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The fifth of
recommendation 6's pieces, and the first door a head opens.

**The finding** (§96): "One recurring door, `rivalCall`, opened by
temper", with "a truce after a named rivalry" among its uses and
"the polite no as the bot's default". Since §114 a house's regard
could be read, and since §115 it weighed on our dates, but there
was nothing to do about it. This is the first thing to do.

**When a head calls** (`KP.truceDue`, pure). A house whose regard
for us is under −3, which is the card's "holding a grudge". Its
head is not a duelist: a duelist never calls. It is not the house
we walked out of: the old house never calls. It is not already in
a truce with us, and its head has not called in the last 96 weeks.
Then each week is a hash of the seed, the house and the week
against the temper's chance: a steward 8 in 100, a broker 5, a
showman 3. Nothing is drawn from the main stream. One call waits
on the Desk at a time, for three weeks.

**The letter** is the head's, and critical: it opens a decision,
and a head calls about this once in two years. Each temper has a
line:

- steward: "A house that spends its year on another house has not
  spent it on its artists. I would like both of ours back."
- broker: "This has cost us both more than it has made either of
  us. I have run the numbers twice."
- showman: "The feud was good television. It has stopped being
  good television."

**The terms** are one sentence, the same in the letter, the scene
and on the card: "they stay off our dates, and we do not sign
anyone they have cut". A truce runs 48 weeks.

**Two answers.** The polite no comes first, so a desk that does
not answer amounts to it, and so does every tool's bot.

- *Decline, politely.* Nothing changes. It goes on the books in
  words and weighs nothing: the house "offered us a truce and was
  politely declined". A call left three weeks unanswered is
  written down the same way.
- *Shake on it.* What the house held against us is struck from its
  books; what it did, and the walkout, stay. The handshake goes on
  them (+1). It costs no money and no trust. Its price is its
  terms.

**In force.** A house in a truce with us is not in reach of our
dates (§115): it does not park, whoever else does. Its card says
until when, and the terms.

**Breaking it.** Signing anyone the house has cut ends the truce
at the signing. Both go on the books: the castoff signed (−1) and
the truce broken (−4), which is heavier than most of what a
handshake strikes. A critical letter says who read the signing
photo as an answer. The player is told before the pen: the board
marks her, "signing breaks the truce with Novaline", and the
signing sheet says it again in red.

**The year runs out.** The week after its last, the truce is off
the file and a critical letter says so, once.

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.26): the wall's ledger counts truces
from zero.

**Measured.** The census bot shakes on it in half its careers, by
seed, so both answers are measured; the other tools' bots give the
polite no. Over 200 careers a head called 79 times, in 68 careers:
38 were shaken on, 39 declined or left unanswered, and 2 were still
waiting at the end. Of the 38 truces, 16 ran their year, 21 were in
force at the end, one went with a house that did not last the
career, and none was broken. Three bands: a head called (68 of
200), a truce shaken on (33), a truce broken (0). Across the long
haul's eleven scenarios, 3 calls, all declined.

**At 1,000 careers on both builds** (§115's law). 381 calls in 333
careers; 186 truces. A date is parked on 4.3 times a career before
and after: 4,205 dates before, 4,204 after. No outcome moved: the
daesang goes home in 74 careers and 75, the first group reaches
number one in 880 and 882, a head-to-head week is lost in 681 and
681, 12 and 12 careers dissolve. Of 352 rows, 127 differ and none
by two standard deviations.

**Not measured by the census: the break.** In 1,000 careers the bot
never signed someone a house had cut while in a truce with that
house. The break is held by the suite, through a real signing and
through the signing sheet's two buttons, and by the browser pass.

**Found while finishing it.** The browser pass passed without
doing what it claimed. Its Sign button opens a sheet, and the
script closed the sheet and signed through the engine instead. It
now taps the sheet's own buttons, and the sheet got the warning it
was missing. The handshake's toast ran off the screen and was
shortened.

**Found by the mutation run.** One broken line hung the suite for
half an hour instead of failing: with the head's mark unset, a
check set the week to a value that was not a number, and the
engine never came back from it. The check now fails by name first,
and the runner treats two minutes without an answer as a crash. On
the full run after that, 60 of 61 were caught; the miss was a
mutation that crashed by its own construction, replaced by a real
one (a truce past its year still shown on the card) with a check.
One guard guarded nothing and was deleted.

Suite_136 (102): the table, when a head calls and when not, the
hash's share over two thousand weeks, the call through the real
weekly with the main stream left where it was, one call at a time,
the scene's words, each answer, silence, a house that stops
standing, the walkout kept, a truce in force on our dates, the year
running out, the break through a real signing, the card, the board,
the Desk, the signing sheet driven through its two buttons, an old
file, a reload, both tools' wiring. Suites 131 and 133 hold the two
letters and the three acts to their lists. Mutation-checked against
61 broken lines, each caught by a named assertion in every suite
that owns the line. A real-browser pass (25 checks, no page
errors): the head calls with the week's hash forced, the Desk
carries the call, the truce is shaken on with the real button and
is on the card, the board and the signing sheet both warn, and
signing through the sheet ends it. Battery 136/136, soak 40 clean,
census 200 clean, longhaul 11 × 620 clean, e2e 137, lockstep
0.11.26.

*Left for the next piece.* The other doors a head could open: a
borrowed stage week, a trade, a joint stage. *Not built:* a price

## §118 Two pieces measured and not built (after v0.11.26 — §96 recommendation 6: the seat in play, the giants' weeks)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. Two of
recommendation 6's pieces were counted before any code was
written, and as the game stands neither has anything to act on.
Nothing shipped. Both are the owner's to call.

**The seat in play.** §96: "The overtake as a two-letter event
('the seat is in play' in December, the ranking in January)."
Counted over 200 careers, four weeks before each January issue:
the gap between first and second on the trades' own score.

| the gap in December | the first year | later years |
|---|---|---|
| Decembers counted | 206 | 218 |
| eleven points or more | 198 | 207 |
| seven to ten | 3 | 4 |
| four to six | 1 | 3 |
| three or fewer | 4 | 4 |

Our house is first in 200 of the 206 first Decembers and in 200 of
the 218 later ones. The seat changed hands in 7 Januaries of 218.
A December letter would have something to say about one year in
twenty.

The reason is the score. Ours is our best group's popularity, four
tenths of the second's, a third of the executive's trust and four
points a daesang. A house's is eight tenths of its prestige and
under half its flagship's popularity. By the first December ours
is far above. *The owner's to call:* whether the trades' ranking
should be a race, which means re-weighing the two scores, or stay
what it is, a record of a lead.

**The giants' weeks.** §96: "The national titans' mega-weeks on
the strip through `announcedWeek` so they crowd you and the date
picker can see them." A giant's next release week is on the file
from the day of its last, so marking it is easy. Counted first:
what releasing near one costs us on the national board, over the
same 200 careers.

| our release | records | top ten | top three |
|---|---|---|---|
| no giant within two weeks | 1,352 | 50% | 7% |
| a giant that week or the two before | 1,675 | 61% | 9% |
| a giant in the two weeks after | 577 | 64% | 15% |

Nothing. Records released beside a giant peak a little higher, not
lower. The summit of the national board is held by the giants'
standing catalog between their releases (v0.10.22), so a new
release of theirs changes little about where ours peaks, and
nothing of theirs touches our reception. A marker on the calendar
would point at nothing.

For the marker to mean something, a giant's week would have to
crowd ours, the way a scene rival's shared week does. That is a
change to difficulty, not a signpost. *The owner's to call.* Also
not built: the torch letter. A giant does not retire in the game
as it stands.

**A note on method.** Both pieces were in the plan, and both would
have passed every check: a letter that is written, lands and reads
well, and a marker that renders. Counting first is what showed
there was nothing under them. The two probes run the census bot's
careers with the engine wrapped, and print one paragraph each.

*What is left of recommendation 6:* the other doors a head could
open (a borrowed stage week, a trade, a joint stage), and the
press.

## §119 Her own questions (SHIPPED v0.11.27 — §96 recommendation 7, the people upstairs and down the hall, part one)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The first of
recommendation 7's pieces: the executive's kind is read.

**The finding** (§96): "The exec's `personality` finally read: a
question family per type". Counted first (§118's lesson). Over 200
careers the Monday meeting sat down 2,941 times and had nothing to
ask 1,626 times. Six kinds of executive are in the data, each with
a sentence of their own at the start of a career. The kind was
copied from file to file and read by nothing.

**What each kind asks**, when the meeting has nothing else. The
older questions come first: the board's solo question, whose debut
lands first, when the second lineup forms.

- the profit hunter, about the quarter: "Twelve weeks from today,
  is there more in the till than the 132 in it this morning?"
- the traditionalist, about the best voice in the trainee room:
  "Half a year from now, is it a better one?"
- the micromanager, about the lowest name on the last evaluation
  sheet: "Take a full month. On the sheet after that, is she
  higher?"
- the trend chaser, about the sound of the year: "When our next
  record lands, is it in the sound of its year?"
- the visionary, about the act the public knows best: "Does the
  next one land harder?"
- the patient executive asks nothing. That is what patient means.

§96 named four. The visionary's is a fifth, in the words of her own
introduction. Each needs something to ask about: a trainee in the
room; a printed sheet with someone below first; an act that could
release a record (standing, debuted, not on hiatus); a record
already out. Nothing here draws.

**Each question is a family** (§93). Three ways of opening it,
picked by hash, never the one she used last time. The question
itself is the last sentence and is the same in all three, so what
is promised does not depend on which she used. This was added after
the count below: a question at 84 meetings in 100 would have been
the same sentence twice a year.

**Two answers.** The promise first, as in every question of hers.

- *On the record.* A promise to this chair, checked by the game. It
  costs nothing until it is judged. Kept, trust +2. Broken, trust
  −2, and twice that under the fund's board seat. These are the
  numbers every promise to her has always moved.
- *A pass*, in her words for it. Free once. A second pass in a row
  costs 1, and so does each one after it: "That is two of my
  questions running with nothing on the record." Anything put on
  her record in between ends the run, and a new chair starts her
  own count. (§96 release 1: no answer is free.)

Silence costs what it always cost her: 1.

**What each promise is held to.**

- the quarter: more in the till, in whole units, twelve weeks after
  the question. The same number is not more. From an empty till or
  the red, the promise is the black.
- the voice: three points better, half a year from the answer. A
  debut keeps it at once. Letting her go breaks it at once.
- the name: a higher number on the first sheet a full month after
  the answer. The sheets between do not count. A debut keeps it;
  letting her go breaks it; a sheet that is never held judges
  nobody.
- the sound: our next record, whichever act releases it, in the
  sound of the year it lands in. Next door to the sound is not in
  it. A record that moves the year's sound keeps it. A year with no
  record breaks it.
- the record: that act's next record landing harder than its last.
  Level is not harder. A last bow first, or a year with no record,
  breaks it.

**One at a time, and hers.** While one of these promises stands she
asks no new one. It is made to her: under the next chair it is set
aside, unjudged, with no letter.

**Overtaken.** A question waits four weeks. If what it asks about
has already happened by the answer, there is nothing left to
promise: the trainee has left the room or debuted, the next sheet
is printed, the next record is out, the act is gone. She crosses it
off: nothing promised, nothing charged, whichever answer is tapped.
Without this a slow answer was a free one.

**The verdict is a letter in her voice**, and critical: it is said
once. "You said the quarter would close above 132. It closed at
133. I like a number that keeps its word." "Yoon Ye-dam: number 6
when I asked, number 6 on this sheet. I notice when a name does not
move, too." The Desk's record lists the promise in words with its
date, and keeps what she said beside the verdict.

**Found while building it: three things on the Desk.**

- A promise that was set aside read "broken". A promise ended by a
  founding, a fresh start, a contract's end or a group's last bow
  is not judged, and the settled list called every one of them
  broken. It reads "set aside" now.
- The settled list named today's chair for every promise. A promise
  made to her question names the chair it was made to.
- A toast was one line, cut with three dots at the screen's edge.
  Most replies in the game are a sentence or two, so most were cut.
  A toast wraps now. It stays 2.2 seconds, plus a twenty-fifth of a
  second for each character past forty, to a ceiling of six. It
  never takes a tap meant for what is under it, and a new one
  replaces the last.

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.27): the ledger upstairs counts from
zero. A promise from before this version has no chair on it and is
judged as it always was.

**Measured, before and after**, over the same 200 careers and the
tool's side worlds:

| over the same 200 careers | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Monday meetings | 2,941 | 2,941 |
| with a question | 1,315 | 2,472 |
| with nothing to ask | 1,626 | 469 |

The census bot steers toward none of the five. It answers each by a
hash of the week it was asked, so both answers are measured; the
other tools' bots always promise. In the census's own count over
its 200 careers she asked 1,083 times, in 168 careers. 501 went on
the record and 510 were passed, 149 of them a second pass in a row
and charged. 163 promises were kept, 298 broken, 12 set aside, and
28 were on the clock at the end. Three bands: she asked (168 of
200), a promise kept (103), one broken (133). Across the long
haul's eleven scenarios, whose bot always promises, she asked 187
times: 77 promises kept, 82 broken, 25 set aside.

| unsteered, over 200 careers | asked | kept | broken |
|---|---|---|---|
| the quarter | 203 | 64 | 19 |
| the voice | 155 | 19 | 32 |
| the name | 221 | 37 | 65 |
| the sound | 282 | 7 | 127 |
| the record | 222 | 36 | 55 |

The sound is the hard one unsteered. The bot picks a concept for
the group and not for the year, and keeps 7 of 134. A desk that
picks the year's lane for its next record keeps it. That is the
trend chaser: an executive who pays for chasing the year and
charges for ignoring it.

**Trust**, the one number this moves, on both builds over the same
200 careers:

| over the same 200 careers | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| mean trust, all weeks | 67.3 | 66.7 |
| mean trust at the last week | 64.1 | 63.1 |
| weeks under 40 | 9.4% | 9.6% |
| weeks at 60 or more | 65.4% | 64.3% |
| weeks at 70 or more | 47.2% | 46.0% |

Trust is 0.6 lower on average under a desk that steers toward none
of the five. By the chair's kind: 1.7 lower under the trend chaser
(70.7 to 69.1), unchanged to the hundredth under the patient
executive (69.14), and 0.4 higher under the profit hunter (67.1 to
67.5), whose quarter the bot mostly keeps.

**At 1,000 careers on both builds** (§115's law). 5,219 questions
in 836 careers; 810 promises kept and 1,417 broken. No outcome
moved: the daesang goes home in 75 careers and 75, the first group
reaches number one in 882 and 881, a head-to-head week is lost in
681 and 684, 12 and 12 careers dissolve. Of 355 rows, 130 differ
and none by two standard deviations. The two that moved most: a
debut anniversary celebrated in 999 careers and 996, and trust
drifting down from above its bar in 848 and 831. The wordings were
added after this run; they draw nothing, and the 200 careers run
after them match the 200 before them in every one of 358 rows.

**Found by the browser pass.** The suite and the first browser
script were written as if a week turned between her question and
the answer. It does not: the week turns at the start of the next
advance, and the desk answers in the week it was asked. The rules
were right for either order. Both scripts were corrected, and the
suite tests the slow answer as its own case. The script also tapped
the first "promise" button on the page, which another scene can
own; it taps hers by its id. The cut toast was seen in a
screenshot.

**Found by the mutation run.** On the first run 131 of 139 broken
lines were caught and none survived, but 8 crashed the suite where
they should have failed by name: with no question on the Desk, a
check read through a promise, a person or a list that was not
there. Each got a guard, and a stand-in nobody could mistake for
the trainee. After the timeline was corrected one line survived:
counting the quarter from the answer and not from the question. The
suite had no late answer to the quarter, and has one now. Seven
guards guarded nothing and were deleted: a filter on a list already
filtered, five checks for things that are always there, and a
rounding of a number that is always whole. On the final run, 153
of 153.

Suite_137 (280): the table; what each kind asks through the
real meeting, and when it has nothing to ask about; who is named,
and the same one every time; the older questions first; the promise
and what it is held to; a pass in each one's voice, the second in a
row, what ends the run; each way a question is overtaken; one

file and a reload; both tools' wiring; the three wordings of each

of letters said once. Mutation-checked against 153 broken lines,

A real-browser pass (38 checks, no page errors): the question
arrives through the real advance button, is promised with the real

weeks on; the micromanager's sheet is the verdict; a trend chaser

older browser passes, lockstep 0.11.27.

*Left for the next pieces.* The annual review at board week, with
trust bands that gate something. The exec-side ledger, and a

## §120 The annual review (SHIPPED v0.11.28 — §96 recommendation 7, the people upstairs and down the hall, part two)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The second of
recommendation 7's pieces, and the smaller half of it: the review,
in words. Probation is the next piece.

**The finding** (§96): "an annual review scene at board week in her
voice with trust bands that gate something visible". Counted first.
Board season is the company answering to its directors: once a
year, at week 46, three answers. The executive's own word on the
desk was a chip, "trust: watched", and nothing else. Over 200
careers and the tool's side worlds there were 424 board seasons:
124 at trusted, 160 solid, 92 watched, 26 thin, 22 gone. Trust went
under 20 in 31 of 203 worlds. Three long ones sat there for 180
weeks or more, with nothing said and nothing done.

Nothing here draws, and nothing here moves a number.

**When the directors have gone** she says three things, in order.

*One fact about the year, in the terms her kind keeps.*

- the profit hunter: the till, against the last review's. "The till
  holds 150. At the last review it held 100. That is the direction
  I am paid to like."
- the traditionalist: the best voice in the building, and whether
  the public has heard it yet.
- the micromanager: how many evaluation sheets she read, and who
  was first on more of them than anyone still in the building.
- the trend chaser: how many records we released, and how many were
  in the sound of the year they landed in.
- the visionary: the record that landed hardest, and whether anyone
  will remember it. A strong record or a sensation is remembered.
- the patient executive: "Year 2, and we are still here: one act
  under this roof, 5 trainees in the room."

The year is the last 48 weeks. The records we inherited are not
ours, and someone who has left the building is not counted.

*Where the desk stands.* The Desk's five words are the engine's now
(`KP.trustBand`), at the lines the chip always drew: trusted from
80, solid from 60, watched from 40, thin from 20, gone under it.
One sentence each. At thin: "The directors asked me whether you are
the right person for this desk. I said yes. I did not say it
quickly." At gone: "... I did not answer them. You should know
that."

*What that opens or closes.* The two gates trust already keeps,
said in words for the first time. Under 45 the board hears no
pitch: "Do not bring me a pitch this year." From 70, and not under
a founder's own board, the founding's gate is open: "And if
investors ever call me about you, I will tell them the truth. You
would like it." Between the two: "Bring me a pitch when you have
one."

**It follows the answer.** Each of the board's three answers is
followed by her review, read after what the answer did to trust. A
board left unanswered is reviewed all the same, after the point the
empty chair costs, in the letter that says so.

**A critical letter, and a line on the file.** `state.reviews`
keeps the latest twelve: the year, the week, who gave it, trust and
its word, the till, the sheets printed so far, and what she said.
The Desk's record lists them, the newest first, each under the name
of the chair who gave it.

**Found by the browser pass.** A board left unanswered is reviewed
three weeks later. Board week is week 46 of 48, so by then the year
has turned, and the review was filed under the next year: "Year 2,
and we are still here", about the year that had just ended. A
review is of the board season's year now.

**Found while writing the suite.** My fixtures took a year for 52
weeks. A year is 48. And reading what she would say made a ledger
on a file that had none; a read changes nothing now.

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.28): no review was ever filed. The
list opens empty and the count starts at zero.

**Measured.** In the census's own count over its 200 careers, 400
reviews, in 200 of 200 careers: 130 at trusted, 161 solid, 81
watched, 23 thin, 5 gone, the five in five careers. Two bands:
reviewed (200 of 200), reviewed with trust gone (5). No career
moved: every one of the census's 358 rows is v0.11.27's. Across the
long haul's eleven scenarios, 132 reviews: 31 at thin and 77 at
gone.

**Found by the mutation run.** On the first full run 87 of 89
broken lines were caught. One survived: no board was answered
late, so filing an answered board under the week’s year passed.
The suite has a late answer now. One crashed the suite where it
should have failed by name, in a check that split a sentence that
was not there, and got a guard. A partial run before it had four
more such crashes, each from an engine that threw inside an
answer; the suite takes a throw as an answer that failed. On the
final run, 89 of 89.

Suite_138 (110): the five words at their lines; each kind's
fact, with its edges; the three sentences in order at each word;
what it opens at each gate, and under a founder; a pure read; her
review after each of the board's answers, read after the answer; a
board answered late, and one not answered; the years on the file,
the last twelve kept, a new chair beside the old; the Desk through
the DOM stub with the real button; an old file and a reload; both
tools' wiring; a hundred and ten real weeks. Suite_131 holds the
letter to the list of letters said once. Mutation-checked against
89 broken lines, each caught by a named assertion in every suite

is a critical letter and a line on the record; a second career is
reviewed at trusted under another kind of executive; a third leaves

board sat in. Battery 138/138,
soak 40 clean, census 200 clean, longhaul 11 × 620 clean, e2e 137,

*Left for the next piece.* Probation: at gone, a dated directive,

## §121 The company's own file (SHIPPED v0.11.29 — §96 recommendation 7, the people upstairs and down the hall, part three)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The third of
recommendation 7's pieces: the history, and a page for it. The
anniversary and the year-end letter are later pieces.

**The finding** (§96): "The company's own file: a durable history
written by the rails that already fire". The company had no
history. Every first was a letter, read once and gone with the
inbox. The manager's title was set to "A&R Manager" at week one,
shown nowhere, and changed by nothing.

**Counted first** (§118's lesson). Over 40 careers the rails fire
in most of them: a first trophy's letter in 44 of 48 worlds, an
award win in 41, a red memo in 25, a succession in 3. And most of
what they mark is still on the state when the letter is gone: a
debut week, the week of the first trophy, each record's peak on the
chart, each act's honors, the settlement, the last bow, the
founding, the label that folded, the week the chair sat down.

**So the file is read, and not written** (`KP.companyFile`, pure).
Nothing writes to it, so nothing can drift from the game it
describes. An old save has its whole file the day it opens, with no
migration. Reading it changes nothing.

**The chapters**, each from the marker a rail leaves:

- the desk: "You took the A&R desk at Hanseong Culture Group." A
  founded label: "... opened its doors, out of HCG." After a second
  chance the desk's week is the new one.
- each debut, with the record of the debut week.
- the first number one on the scene chart: the company's, and this
  desk's when the company's came before it.
- the first music-show trophy: the company's, and this desk's. This
  desk's is dated by the record that won it; no rail keeps its
  week.
- each year-end honor, dated by its ceremony. The daesang is said
  in its own words.
- the first settlement; a last bow; a label that was dissolved
  before this one; a chair who sat down after the desk did.

Weeks before this desk's own are the company's past: the act it
inherited debuted, went to number one and won its trophies "before
your time". The file is in order of the weeks; within a week by
kind; two of a kind by their words.

**What the manager is called** is what the file proves under this
desk (`KP.managerTitle`): an A&R manager; a senior one once an act
has debuted under this desk; the head of A&R after a year-end honor
for any of our acts; an executive producer after a daesang. A
founder is a founder. What was won before this desk does not count.

## §122 The written record (SHIPPED v0.11.30 — §96 recommendation 7, the people upstairs and down the hall, part four)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The fourth of
recommendation 7's pieces: the chapters §121 could not read.

**The finding** (§121's own list): "Not on the file yet, because no
rail leaves a marker: the week of a succession before the last one,
a red episode, the fame breakthrough, and the week this desk won
its first trophy."

**Counted first** (§118's lesson), over 200 careers of three years
and the tool's side worlds, 203 worlds in all:

| the rail | fires | in worlds |
|---|---|---|
| the accountant’s memo | 200 | 124 |
| the staff meeting | 44 | 42 |
| the creditors’ letters | 4 | 4 |
| the final notice | 2 | 2 |
| a succession | 3 | 3 |
| the breakthrough | 2 | 2 |
| this desk’s first trophy | 203 | 203 |

Three things followed from the count.

- Of 200 red episodes, 92 lasted one week. A short week is not
  history. The bar is the staff meeting, four weeks behind, where
  every file on the roster takes the month the company could not
  pay.
- A chair's era runs five to seven years, so three years never see
  a succession: the three counted were in the tool's long side
  worlds. A long career sees several, and the file kept only the
  last.
- In all 203 worlds the file dated this desk's first trophy by the
  record that won it: one to three weeks before the night.

**The record** (`state.annals`). A mark is a week, a kind, and the
words it needs. It names what it is about and reads nothing else
off the state, so it outlives the act it names. The rail writes it
as it fires (`KP.fileMark`), and the file reads it. Five kinds:

- *chair*, at every succession: who sat down, after whom, and how
  long the chair had been held. "CEO Seo Hae-won took the chair.
  CEO Kang Min-ho had held it 8 years."
- *trophy*, the night of this desk's first trophy: the act, the
  stage, and the record it was promoting. "VINITE won Pop Wave with
  “Getaway”: the first under this desk." It is the first win by any
  act of ours since the desk began. Two stages in one week are one
  night.
- *breakthrough*, the first record to chart from a label nobody had
  heard of. Once a company.
- *red*, at the staff meeting: "The red weeks. The company fell far
  enough behind on what it owed that the staff held a meeting
  nobody called."
- *redCleared*, when the count runs back to zero, with how far it
  had gone: the staff meeting, the creditors' letters, or the final
  notice. An episode that never reached the meeting clears with its
  letter and no chapter.

A mark of any other kind is refused, loudly. The state's own check
names a mark of no kind, with no week, dated after today, or dated
before this desk began.

**The two firsts.** The marker still says when the company's first
trophy was won. The mark says whose night this desk's was. When
they are the same night it is said once, by the mark: "... the
first music-show trophy in the company's history."

**The record is the company's.** A founding or a last statement
closes it. The next label's record opens empty, as its lineups do.

**Found while building it: a founded label had no firsts.** The
last statement gives the dead label its first trophy and its first
daesang to keep (audit v0.11.3: "the next company's first is a
first"). The founding did not. At a founded label the first trophy
was never a first: no letter in capitals, no word in the boardroom,
no change in the members. Its first daesang got none of a first's
treatment. And §121's page listed the old house's first trophy as
the new label's past. The founding follows the last statement's law
now. *This changes play at a founded label*: its first trophy and
its first daesang are firsts. The census bot founds nothing, so no
census row can show it. The long haul's founder scenario founds a
label, and ran clean.

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.30).

- The record gets the marks the markers can still prove. The chair
  of the day, when she sat down after the desk did, with nobody
  named before her. The breakthrough, from the week an act still
  carries. This desk's first trophy as the file dated it until now,
  by the record that won it, in the words it had.
- A chair before the last, and a red episode already over, left
  nothing to read. An episode past its meeting on the day of the
  load gets its clearing and not its meeting.
- A label founded before this version gives the old house back its
  firsts. Its own first trophy is dated by the record that won it,
  its own first daesang by the honor, and either may be none.
- A desk that had already won gets no second first. The rail reads
  the acts' own last win, which an old save has, and not the
  record, which it did not.

**Measured: old saves.** 63 real careers were saved by v0.11.29 and
loaded by this build. The file reads word for word as it did in 61.
In 2 it is the same with the breakthrough added, which the old file
could not tell. None differs otherwise, and all 63 pass the state's

## §123 The bar holds its line (SHIPPED v0.11.31 — a repair found in a screenshot)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. Not on §96's
list. A fault seen in §122's browser pass, older than it, and
measured before it was touched.

**The finding.** The top bar is five things on one line: the
label's short name, the date, the advance button, the till, the
menu. They do not fit a phone. When they did not, every part gave
way at once: the date broke in the middle, and so did the till.

**Measured first**, in a real browser, over 360 cases: six widths
from 320 to 430 px; five names (the house's own, a short one, eight
letters, one with a hyphen, the widest nine); six tills from
nothing to six digits; the first year and the twelfth.

| on the old stylesheet | of 360 |
|---|---|
| the date broken onto a second line | 307 |
| the till broken onto a second line | 307 |
| a name broken at its hyphen | 71 |
| the bar wider than the screen | 51 |
| the bar taller than the room the page leaves it | 152 |

In those 152 the bar covered the top of the page. At 360 px, the
commonest Android width, the house's own name was broken with every
till. At 390 px it held only while the till had three digits.

**The rule now.** The date and the till never break in the middle,
and the button never gives up its words. When the bar is short of
room the left block gives, in this order:

1. the date drops under the name, whole;
2. the name is cut with three dots;
3. on a 320 px screen, last, the date is cut with three dots.

At 400 px and under the date is always under the name. At that
width it fitted beside the name only while the till had three
digits, and a bar that changes shape as the till grows reads as a
fault. Above 400 px the date is beside the name wherever one line
has room with 4 px between the parts, and under it wherever not.

Under 375 px the button gives up 6 px of padding. Under 350 px it
gives up more, and the till moves 6 px nearer the menu. Nothing
else changes size.

**What holds**, over the same 360 cases:

- nothing breaks, nothing overlaps, nothing runs off the screen,
  and at least 4 px stand between the button and its neighbours;
- the bar is 56 px tall at most, inside the 58 px the page leaves
  for it, and 54 px on one line as it was;
- at 360 px and wider the date is whole, the house's own name is
  whole, and an eight-letter name is whole;
- a name is cut only once the date is under it. At 360 px and wider
  only the widest nine letters are;
- at 320 px the date is whole in the first year up to a five-digit
  till, and cut in the twelfth from a four-digit one.

**What changed where nothing was wrong.** Of 288 of those cases
(without the hyphenated name), 52 fitted on one line before. 38
still do. In 14 the date is under the name now: 9 at 390 px and
under, by the rule, and 5 above it that had less than 8 px to
spare.

**The test is the repo's own** (`test/e2e_topbar.js`, 32
checks, three seconds). Layout cannot be checked in the DOM stub,
and the browser passes written for each release live outside the
repository. This one is in it, beside the walkthrough, and the
README's ritual lists it. Run against the old stylesheet it fails
15 of its checks by name.

**Found by the mutation run**, in four rounds.

- First run, 16 of 29 caught. Seven survivors were declarations
  that did nothing: a button told not to break that cannot, two
  minimums a clipped box already has, two line heights, two margins
  the narrow rules did not need. Deleted. Three pointed at two gaps
  in the test: a name with a hyphen, and text spilling out of a cut
  box. Three pointed at slack in the narrowest rule.
- Second run, 18 of 22. One more gap: a date that could not be cut
  ran over the button, and the test measured the wrong edge. One
  rule began at 380 px and was needed only under 375: it has its
  exact bound now. Two declarations had slack. Both were deleted,
  which broke the claim at 320 px, so one came back.
- Third run, 22 of 23. Nothing pinned where the tightest rule
  begins. Each band of widths is pinned exactly now.
- Fourth run, 23 of 23. On the final run, 23 of 23.

Eight declarations were deleted on the way and four gaps in the
test were closed. Six more had gone before the first run: they
repeated the defaults.

**A mistake on the way.** The narrow-screen rules were first
written above the button's own rule, which overrode them. They did
nothing, and the measurement showed it. They sit below it now, and
one broken line holds them there.

**No simulation changed.** Every one of the census's 363 rows is
v0.11.30's.

Battery 140/140, soak 40 clean, census 200 clean, longhaul 11 ×
620 clean, e2e 137, the top bar's own test (32), the fourteen
older browser passes, lockstep 0.11.31.

## §124 The year's close (SHIPPED v0.11.32 — §96 recommendation 7, the people upstairs and down the hall, part five)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The fifth of
recommendation 7's pieces: "a year-end letter at week 48 from the
company to itself as the yearly accounting". Taken ahead of the
anniversary: it reaches every career every year, and the
anniversary can reuse its reader.

**Counted first** (§118's lesson). Over 200 careers every week of
the year writes about twelve letters, and the inbox keeps five and
the critical ones. Week 48 writes fifteen and keeps five and a
half. A critical letter is added to the five and pushes nothing
out, and the feed has drawn its own stream since v0.10.30. So a
letter of words in the last week of the year lands every time and
moves no outcome.

**What the company writes to itself.** One letter, the company's,
critical, in the last week of the year: an opening, then four
things in a fixed order.

- *The headline*: one chapter of the year from the company's file
  (§121, §122), the first there is of these: the daesang, an honor,
  this desk's first number one, its first trophy, the breakthrough,
  a debut, a settlement, a new chair, a last bow, the arrears
  cleared, the red weeks. Of two of a kind, the file's last. A year
  with none: "No headline: a quiet year on the file."
- *The work*: the records that came out in the year, the best
  place any of them reached, and the trophies they won.
- *The people*: acts that debuted, people who signed, people who
  left, acts that took a last bow. A year with none: "nobody came
  and nobody went".
- *The books*: what came in, what went out, the till, and how far
  it moved.

"The year closes, and Hanseong Culture Group writes to itself, as
it does once a year. Year 1. The headline: VESPER4 took Artist of
the Year. The work: 4 records out, the best at number 1, and 5
trophies. The people: one act debuted, 3 signed. The books: 2231
came in and 1939 went out. The till closes at 412, up 292."

The opening is a family of three (§93), picked by hash and never
last year's.

**Read, not written** (`KP.yearAccount`, pure). The tallies are
read off the state, for this year or any before it: records by
their week, honors by their ceremony, signings and leavings by the
chapters on each person's file (§90). A year is the calendar's. A
desk that began inside it answers for its own weeks.

**Two things are kept** (`state.yearLedger`), because nothing else
holds them: what came in, which the flows add up as they happen
(corrected in v0.11.35, §127: the flows missed part of it, and it
is counted at the till now), and the till the year opened with. What went out is what came in
less what the till gained. The sum is given only when it adds up.
A till that gained more than came in was fed from outside the
books, and then the letter gives the till and how far it moved.

**The closed year is filed** (`state.years`, the last twelve) with
what was said. The company's page (§121) lists the years above
this desk's chapters, the newest first: "Y2 · 3 records · 14
trophies · 2 honors, the daesang among them · 1 debut · till 3975".

**A move closes them.** The years are the company's, like its
written record. A founded label's first year opens with its war
chest; a second chance's with what its door gave.

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.32). The years already closed under
this desk are filed from what the state still shows, with no till
and nothing said. The year in hand keeps its books from the day of
the load, so its letter gives the till and not the sum. The year
after is whole.

**Measured.** Over 200 careers the company closes 400 years, two a
career, and every letter lands. 394 of them have a headline, and
all 400 give the year's sum. They count 2,056 records, 2,495
trophies, 995 honors, 353 debuts, 1,287 signings and 12 leavings.
Two bands: a year closed (200 of 200), a year with a headline
(200). No career moved: every one of the 363 rows the census had
is v0.11.31's. Across the long haul's eleven scenarios, 620 weeks
each, 128 closed years are on file, 38 with a headline. On a wider
run with the tool's side worlds, 424 letters were written and 424
landed; the till in the letter was the till after the week in all
424; the three openings were used 138, 134 and 149 times, never
the same two years running; and the sum failed to add up in 1
year of 421, where a tool sets the till by hand.

**Found while building it.** The first rule for a whole year's
books asked only that they had opened by the year's first week. A
fixture that jumped a year without closing it then read last year's
opening till as this year's. The books count only when they opened
with the year. Two guards in the account guarded nothing, since a
week that is missing is in no year, and were deleted.

**Found by the mutation run.** On the first run 108 of 112 broken
lines were caught and none survived. Four crashed the suite where
they should have failed by name: it read the second filed year, a
list the backfill had not returned, and books a load had not
opened, each without looking first. Each read is guarded. On the
final run, 112 of 112.

**Found by the browser pass.** Nothing in this piece. One thing
older than it: in the Desk's inbox the tag DEVELOPMENT is wider
than its column and runs into the letter beside it. It is a later
piece.

Suite_141 (92): the year's books at a career's start; what the
flows add to them; each tally from its marker with its edges (the
year's first and last week, the week a desk began, a year still
running, any year before); the headline's order, step by step; the
books' three states; the letter's three openings and each of its
four parts in words; the close through its real week, twice, and
at the epilogue, and thirteen times for the twelve kept; fifty real
weeks to a letter in the inbox; a founding, a last statement and a
second chance; an old file's years, and the real load with the two
closes after it; the company's page through the DOM stub; the

said once. Mutation-checked against 112 broken lines, each caught
by a named assertion in every suite that owns the line. A
real-browser pass (23 checks, no page errors): the real advance
button turns the last week of a first year and the letter is on
the Desk with its headline, work, people and books; forty-eight
real weeks on the second year closes with another opening and the

closed years listed without a till, and three real weeks on its

## §125 The tag takes the line (SHIPPED v0.11.33 — a repair found in a screenshot)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. Not on §96's
list. A fault seen in §124's browser pass, older than it, and
counted and measured before it was touched.

**The finding.** A letter's row is a tag in a 62 px column with the
letter beside it. The tag is one word, the kind of the letter, and
it cannot break. A word wider than the column ran on into the
letter.

**Counted first.** Over 200 careers the engine writes fourteen
tags, and the source holds no others. Three are longer than the
column: DEVELOPMENT, RELATIONSHIP and BREAKTHROUGH.

| over 200 careers, 29,440 weeks | a tag run into its letter |
|---|---|
| weekly reports with at least one | 29,423 (99.9%) |
| rows of the weekly report | 71,350 of 214,196 (33.3%) |
| weeks with at least one on the Desk | 17,737 (60.2%) |
| rows of the Desk's inbox | 28,068 of 411,359 (6.8%) |

The weekly report shows it most. Its rows from the spotlight, two
a week, are tagged DEVELOPMENT.

**Measured**, in a real browser, at six widths from 320 to 430 px,
in the face the app names and in two others. The column is fixed,
so the fault was the same at every width.

| the tag | its word | into the letter |
|---|---|---|
| BREAKTHROUGH | 92 px | 19 px |
| DEVELOPMENT | 83 px | 10 px |
| RELATIONSHIP | 82 px | 9 px |
| EXECUTIVE | 64 px | none, 9 px short of it |
| SHOWCASE | 64 px | none, 9 px short of it |

The other nine fit the column. In the widest face measured the
three ran 16 to 27 px into the letter, and SHOWCASE stopped 5 px
short of it. The other mail rows were measured too, 654 cases a
face: a date, a year, a record's kind, a save slot. None runs past
its column.

**The rule now.** The letter starts 73 px in on every row, where it
did. A tag up to 69 px wide stands beside its letter, so 4 px
always stand between them. A wider tag takes the line, whole, and
its letter starts directly under it, in its own column.

Eleven of the fourteen tags sit where they sat, and so does every
letter. A row whose tag takes the line is 15.5 px taller. That is
38 px on an average weekly report, and 15 px on the Desk.

**Why not a wider column.** A column wide enough for BREAKTHROUGH
in the widest face measured would take 31 px from every letter on
every row, a seventh of its width on a 320 px phone, to seat three
words in fourteen. And it would hold only the words written so
far. The rule holds for any word in any face.

**Why not shorter words.** The tags are the game's own words. A
shorter one is the owner's call, not a repair.

**The test is the repo's own** (`test/e2e_mail.js`, 41 checks,
three seconds), the third browser test, and the README's ritual
lists it. It holds the rule for the fourteen tags and for a ladder
of 49 made-up words whose widths step across the line a quarter px
at a time, so the line is pinned to the px and the rule is held for
a tag nobody has written yet. Each is measured in the Desk's inbox
and in the weekly report at six widths, 756 rows. Then the other
mail rows, which must keep the column they had; eight real weeks
by the real button; and the company's page, a file and the system
sheet as a real career shows them. Run against the stylesheet as
shipped in v0.11.32 it fails 11 of its checks by name.

**Found by the mutation run.** Nothing. On the first run 17 of 17
broken lines were caught by name. One thing went before it: the
letter's rule first named its grow and shrink as well as its
basis. Both were the defaults, and a broken line for either would
have changed nothing. On the final run, 17 of 17.

**Found by the browser pass.** Nothing in this piece. One thing
older than it: on a 320 px phone the Desk's strip of five tabs is
12 px wider than the screen, the last tab is cut, and the page
slides sideways. It is the next piece.

**No simulation changed.** Every one of the census's 365 rows is
v0.11.32's.

A real-browser pass (32 checks, no page errors): real weeks by
