## §126 The tabs keep to the screen (SHIPPED v0.11.34 — a repair found in a screenshot)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. Not on §96's
list. A fault seen in §125's browser pass, older than it, and
measured before it was touched.

**The finding.** A strip of tabs is one line of equal parts, and a
tab cannot be narrower than its word. When the words did not fit,
the strip ran on past its box and past the screen, and the whole
page slid sideways with it.

**Measured first**, in a real browser: every strip a real career
shows, ten of them in 41 states, at ten widths from 280 to 430 px.
The narrow widths matter. A phone with its page zoom raised is
narrower than 320 px.

| the Desk's five tabs, as shipped | |
|---|---|
| the screen they need for one line | 352 px |
| at 340 px | 9 px out of their box |
| at 320 px | 12 px off the screen, the last tab cut |
| at 300 px | 32 px off the screen |
| at 280 px | 52 px off the screen |

One more strip ran out of its box: the four training loads, by 4
px at 280 px. The other eight fit at every width. In the widest
face measured the Desk's tabs need 376 px.

The count on Offers was counted too. Over 200 careers it shows in
42% of weeks and never passes 8. It sits under the word, so it
changes nothing about what the strip needs.

**The rule now.**

1. A strip of tabs never runs off. When its tabs do not fit one
   line, the last of them take the next.
2. Under 360 px a tab gives up 2 px of padding on each side and
   most of its letter-spacing. The Desk's five tabs then need 311
   px, so on a 320 px phone they are on one line with 9 px to
   spare.
3. At 360 px and wider nothing changes.

**What holds.**

- from 280 to 430 px no tab runs off the screen or out of its box,
  no word spills out of its tab, and no page is wider than the
  screen;
- the Desk's five tabs are on one line from 312 px, with a count
  on Offers or without, and under that the fifth takes a second
  line;
- a file's five tabs are on one line at 320 px, where the fifth
  sat alone on a second;
- at 360, 390 and 430 px every strip compared is pixel for pixel
  what v0.11.33 drew, 15 of 15.

**The test is the repo's own** (`test/e2e_strips.js`, 23
checks, eighteen seconds), the fourth browser test, and the
README's ritual lists it. It walks every strip a new career shows,
with each count on Offers, at eight widths from 280 to 430 px, and
twelve made-up strips of three to nine tabs of short, middling and
long words. The law it holds is free of the face: a strip is on
one line wherever its tabs fit one at their narrowest, and on more
wherever they do not. Run against the stylesheet as shipped in
v0.11.33 it fails 9 of its checks by name.

**Found by the mutation run.** On the first run 12 of 13 broken
lines were caught. The one that got through set the narrow tab's
letter-spacing to none. A spacing of none reads as the word
"normal" and not as a number, and the check let a reading that was
not a number pass. It fails one now. Second run, 13 of 13. On the
final run, 13 of 13.

**Mistakes on the way.** Two, both caught by measuring.

- The first narrow rule began under 350 px and kept more of the
  letter-spacing. It left the Desk's tabs 2 px short at 320 px,
  where they wrapped. And it made them wrap at 350 px, where the
  old strip had run 2 px out of its box unseen. The widths had
  been worked out by hand. Measured to the tenth of a px, the rule
  begins under 360 px and gives up more.
- The narrow rule first restated the tab's top and bottom padding.
  A broken line there would have changed nothing the test sees. It
  names the two sides only now.

One line went. The file's strip carried its own instruction to
wrap, and every strip has it now.

**Left as it is.** The count on Offers sits under the word at
every width, as it has since v0.11.6, and the strip is one line
taller in the weeks it shows. That is a look and not a fault, and
it is the owner's to call. The bottom nav was measured too. It
holds down to 260 px, with its last word 3 px from the edge at 320
px.

**No simulation changed.** Every one of the census's 365 rows is
v0.11.33's.

A real-browser pass (28 checks, no page errors): a new career
through the front door on a 320 px phone has the Desk's five tabs
whole, on one line, in their box; real weeks by the real button
put a real count on Offers and the line holds; on a 300 px screen
the fifth tab takes a second line and nothing runs off; a real
career saved by v0.11.29 shows its Desk, a file, the studio and
the industry page under the rule; and the strips at 360 px and
wider are compared pixel for pixel with the last build.

## §127 The till's one door in (SHIPPED v0.11.35 — a repair of §124's books)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. Not on §96's
list. A defect in §124, shipped in v0.11.32, found by the first
look at the next piece and counted before it was touched.

**The defect.** At the year's close the company writes "X came in
and Y went out". §124 fed X from the quarter's books: every entry
above nothing was taken as money that came in. The books were
never that. They enter some takings net of their cost, and some
not at all:

- a unit era's takings and its cost were in no book;
- the lightstick, the fan meeting and the last concert were
  entered as one net figure;
- the monthly stipend was netted against the month's bills in one
  line, and in no book.

So X was short, and Y, which is X less what the till gained, was
short by the same amount. The till's close and its move were
always right.

**How it got through.** §124 checked that the sum "added up", and
the check was that Y was not below nothing. That catches a till
fed from outside. It cannot catch a count that is short.

**Counted first.** Over 200 careers and their side worlds, 424
years closed:

| | |
|---|---|
| years whose letter said too little came in | 424 of 424 |
| what the letters counted | 1,096,634 |
| what the tills took | 1,265,633 |
| short by | 13.4% |
| in the middle year | 14.2% |
| in the worst year | all of it |

Every year was short, because every year takes in its stipends.
In the worst year the books saw nothing come in at all.

One real career, the same year, before and after: "1453 came in
and 750 went out. The till closes at 5283, up 703." and "1597 came
in and 894 went out. The till closes at 5283, up 703." The 144
between them is twelve stipends.

**The rule now.** Every credit to the till passes through one
function, `KP.takeIn`, and the year's sum counts it there. The
books keep their own entries and no longer feed the year. What
went out is still what came in less what the till gained, and now
that is every debit.

Thirty-four lines in twenty-one files go through the door. Two
lines that netted are two steps now: the stipend comes in and then
the month's bills go out, and the last night's takings come in and
then its cost goes out. The till is a whole number at every step,
so the arithmetic is the same to the last bit, and no career moved.

**Held three ways.**

- *By the source.* The suite reads every file of the engine and
  the screens. One line adds to the till, and it is the door's
  own. Every plain assignment to the till is one of six that set a
  company's till when it opens or folds, or one of five clamps that
  can only lower it.
- *By the suite.* A unit era, the lightstick, the last concert and
  the month's turn each go through their real line with the till
  watched from outside the engine. Two real years close, and in
  each what the letter counts is what the watched till saw.
- *By a new audit* (`tools/audit_till.js`). It plays the soak with
  the till of every world watched and asks of every rise where it
  came from: the door, a company's opening till, the tool's own
  hand, or a line it then names. Run on the tree as shipped in
  v0.11.34 it names 29 lines.
  Run on this one: 22,010 credits came through the door, 489,420 in
  all, and the year’s ledgers took every one.

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.35). What the year in hand has
counted cannot be made whole, so its books open again on the day
of the load. Its letter gives the till and not the sum, and the
year after is whole. The years already filed keep the sums they
were given, which are short, and the letters already in the inbox
are not rewritten.

**The quarterly statement is untouched.** It never claimed a
total: it gives each stream net and puts the rest under
operations, and that still adds up.

**No simulation changed.** The census's output is v0.11.34's to
the byte. The long haul says the same of every scenario. One save
is a kilobyte larger: at a blank-page label the stipend had kept
letters from giving a sum, and they carry one now.

**Found while building it.** The door first raised the till and
then opened the year's books if they were not open. Books opened
that way would have opened with the credit already in the till and
counted it as well. The books open first now, and a broken line
holds the order.

**Found by the mutation run.** On the first run 22 of 23 broken
lines were caught. The one that got through broke the audit
itself: the suite only read the tool's text. The audit is a module
now. The suite takes its watcher and its report and holds them on
a small case of its own: a credit through the door, a world loaded
from a save, an opening till, a line that goes round the door, a
door that miscounts, and an audit that saw nothing. Second run, 31
of 31. On the final run, 31 of 31.

**Mistakes on the way**, each caught by a first run.

- The suite's fixture for the month's turn looked for it among the
  phases a module registers. It is in the driver's own list. The
  fixture plays real weeks at an empty label now.
- The fixture for two real years played an idle desk, and an idle
  desk is dissolved in its twenty-eighth week. It has a till deep
  enough for two idle years now.
- The same fixture looked for both letters at the end, in an inbox
  that keeps sixty. Each is checked the week it lands.
- The probe that counted the defect took a company's opening till
  for a credit, twice.

Suite_142 (51): the source held to one door; the door's own
arithmetic and its order; the books left to themselves; the four
credits the books missed, each through its real line; two real
years against a watched till; the letter from a till moved by
hand; an old file from v0.11.34, one from before the year's close,
and one of this version; the audit on its own small case. Suite_141
holds the count to the door. Mutation-checked against 31 broken
lines, each caught by a named assertion in every suite that owns
the line. A real-browser pass (15 checks, no page errors): a
real career saved by v0.11.34 in the middle of its fourth year
opens with its books opened again and its three filed years as
they were; twenty-eight real weeks by the real button close that
year with the till alone, every credit the watched till saw having
been counted; forty-eight more close the next with a sum that is
what the watched till saw come in and go out.

620 clean, the till audit clean, e2e 137, 32, 41 and 23, the
seventeen older browser passes, lockstep 0.11.35.

## §128 The label's birthday (SHIPPED v0.11.36 — §96 recommendation 7, the people upstairs and down the hall, part six)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The sixth of
recommendation 7's pieces: "a company anniversary on the founding
week reusing the group anniversary's family". Set aside once, for
§127's repair, which its first look uncovered.

**Counted first.** A founding week is on file for a founded label
and for no other company: a salaried desk's house was there before
the career began. So the piece reaches founded labels only.

| | |
|---|---|
| census careers that ever live at a founded label | 0 of 200 |
| long-haul weeks lived at one | 2,802 of 6,817 |
| labels in the long haul | 5 |
| birthdays that come round there | 56 |
| of those, in the week the year closes | 12 |
| of those, while a last statement waits | 0 |

On a birthday week the inbox writes about five letters and keeps
four, and a critical letter lands on top of those. The census
cannot see this piece at all. It is held by its suite and by the
long haul.

**What the label writes.** One letter, the company's, critical, in
the week its doors opened, each year: an opening, then and now,
and a last line.

- *Then*: what it came out of, if it came out of a house, and what
  was in the till the day it opened. Both are on the founding.
- *Now*: the acts on stage, the people under contract, the
  trophies and honors since the doors opened, and the till.

"It is one year to the week since HOMEWARD opened its doors. It
started out of HCG with 278 in the till. Today it has no acts,
nobody under contract, no trophies on the shelf, and 304 in the
till. The first lease is framed by the lift now. The staff signed
the back of it."

The opening is a family of three (§93), picked by hash and never
last year's, and each opening has its own last line. The age is
said in words up to twelve.

**Then and now, not the year.** A blank page's birthday falls in
the week its year closes, and the year's letter has already
counted the year. So the birthday counts nothing of the year. It
sets what the label started with beside what stands there today.

**Read, not written** (`KP.labelAge`, `KP.labelStanding`, pure).
The founding is on file. The shelf is read off the records and the
honors since it, with the file's own readers (§121). One thing is
kept: which opening was used, on the founding itself.

**Words only.** An act's anniversary lifts its members' morale
(§41). The label's moves nothing. The census’s output
is v0.11.35’s to the byte, and the long haul says the same of
every scenario but for its new count and the size of a save.

**Old saves.** Nothing to migrate: the birthday is counted from
the founding a save already holds. A label that has kept no
opening says its next one as any first.

**Found while building it.** Two guards guarded nothing and were
deleted. The age asked that the week be after the founding, and
the founding's own week is nought years by the arithmetic. The
shelf asked that a record be no later than today, and no record
is. And §127's defect: the first look at a blank page's birthday
showed its year's letter giving no sum.

**Found by the mutation run.** Nothing. On the first run 39 of
39 broken lines were caught by name, and on the final run the
same.

**Mistakes on the way.**

- The first count was wrong: 70 birthdays in 3,402 weeks. The long
  haul plays copies of a career side by side to see that two runs
  agree, and the count took those copies for careers. The long
  haul's own count, 56, did not match it, and that is how it was
  seen.
- Two of the suite's own expectations were wrong on its first run.
  One joined a value that was not there, and one counted the
  birthday week itself among the weeks before it.

**The long haul's check, tried.** The suite only reads the long
haul's text, and §127 showed what that is worth. So the check was
run against an engine whose birthday comes a week late.
The first trial found nothing. The check had asked the engine when
a birthday was due, and a wrong engine agreed with itself. The
check works the week out from the founding now. The second trial
stops at the long haul’s limit, 61 problems, and every one is the
birthday’s: 21 birthdays that came round with no letter, 20 letters
in a week that is no birthday, and 20 that give the wrong age.

Suite_143 (48): the age at a salaried desk, a blank page and a
label founded in the middle of a year; the standing from its
markers, with an act that took its last bow, a lineup not yet
debuted, a ceremony before the founding and one after, and an old
file that does not say what the label opened with; the letter's
three openings each with its last line, never last year's, and
every part of then and now in words; the week it comes round, the
weeks it does not, a salaried desk, a label at its last statement,
and its place after the year's close; real weeks at a blank page
through two birthdays, at a label founded in the middle of a
career, and through a second chance by the blank door and by the
salaried one; the save; the list of letters said once. Suite_131
holds the letter to that list. Mutation-checked against 39
broken lines, each caught by a named assertion in every suite that
owns the line. A real-browser pass (14 checks, no page

real label founded under v0.11.35 opened and played to its first
birthday, a year to the week after the founding; and thirty real
weeks at a salaried desk, across a year's close, with no birthday
letter in any.

## §129 The greenlights on the record (SHIPPED v0.11.37 — §96 recommendation 7, the people upstairs and down the hall, part seven)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The seventh of
recommendation 7's pieces: "a small exec-side ledger so the pitch
she granted and the greenlight honoured are remembered in words".
The other half of that sentence, a succession that hands over a
record and not a number, is a piece of its own and comes next.

**Counted first.** A greenlight is never thrown away. Each one is
on the state with the week it was given, where it came from and
what came of it. No screen listed them.

| | |
|---|---|
| census careers given at least one | 195 of 200 |
| greenlights in all | 347 |
| kept | 169 |
| left dark | 24 |
| still open when the census stops | 154 |
| that came from a pitch | 192 |
| from the turn of the generation | 148 |
| from the board's own read of the room | 7 |
| pitches taken upstairs, and refused | 326, 134 |
| long-haul careers given at least one | 7 of 11 |
| greenlights there | 68: 2 kept, 59 left dark, 6 open, 1 set aside |

So nearly every career has something to list, and most have two.

**What the record says.** One row for each on the Desk's Record
tab, the newest first: the week it was given, the chair who gave
it, what was greenlit, where it came from, and what came of it.
From a real career:

"CEO Moon Sang-chul greenlit a new group. It came from your pitch.
*kept* ELRISE II debuted Aug · Wk 4 · Y2, inside the window."

"CEO Moon Sang-chul greenlit a new group. It came from the
generational directive. *left dark* The window closed Jan · Wk 2 ·
Y5 with no stage in it."

An open one says when its window runs to. The section sits after
the promises and before the annual review, and a desk that was
given nothing has no section.

**Read, not written** (`KP.greenlights`, pure). Two names are kept
that nothing held. The chair's is stamped on a greenlight as it is
given, the way a promise to the chair and an annual review already
carry theirs. The act's is stamped as its debut keeps the
greenlight. So a row is read off the greenlight alone, and needs
no act on the file. The words for what was greenlit are the ones
the pitch's own note uses, from one helper.

**Found while counting: a greenlight crossed the wall.** A founding
and a second chance set aside every open promise and left the open
greenlights as they were. So a greenlight the old house gave stayed
open at the next house, and was kept or left dark there.

| | |
|---|---|
| desk changes in the long haul | 4 |
| of those, with a greenlight open that day | 1 |
| desk changes in the census | 2 |
| of those, with a greenlight open that day | 0 |

In the long haul's founder career the old house gave a greenlight
in week 142. The label was founded in week 151, and in week 161
its first act "kept" the old house's greenlight, and the label's
chair wrote that it "was kept, on time, with a stage in it".

One real saved career, a label founded in week 141 that still
carried the old house's directive, played the same forty weeks
before and after. Before, in week 195 the label's chair says "We
greenlit a project and the floor stayed dark", and trust falls
from 54 to 51 for a greenlight the label never gave. After, the
directive is set aside when the save loads, nothing is said, and
in week 201 trust stands at 52 where it stood at 49.

**The rule now.** A greenlight is the house's that gave it. When
the desk moves to another house, one still open is set aside
unjudged (`KP.closeGreenlights`), as an open promise already was.
The calendar upstairs opens with the new house: a pitch closes it
for eight weeks and a refusal on doctrine for forty-eight, and the
new house's board heard neither. The record lists this desk's own,
from the week the desk began.

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.37). Each greenlight is named as far
as the written record proves who sat in the chair that week
(`KP.chairProven`). With no change of chair on the record it is
the chair sitting now. Before or after a change it is the one the
mark names. In the week of a change two people sat there, so
nobody is proven and the row says "The chair of the day". One
that was kept is named for its act while the file still holds the
act, and else its row says "An act". A greenlight the last house
gave that is still open is set aside.

**The state's own check.** One line in `KP.validateState`: a
greenlight still open was given under this desk.

**What moved.** The census’s output is v0.11.36’s to the byte: no
desk change there had a greenlight open. In the long haul one
career moved, by one letter: the founder’s label no longer writes
that the old house’s greenlight was kept. Every scenario’s line is
the same but for the new count.

**The long haul's check, tried.** The suite only reads the long
haul's text, and §127 showed what that is worth. So the long haul
keeps books of its own: which greenlights it has seen, who sat in
the chair when each appeared, and which were on file the day the
desk moved. It asks the engine for none of that. It was then run
against four engines broken on purpose.
A founding that leaves the old house’s greenlights open. A
greenlight that carries no name. A record that lists the last
house’s. A record that says every greenlight is still open. Each
run stopped at the long haul’s limit, 61 problems, and every one of
them names a greenlight. On the tree as it stands the same run is
clean.

**Found by the mutation run.** Nothing. On the first run 58 of 58
broken lines were caught by name. The repair told below made the
list 63, and 63 of 63 were caught on the next run and on
the final one.

**Mistakes on the way.**

- The first draft read a kept row's act off the file. A label at
  its last statement has no acts on the file while it waits for a
  door. There the record threw, and the state's check raised a
  false alarm. No run found it: no dissolved career in the census
  or the long haul had a kept greenlight. It was found by reading
  the diff while the first check chain ran, and the chain was
  stopped. The debut stamps the act's name now, the record reads
  nothing but the greenlight, and the check that leaned on the
  acts is gone. The suite dissolves a label with a kept greenlight
  and reads its record.
- Three of the suite's own expectations were wrong on their first
  runs: two week names worked out by hand, and the name of the
  field that holds the Desk's tab.
- The first count took three of the census’s side worlds for
  careers: 203 worlds, not 200. The three were given nothing, so
  the figures above did not move. The second count matched no
  career at all on its first run: it looked for a career by the
  state’s own seed, which is a number.

**Found and not fixed here.** A screenshot from the browser pass

## §130 The review's own year (SHIPPED v0.11.38 — a repair of §120's annual review)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. Not on §96's
list. A defect in §120, shipped in v0.11.28, seen in a screenshot
from §129's browser pass and counted before it was touched.

**The defect.** When the directors have gone the executive says one
fact about the year. Two of the six kinds hold the year against
the review before it: the profit hunter the till, the micromanager
the evaluation sheets. §120 took "the review before it" to be the
last one on the file, whoever gave it. After a founding or a
second chance that is the last house's review. And with no review
on the file, the micromanager's count began at the career's first
sheet.

So at a new house a profit hunter held the label's till against
the old house's, and a micromanager counted sheets that the old
house's floor was read on.

**How it got through.** §120's suite never moved a desk, and the
reviews it put on the file carried no week.

**Counted first.**

| | long haul | census |
|---|---|---|
| reviews given | 132 | 400 |
| given after a desk change | 44 | 4 |
| the first under a new desk | 4 | 2 |
| whose "last review" was the last house's | 2 | 0 |
| that said something untrue | 1 | 1 |

Both untrue ones were a micromanager's count: "I read 6
evaluation sheets this year" at a house that had held none, and "I
read 11" at a house that had held 4. No profit hunter sat at a new
desk's first review in either run. That one was seen on a real
saved career. So the defect is rare. It needs a desk change, and
then one of two kinds of chair at the next review.

**One real career, before and after.** A save from week 141,
walked out of that week to found a label. The label's first
review, a week later:

"The till holds 320. At the last review it held 652. I am paid to
notice the direction."

"The till holds 320. Next year I will have a number to hold it
against."

The 652 was the old house's till, at the old house's last review.

**The rule now.** The year is held against the last review given
under this desk. A desk's own review is never in the week the desk
began, so that week's is the last house's. With none of its own,
the profit hunter says there is no number yet, and the
micromanager counts from the sheets the career had seen when the
desk began. That count is noted when the desk moves
(`KP.evalDeskOpens`, beside §129's sweep). The name the
micromanager gives, the one who "was first on more of them", is
taken from this house's sheets only.

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.38). At a desk that has moved, what
the career had seen when the desk began is worked out: the
ledger's count less the showcases held since, which are on the
trainees' own histories. The histories keep twelve months, and a
desk older than that has a review of its own to count from. The
reviews already filed keep what they said, and so do their
letters: a file that holds the wrong sentence goes on holding it,
and its next review is right.

**What moved.** No simulation changed: the repair is in what is
said. The census’s output is v0.11.37’s to the byte, and the long
haul says the same of every scenario but for its new count. Two
sentences read differently. In the census one career’s chair says
“I read 4 evaluation sheets this year” where it said 11. In the
long haul one says that no sheet reached the desk where it said 6.

**The long haul's check, tried.** The long haul keeps its own
count of the sheets since the last mark, which is the desk's last
review or the day the desk moved. It reads the ledger week by week
and holds a micromanager's sentence to that count. It was run
against four engines broken on purpose.
A review held against whichever review came before it. A count that
begins at the career’s first sheet. A second chance that notes
nothing. A review that does not note what the career had seen. Each
was flagged, the first three by the chair’s own sentence: “6” and
“16” at a house that had held none. On the tree as it stands the
same run is clean.
It does not hold the profit hunter's till. None of its eleven
careers seats one at a new desk's first review, so that check
could not be tried there. The suite and the browser pass hold it.

**Found by the mutation run.** Nothing. On the first run 27 of
27 broken lines were caught by name, and on the final run the
same.

**Mistakes on the way.**

- Six checks of §120's own suite failed when the engine began to
  read a review's week: five of its fixtures put reviews on the
  file with no week, or in week 1. A filed review always carries
  its week. The fixtures were given weeks, and nothing else in
  that suite was touched.
- Two of the new suite's expectations were wrong on its first run:
  a sentence cut one character short.
- The browser pass was wrong twice on its first run. A review is
  filed when the board season is answered, not when it opens. And
  the pass switched the app out of the epilogue by hand, which left
  the week's button hidden. The third career is taken through the
  door before the browser opens it now.

## §131 The handover (SHIPPED v0.11.39 — §96 recommendation 7, the people upstairs and down the hall, part eight)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The eighth of
recommendation 7's pieces, and the second half of the sentence
§129 began: "and succession transfers a record instead of a
number".

**Counted first.** When a chair's era ends, the next one is given
35 parts in 100 of the distance the old trust stood from 55, a
letter, and a first meeting. The letter said the new executive
"has read the file — every number, every promise, every year". The
meeting said "{the one who left} rated you highly. I inherited the
rating, not the reasons."

| | |
|---|---|
| changes of chair in the census's 200 careers | 0 |
| in the long haul's 11 | 12 |
| the meeting said "rated you highly" | 12 of 12 |
| of those, the desk stood at thin or gone | 12 of 12 |
| the last review the one who left gave read gone | 11 of 12 |
| greenlights under the chairs who left | 54: 2 kept, 45 left dark, 7 open |
| promises upstairs under them | 43: 10 kept, 15 broken, 3 set aside, 15 open |
| the number, the day before and the day after | 0 to 36 nine times; 32 to 47; 25 to 45; 18 to 42 |

So the line was said every time, and every time it was untrue. The
census never lives long enough to hear it: no career there reaches
a change of chair. This piece is held by its suite and by the long
haul.

**What the next chair is handed.** The record under the one who
leaves (`KP.chairRecord`, pure), read off what the file already
holds:

- the greenlights that chair gave, and how many were kept and left
  dark (§129's own rows, by the name each carries);
- the promises made upstairs while they sat, and how many were
  kept and broken. A promise to the chair's own question carries
  their name (§119). Any other is theirs by the week, as far as the
  written record proves who sat (§129);
- the word of the last review they gave under this desk (§120).

The letter says it in one sentence. From a real career:

"The new executive has read the file CEO Moon Sang-chul left: 2
greenlights, one kept and one left dark; 5 promises upstairs, one
kept and 3 broken; and a last review that read “gone”."

A chair who gave no review leaves "no review of theirs on the
file", and no word is put in their mouth.

**The rating, named truly.** The first meeting carries the rating
the next chair inherits: the last review's word, or, from a chair
who gave no review, where the desk stood the day they left. The
line has five forms now, one for each of the Desk's words:

| | |
|---|---|
| trusted | rated you as highly as this house rates anyone |
| solid | rated you well |
| watched | was still reading your work twice |
| thin | kept you on, and not by much |
| gone | had stopped answering for you |

One real career, the same weeks, before and after. The desk stood
at 0 and the last review read gone. Before: "CEO Moon Sang-chul
rated you highly." After: "CEO Moon Sang-chul had stopped
answering for you." The rest of the line is as it was: "I
inherited the rating, not the reasons."

**The number is untouched.** Trust carries as it did. Whether the
record should move it is the owner's to call, and it is put below.

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.39). A first meeting already open on
the Desk was opened with the old line. It is given the last
review's word, so what it says now is true. Where the one who left
gave no review the meeting is left as it was: the number has been
carried since, and proves nothing.

**What moved.** No simulation changed: the piece is in what is
said. The census’s output is v0.11.38’s to the byte, since no
career there changes its chair. The long haul says the same of
every scenario but for its new count, and writes the same number of
letters: twelve of them read differently.

**The long haul's check, tried.** The long haul keeps books of its
own for each chair of a desk: the greenlights and the promises
upstairs it saw appear while they sat, and the last review it saw
them give. When the chair changes it holds the letter's six
figures, its review and the meeting's rating to those books. It
was run against seven engines broken on purpose.
Kept and left dark the wrong way round. Every promise upstairs
counted for whoever leaves. A meeting that carries no rating. A
letter that says nothing of what was left. A rating read off the
number and not the review. The oldest review given for the last. A
letter that names the one who arrives. Each was flagged by name, in

**Found by the mutation run.** One guard that guarded nothing. The

## §132 The chairs stay with the house (SHIPPED v0.11.40 — a repair of the founding, found counting the staff)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. Not on §96's
list. A defect in the founding, as old as the staff (v0.10.6,
§79), found while counting for the next piece of recommendation
7, the staff given years.

**The defect.** The card for the door says "everything you built
stays behind — as the competition". The founding leaves the
groups, the roster, the record, the greenlights and the sheets
with the old house (§122, §129, §130). It never swept the staff.
A founded label opened with the old house's chairs still sat in
its building: their names, how well known they were, their weeks
in the chair counted from the old house, and "here since the
beginning — the résumé is this company" on their files. The
dissolution has always swept them, under a comment that says it
copies "the founding's sweep". The founding never got the line.

**How it got through.** The census's player never founds a label.
The long haul founds one, and nothing there kept books of who
sat.

**Counted first.**

| | |
|---|---|
| foundings in the census's 200 careers | 0 |
| in the long haul's 11 | 1, with 8 chairs carried |
| in forty founder careers run for this | 40 |
| chairs sat in those forty labels the day they opened | 317 |
| of them carried from the old house | 317, every one |
| by the trades' word for them | 61 a name, 69 known, 65 unknown, 122 working |

**The rule now.** A house keeps its staff when the desk moves. The
next building opens with four of its own, the vocal coach, the
dance coach, the performance director and the scout: new people,
working names, sat from the week the doors open. The A&R, the
marketing and the studio chairs are open, as at any beginning.
One mint does it for the founding and for a second chance alike
(`KP.seatBuilding`), and with the chairs go the posting that was
up and the market's memory of the last ones. The founding letter
says it and names the four. From a real career:

"Its staff stayed with it: Coach Shin, Coach Nam, Director Baek
and Scout Yoon took the bet on you, and sit in the new label’s
chairs."

The card for the door names what stays behind before it is
walked through: "the groups, the trainees, the staff".

**One real career, before and after.** The same founding, in week
164, with 314 in the till. Before: eight chairs sat, six of them
names the trades know and two known, every one filed as sat
since before the label existed. Letting them all go would have
cost 280 of the 314. After: four working chairs, just arrived.

**What it does to a founded label.** The same forty careers, with
and without the repair.

| | carried | its own four |
|---|---|---|
| chairs sat the day the label opened | 7.9 | 4 |
| weeks to the first debut | 10.1 | 10.0 |
| debuted inside the 72 weeks | 39 of 40 | 40 of 40 |
| the first record's reception | 43.3 | 45.1 |
| weeks in the red | 5.0 | 3.2 |
| labels that dissolved later | 11 | 8 |
| calls from outside for a chair | 49 | 19 |

So a label that opens with its own four is not the harder start.
The names that came across drew the calls: 40 of the 49 were for a
carried chair, and a raise costs 25 from a till of about 200. Forty
careers are few. The difference in dissolutions is inside what
another run of luck gives, and is set down as measured, not as a
finding.

**Old saves** (migration 0.11.40). A label founded before this
version has lived with the people who came across, and keeps
them: the same names, as well known as they were, worth what
they were worth. What is corrected is what the file says. Each
is filed as sat in this label's chair since the week it opened.
The line "here since the beginning" comes off the résumé, or
"here before you" where the old house was a second one, and one
true line goes on: "came across from HCG at the founding". The
records a studio chair made for the old house stay on their
file.

**Records for this house, counted one way.** The Building tab
said "1 record for this house" of a producer whose one record
was the old house's, and the second chair opened on such
records. The card, the second chair's gate and its own card now
count the same thing (`KP.seatMade`): the records that landed
after the chair was taken. On a file made by this version that
is every record a chair has.

**The file's own check.** A chair filed as sat since before its
building opened is a complaint, by name and week.

**Found on the way.**

- A label founded out of a second house dated its desk from the
  day that house hired the desk, not from its own founding
  (`KP.deskSince`). Its record would have listed the second
  house's greenlights, and its first review would have been held
  against the second house's (§129, §130). No counted career
  takes that road: a house folds, another hires the desk, and
  the desk walks out of that one. The suite takes it by the real
  doors. The desk dates from the later of the two now, and the
  last statement reads the same week.
- Two chairs of one building could answer to one name. The four
  of a second chance were each named by hash from eight family
  names, and nothing kept two coaches apart: the long haul's
  insolvent career opened its second building with two called
  Coach Yoon, one of the five second chances counted. A name
  already taken in the building is passed over now.
- The long haul’s check of the walkout asked the file where the
  label was founded from. A founded label that later dissolved made
  the old house’s true entry look wrong: eight of the forty founder
  careers, each flagged, none of them a defect. The tool keeps its
  own book of the house the desk walked out of.

**What moved.** The census’s output is v0.11.39’s to the byte: no
career there founds a label, and its two second chances are seated
as they were. Ten of the long haul’s eleven careers read as they
did, line for line. The founder’s reads differently from week 151,
the week it walks out.

**The long haul's check, tried.** The long haul keeps books of
its own: every chair it has seen sat, and the week the desk last
moved. At a desk change it holds the next building to four new
chairs, sat that week, working names, each under its own name.
Every week it holds each chair's first week to the building's.
It was run against seven engines broken on purpose.
A founding that does not sweep the chairs, which is the engine as
it shipped. Chairs that keep the week they were minted with, at a
founding and at a second chance. Two chairs under one name. A
label’s chairs minted under the old building’s count, so they are
the old people again. A second chance that seats nobody. A building
that opens with names the trades know. A walkout left off the old
house’s books. Each was flagged by name. On the tree as it stands
the same careers are clean, and so are forty founders, where the
tool as it shipped flagged eight.

**Found by the mutation run.** One real edge, and three faults of
the suite's own.
The first run caught 50 of 54 broken lines by name. Two of the four
that got away crashed the suite, where the law is that it fails by
name: it read a file that had not loaded. One was a fixture that
gave the label the old house’s name, so a résumé that named the
wrong house read right. And one was real: the card counted a record
that landed the very week a chair was taken, and that record landed
before it was. The rule became “after”. The second run caught 54 of
54, the third 58 of 58 once the second chair’s gate was held, the
fourth 61 of 61 with the second house’s line and the card for the
door, and the final run the same.

**Mistakes on the way.**

- The first draft of the mint took the week as a third argument.
  Both callers passed the week it already knew. And the
  migration and the file's check each guarded against a chair
  that is on the file as nothing, which no file holds. All three
  were deleted on reading the diff, before the mutation run.
- One of the suite's expectations was a miscount: six chairs
  where the fixture had seven.
- The browser pass was wrong once on its first run: it read the
  company's name as if it were the company.
- One fixture of §128's suite built a founded label by hand,
  with chairs sat since week 1. The file's new check refused it.
  The fixture was given a label's own chairs, and nothing else
  in that suite was touched.
- Reading the diff before the long run found two things the
  runs had not. A chair that came across from a second house
  kept "here before you" on its résumé. And the card for the
  door did not say the staff stays.
- The probe that counted the carried chairs counted by first
  week, and was one short: a chair hired the very week of the
  founding. The script that fills this section stopped on it.
- A draft of this section said eight broken engines. There were
  seven, one of them run on two careers.

Suite_147 (79): the mint, its four chairs, their week, their
word, their résumé and their file numbers, the posting and the
market's memory cleared, the names with and without a clash; a

through the blank door and the salaried one, named by the

## §133 The credits (SHIPPED v0.11.41 — §96 recommendation 7, the people upstairs and down the hall, part nine)

Owner: *"Break remaining work into smaller pieces"*. The ninth of
recommendation 7's pieces, and the first of the staff given
years: "credit on the eras she coached". §96 found the staff
"hired as people through the best-composed scene in the company
slice and then kept as multipliers: no review, no credit, no
leaving on their own terms".

**Counted first.** Nothing on the file said what this house did
while a chair sat. The call from outside said "the industry reads
your credits and hires your people", and there were no credits to
read.

| | census, 200 careers | long haul, 11 |
|---|---|---|
| chairs that work an era, sat at the end | 1000 | 55 |
| of them with an era or more behind them | 973 | 26 |
| eras behind them, in all | 11682 | 301 |
| calls from outside for such a chair | 105 | 19 |
| of those, for a chair with no era at this house | 15 | 7 |
| such chairs that left a house that went on | 495 | 142 |
| eras behind the ones who left | 4389 | 1231 |

So the sentence was said of a chair with nothing at this house in
15 of 105 calls in the census and 7 of 19 in the long haul. Those
chairs came with a name, or the house was in its red weeks: the
call was never for a credit.

**The credit.** Read off the file, and nothing is kept
(`KP.seatCredit`). It is the résumé's own law (§79): it says where
they were, never what they did there.

- A chair that works an era, the vocal coach, the dance coach,
  the performance director, the A&R lead and the marketing lead,
  is credited with the eras that landed after they sat, by how
  each closed (§100): with a trophy, warm, quietly, cold, or
  still running. An era that landed the very week a chair was
  taken landed before it was (§132).
- A studio chair is credited with the records made here (§132).
- The scout is credited with those of the roster who signed on
  their watch, and how many of those have debuted.

No number here is what a chair is worth. The same eras stand
behind every chair that sat through them, and the results arrive
tangled with everything else, as they always did.

**Where it is said.**

- *The chair's card*, under the résumé: "In the room for 17 eras
  of this house: 8 closed with a trophy, 2 warm, 4 quietly, 3
  cold." A scout's: "Of the 17 on this house’s roster, 7 signed
  on their watch, and 3 of them have debuted." A chair with
  nothing behind it has no such line.
- *The call from outside* says what the industry read: "What it
  read: 17 eras for this house, 8 of them closed with a trophy."
  Of a chair with a name and nothing here it says so: "Sa Seon-mi
  has no credit at this house yet: the call is for the name they
  came in with." A chair with neither is only ever called in the
  red weeks (§86), and the scene says that.
- *The goodbyes*, when a chair is let go, replaced at an
  interview or takes the offer: "On the résumé that leaves with
  Kang Byung-chul: 17 eras for this house, 8 of them closed with
  a trophy."

**Found on the way.** A chair that walked on an unanswered call
went without a word. The road manager's unanswered counter-offer
has always written a letter. A chair's wrote none: the chair was
simply open the next time the Building tab was looked at. No run
could have found it, because the tools' players answer every
call. It was found reading the code for the goodbyes. Now a
letter says who took them, which chair is open and what went
with them, and it is one the week's budget cannot cut
(`seatLapsed`, on the one-shot list of §112).

**One real career, before and after.** A save from week 164, four
of its chairs sat since the first week.

Before, the call for the vocal coach and the call for a writer
eight weeks in read the same: “the industry reads your credits and
hires your people.” After, the first goes on: “What it read: 17
eras for this house, 8 of them closed with a trophy.” The second
says: “Sa Seon-mi has no credit at this house yet: the call is for
the name they came in with.”

Before, a call left unanswered for the dance coach wrote nothing at
all. After: “The offer sat on the desk until it answered itself:
Coach Cha signed with Aurum Media, and the head dance coach chair
is open. On the résumé that leaves with Coach Cha: 17 eras for this
house, 8 of them closed with a trophy.”

**What moved.** No simulation changed: the piece is in what is
said. The census’s output is v0.11.40’s but for one line: the
average save is 579 KB where it was 578, because the goodbyes it
holds say more. Every count and every band is the same. The long
haul says the same of every career, line for line, and writes the
same number of letters. The tools’ players answer every call, so
the new letter is never written there: the suite and the browser
pass hold it.

**The long haul's check, tried.** The long haul keeps books of
its own for every chair: which records landed in a week the
chair began sat, how each closed by the tool's own reading of the
close, and the week each of the roster came on to it. Every week
it holds each chair's credit to those books, and each call from
outside to what they hold. It was run against ten engines broken on
purpose.
Every era on the file counted, whenever the chair sat down. Every
closed era closed quietly. Nothing ever still running. Everyone on
the roster signed on the scout’s watch. Everyone who has debuted
counted for the scout. A call that does not say what was read. A
call that says credits were read whatever the chair has. The warm
ones named the best where there is a trophy. A chair with a name
told the call is for the red weeks. A chair with neither told it is
for its name. Each was flagged by name. On the tree as it stands
four careers are clean, and the whole run holds 37040 weeks of a
chair’s credit and 19 calls to the books.

**Found by the mutation run.** Nothing. 76 of 76 broken lines were
caught by name on the first run, and on the final run the same.

**Mistakes on the way.**

- The first trial left one broken engine unflagged: a call that
  says credits were read whatever the chair has. The career it
  ran on has five calls, every one for a chair with credits. The
  check was sound, and the trial was not trying it. Two careers
  that do have such calls were added, and it is flagged in both.
- The chain did not start the first time. The script was made
  from the last one by renaming, and the renaming changed the
  name of the scratch folder inside it. Nothing was checked and
  nothing in the tree was touched. A copy of the tree it had
  written to the wrong place was removed.
- The probe that counted first read a scout's signings off each
  person's chapters, which are kept forty to a person. In the
  long haul it found none of them on a stage, which was the
  chapters falling off the end of long files. The credit reads
  the week a person signed, which is kept.
- The first draft read the scout's credit off the week a person
  came to the board. That counts people a rival signed first. It
  reads the week they signed with this house.
- Three comments said the credit had to be read while the chair
  was still sat. It does not: the read takes the chair itself.
  The comments say what the lines do now.

Suite_148 (66): the eras after a chair sat, before, the very
week and after, closed each way, never closed, still running and
in its last promotion week, a second act, a retired act and two
acts in promotion; the five chairs that work an era; the words in
full and in a clause, for one era and for many, each way they can
stand; the scout, by the week each of the roster signed, with a
roster entry that has no file; the studio chairs; the card, its
place and its absence; the call, for a chair with credits, with a
name and none, with neither, for a producer, for a scout and for
a chair since emptied; each goodbye with something to take and
with nothing; a chair kept with a raise; the call left
unanswered, its letter, its place on the house's books, and two
real weeks that land it. Mutation-checked against 76 broken
lines, each caught by a named assertion. A real-browser pass
(12 checks, no page errors): a real career saved by v0.11.34
opens with what each chair was in the room for on its card; the
marketing lead is let go through the real button, and the letter
says what the résumé takes; a call for the vocal coach says what
the industry read, and "Wish them well" through the real button
writes what goes across the street; a call for a writer eight
weeks in says it is for the name; a call left unanswered for
real weeks takes the dance coach, and the letter lands.
Battery 148/148, soak 40 clean, census 200 clean, longhaul 11 × 620
clean, the till audit clean, e2e 137, 32, 41 and 23, the twenty-
three older browser passes, lockstep 0.11.41.

## §18 Watch items

Re-checked every soak; either fixed or watched, never silently tolerated.

- **regionStory band floor lowered 10%→2% (v0.9.1)** — the stronghold
  threshold (75) sits in the tail of the 140-week best-region
  distribution (median ~71, unchanged by aging — verified against the
  v0.9.0 baseline). If human play never sees a second-home story in a
  long career, consider lowering `strongholdNarrativeAt` instead.
  *Resolved v0.9.4*: the home circuit lengthened tours (fewer overseas
  legs per career, map ~3pts cooler, band went 0/40) — threshold moved
  75→72 exactly as this item prescribed; band back to 5/40.

- **showDarling band flipped ceiling→floor (v0.9.10)** — careers now
  open with a six-year act holding two trophies per stage; a bot that
  keeps them winning reaches `darlingAt` (7) in ~38/40 worlds, and
  that is the designed shape of "still selling", not wallpaper. The
  band now guards the floor (30%): no darlings would mean broken
  stages. If human play finds the dynasty coverage line stale by
  year two, vary the `showDarling` feed/memory templates before
  touching `darlingAt`.
- **gaffeSeen ceiling lifted 0.90→1.00 (v0.9.11)** — the second job
  pushes followings past `gaffeMinSocial` and fatigue past the tired-
  posting bonus, so ~37/40 careers now see at least one trended
  posting incident in 140 weeks. One 2am storm per three-year career
  is realism. If human play reports storm fatigue, tune `gaffeChance`
  down before touching the second job's payoffs.
- **Daesang giants back at 140 (0.9.13; peaked 148 in v0.9.12)** —
  the three upward steps countered ALL-TIME trophy inflation; the
  audit year-scoped the trophy term, removing that inflation, and
  the bar stepped back (12/40 daesang at 140 with year tallies).
  The era-indexing prescription stands if creep returns.
- **The stature bill governs, not yet plateaus (v0.9.14)** — the
  620-week trajectory is ~5.7–6.9k with the sink vs ~8.9k without
  (~25% damped). Pushing statureCostPer past ~0.015 provably
  starves the mid-game (the bots ship lean under pressure and the
  income collapses — measured at 0.02). A true plateau waits on
  the map's LATER sinks: enlistment eras cut income (slot 8), the
  imprint costs seed capital (slot 13), and elastic optional
  spending (tutors, wardrobe) arrives with slots 9 and 14. Revisit
  the trajectory after each; the probe lives in audit_longhaul.
- **dealClawedBack censuses 0/40 with the obligation-aware bot
  (v0.9.15)** — the 4-week tour gate means the auto-player simply
  never books the road over a sponsored appearance, so the
  two-miss termination path goes unexercised in soak (round one,
  gate-less, proved it fires: 23/40). Band floor is 0 so this is
  legal; the mechanism is held by suite 056. If human play never
  sees a clawback either, the road is too polite — widen
  missRescheduleWeeks so a mid-tour rebooking can land mid-tour
  again.
- **Producer cooling runs dormant in soak (v0.9.17)** — the bot
  picks the best hook, which is definitionally the push, so
  `pr.snubs` never accumulates in the census (0/40). The mechanism
  is suite-held. Human play picks for concept, taste, and members —
  watch whether the cooling ever fires there; if the owner never
  sees a producer cool, surface the push more loudly in the studio.
- **The whole member desk runs bot-dormant (v0.9.20)** — the walkout
  needs five stacked grievances on one person plus an empty tank, and
  the bot's sit-downs prevent both (0/40); the three verbs are
  player-only by nature. All suite-held. Watch human play: the
  walkout SHOULD eventually reach an owner who holds solos back and
  breaks promises — if it never does, lower grudgeAt before touching
  the chance.
- **The unasked greenlight and the trainee walkout run bot-dormant
  (v0.9.19)** — the bot always pitches before the floor gets loud
  (0/40), and it renews every believer under the age wall while her
  decline needs morale the bot never lets crater (0/40). Both rails
  suite-held. Watch human play: if the owner never sees the board
  move first, raise roomPressureChance; if no trainee ever walks,
  the decline thresholds are too kind.
- **Mandate lapses sit at 24/40 (v0.9.19 first soak)** — the blind
  bot pitches with four free names, aging-out eats the bench, and
  the window dies for −3 trust before a re-ask. Real friction,
  correctly priced. If human play finds windows dying through no
  fault (a poached room, a red quarter), consider pausing the lapse
  clock while the books are on warning before lengthening windows.
- **The slump runs dormant in soak (v0.9.18)** — entry needs
  morale < 42 AND confidence < 45 AND a fresh wound, and the
  sit-down-happy bot never lets both crater (0/80). The whole
  rail (entry, damp, shield, talk, the stage exit) is suite-held.
  Watch human play — a neglected second group after a missed
  comeback is the natural door. If the owner never sees a quiet
  era, raise enterMoraleBelow before touching enterChance.
- **The fiscal ceiling has been chased three times (0.9.18.1)** —
  0.45→0.65→0.75→0.85, each time because a designed-cost or
  designed-pressure release moved the operating point up while the
  poverty tail stayed healthy (latest: 80-seed min end-budget 2065,
  none below 300). The warned-count band is drifting toward
  weather. Next flap: stop chasing and re-point the census at the
  tail itself (orgs ending under ~300, ceiling ~0.05) — that is
  the poverty-spiral regression this alarm exists to catch.
- **holdoutMet runs bot-dormant (v0.9.33)** — the bot signs early,
  before heat and board-training push anyone over the holdout line,
  so it never OFFERS below a bar (0/40); it still wins holdouts
  through the lane door (11/40) and loses one to a power in every
  world (40/40). The decline arc is suite-held and the e2e hits it
  live. Watch human play: the owner scouts hot kids and WILL meet
  the no — if the no never converts (no call-backs, no courtship
  wins in reports), lower powerScore or laneRep before touching
  talentMin.
- **The service is soak-invisible by age math (v0.9.23)** — no male
  idol reaches notice age 26 inside 140 weeks (prospects generate
  14–22), so both service bands assert silence [0–10%] and the
  positive coverage lives in the longhaul's haul-service scenario.
  If the generation curve ever ages up, or a legacy boy group ships,
  re-point the soak bands at real activity instead.
- ~~**Rival acts do not enlist (v0.9.23)**~~ — closed v0.9.24 on
  the owner's order: rival boy acts now carry the window (warm acts
  rotate short-handed, cool acts pause whole, returns punch), and
  the longhaul holds a rival-side wall invariant.
- **The offer has two answers, not three (v0.9.24)** — accepting
  the imperial house's job (running THEIR machine) is a new game
  mode, deferred to the succession/board era (slot 12) where
  executive machinery lives; the scene ships with decline and
  leverage, and the body plays the temptation honestly. If the
  owner wants the third answer sooner, it is a real build, not a
  toggle. *v0.9.32 update*: the succession/board machinery it
  needs now exists (§73); the accept path remains a ruled build
  awaiting the owner's call.
- **Generation cadence is ruled, not measured long (v0.9.24)** —
  minYears 4 with a 2-year backdated seed gives a first turn near
  year 2 and ~4-year waves after; the longhaul prints gen counts.
  If 13-year runs stack more than ~3 turns, raise minYears before
  touching the torch or landmark triggers.
- **clamorHeld measures choice now, not cadence (v0.9.18)** — at
  first soak 100% of orgs paid resentment ticks because settling
  needs a release and the release cadence (~20wk) outruns the
  clock; the promise-pause (an open soloPromise stops the ticks)
  dropped it to 13/80, the orgs that held or let a promise lapse.
  If the band floods again, check the promise path before the
  pacing constants.
- **The resignation letter never fires in soak (v0.9.16)** — the
  sensible bot keeps trainee morale above the quit line in all 40
  worlds (0/40), so the scene is suite-held only. This is the
  burnout-census pattern: the mechanism triggers under neglect a
  decent policy never produces. Watch human play; if the letter
  never arrives there either, raise quitMoraleBelow before touching
  tenure.
- **schoolHot runs rare (1/40, v0.9.16)** — one it-girl arc plus a
  debuted alum is barely enough to cross 75 in 140 weeks; longer
  careers cross more. If the owner never sees a school get hot,
  lower hotAt to 70 before juicing the rep gains.
- **People-file growth accelerated by the school pipeline
  (v0.9.16)** — classes and trips mint extra prospects: ~90 more
  files by week 620 (~725KB vs ~619KB saves). The age-out sweep
  handles the unsigned; the growth rides the same curve as the
  rival-native item below and shares its remedy.
- ~~**No senescence (0.9.13 audit A4)**~~ — closed v0.9.32: age
  bites at 28 (growth, recovery) and pays back in floor (stage
  IQ), words never meters; the legacy act makes the crossing
  near-universal in soak (39/40, floor-guarded).
- **Trust saturates high by year 3 (0.9.13 audit B4)** — gains
  outpace every loss path at scale; gates lose tension. Candidate:
  slow drift toward startTrust, or stature-scaled expectations.
  *Overtaken by the sink (v0.9.18)*: the founder probe measured
  trust hovering 40–60 across 13 bot years under the fiscal
  warnings — saturation is gone at bot policy, and the founding
  gate (70) is now the hard one. The longhaul grants the
  collateral when trust ALONE gates founding by week 150, because
  that audit soaks the founded shape; the soak owns the odds.
  *Closed v0.9.32*: the drift clock ships anyway — above 75, −1 per
  month toward 75, deliberately ABOVE the founding gate so the gate
  stays winnable while the summit stops being ownable.
- **Rival-native file growth (0.9.13 audit)** — ~25 files/year,
  ~half the save by year 13, quota breach ~a century out. If it
  ever matters: tombstone-compress members of long-retired acts
  (keep name/history, drop talent cones).
- **Burnout census runs cold** (0/40 orgs with the cautious auto-player;
  band top 45%). The mechanism triggers under sustained heavy load (suite
  003 forces it), but a sensible policy never sees it. Watch whether human
  play produces it; if not, fatigue soft cap may be too forgiving.
- **Rival steals at 40/40 seeds** — band-legal but pinned at the top; if
  players report the board feels like a fire sale, tune
  `rivalSignHotChance` down.
- ~~**Whitecliff unused** at RIVALS.count=2~~ — retired v0.4.0: the
  opening scene seeds all three rivals and the lifecycle grows the field
  to as many as six.
- **Chart top-three pinned at 40/40** (v0.4.0 soak) — band-legal at the
  top edge. The player's fresh releases usually outscore the rivals'
  decayed entries. If the owner reports the chart feels easy, raise rival
  act quality or add release-week clustering.
- **Feed tone** — the negative content law is tested, but *funny* cannot
  be asserted. Watch the owner's screenshots; stale or repetitive posts
  mean the template pools need widening (they are data, cheap to grow).
- **Overwork benchings at 40/40 max-pace runs** (v0.4.2) — the harness
  never volunteers extra idle weeks, so every soak org eventually eats a
  benching. Band-legal and arguably the point of the hard version, but
  if the owner reports the medical letters feel constant in human play
  (humans breathe more than the bot), lower `OVERWORK.chance` or raise
  the threshold before touching the rest window.
- **Sit-down treadmill** (v0.1.2): the soak auto-player, mediating every
  friction eagerly, runs ~16 sit-downs per org over 84 weeks. Band-legal
  and partly a policy artifact, but if human play feels like relationship
  whack-a-mole, consider longer-lasting mediation effects (a "settled"
  grace period) before touching drift again.
- **`ScheduleBlock`, `Contract`, `Market` domain objects** from brief §17
  are not yet modeled; weekly training assignment stands in for schedules
  in the slice.

> Found-by-process: the launch economy death-spiraled (stipend 6 vs upkeep
> 18/month) — every soak org hit ₩0 before production; retuned to 12/0.25.
> Also fixed pre-ship: ceiling clamp could mint 101-cap cones; module-level
> id counter interleaved parallel states (moved to `state.nextPersonId`);
> modal stopPropagation swallowed every sheet button (e2e caught it).
> Next: owner plays the slice; feel report decides Phase 2.

> **Planning note (docs-only, post-v0.1.0)** — Owner set the next
> direction while testing the slice: *"making everything procedural.
> every run should feel different. no need to code anything yet while I
> test."* Audited what is static across runs (company, rivals, objective,
> opening trainees, staff, and all shallow content pools — measured
> numbers in §17) and specced the v0.2.x procedural line: content
> generators → generated staff → generated companies → scenario hook
> library → executive mechanics → drifting market trends → pre-history.
> Gated on the owner's v0.1.0 feel report. No code written.

> **v0.1.1 — first feel report, answered** (owner played on GitHub Pages)
> Owner's words, all four delivered: *"move advance week to the unused
> space at the top of the page between the week and currency"* — the
> Advance pill now lives in the topbar, always reachable, and the floating
> button is gone. *"quickly change their intensity from this page without
> having to click through the individual profiles… maybe a dedicated
> training page"* — new Training sub-tab in Talent: every trainee's focus
> chips and intensity control inline; members in debut rehearsals shown as
> schedule-owned. *"I need a way to release a trainee"* — releaseTrainee
> with rails (no lineup members, no idols, no refunds, close friends named
> in the confirm and shaken by the exit); suite 006 added. *"trainees skew
> too old. probably shouldn't be seeing many in training at 20+"* —
> diagnosed: uniform 16–23 put 48% of the pool at 20+, mean 19.4. Retuned
> to weighted 15–23 (`GEN.ageWeights`): mean 18.0, 21% aged 20+, guarded
> by suite 001 and a new observatory age census.

> reception median 53), e2e 38/38, lockstep green. Rode to main.

> **v0.1.2 — conflict gets a handle** (second feel report)
> Owner: *"a lot of conflict and no way to do anything about it other than
> hope it works out."* Diagnosis confirmed and quantified: the drift model
> was structurally biased down — always-negative penalty terms, no repair
> force — leaving 65% of pairs tense-or-worse by week 40 (36% in "open
> conflict", which §8 had promised was rare). Two-part fix: (1) drift
> rebalance — neutral compatibility mean, professionalism-scaled reversion,
> cool-off for feuding pairs trained apart (separation is now a real
> lever); (2) **the sit-down** — mediation with cost, cooldown, and
> personality-shaped odds, resolved in prose, surfaced as friction cards
> (problem + handle together) in dossier, group room report, and builder.
> Tuning took two soak rounds: the first pass left 22/40 orgs ending
> conflict-heavy (new census band FLOODed) because shared-focus corrosion
> kept mediation on a treadmill; softened it and strengthened reversion →
> 5/40, in band. Week-40 texture now ~20% tense, ~1% open conflict, warmth
> intact (27 close pairs vs 26 before — the game did not go bland).
> Numbers: battery 7/7 (suite 007 added), soak clean with two new
> relationship census bands, e2e 42/42 (stages a conflict, resolves it
> through the UI), lockstep 0.1.2. New watch item: sit-down treadmill.
> Rode to main.

> **v0.2.0 — the comeback loop** (owner finished the slice: *"I created a
> group, they debuted... now what?"* — chose the comeback loop over
> starting the procedural line, which renumbers to v0.3.x)
> The debut is now the first release, not the ending. Objective ladder:
> every resolved directive summons the next as an executive letter with a
> reinvestment grant — comeback targets that move with the story, gentler
> deadline penalties, always "one more window." Popularity founded at
> debut, compounded by comebacks, decaying in the room between releases;
> worded (burning/hot/warm/cooling/fading), never a meter. Promotion
> cycle: 4 hot weeks then real recovery — which killed a live bug found
> during design: idols kept their training intensity forever and pegged at
> 100 fatigue post-debut; the migration repairs afflicted saves with a
> narrated management-review letter. Charts-lite peaks + weeks per
> release; discography on the group page; Studio reopens each cycle with
> fresh demos; era accents follow the new concept. Also new: **the
> spark** — a big hook plus a magnetic performer can catch fire (+4..10,
> fancam note in the PR digest) — added after the observatory declared
> sensation debuts EXTINCT; the sensation band edge was then calibrated
> against a measured 200-seed distribution (78 → 75, ~3.5% of debuts).
> Numbers: battery 8/8 (suite 008: ladder, cycle, decay, fatigue
> recovery, migration, determinism), 140-week 40-seed soak clean with 12
> census bands (8.0 releases/org, every org loops, fanbases survive),
> e2e 48/48 (plays a full comeback cycle), lockstep 0.2.0 (23 modules).
> Rode to main.

> focus: music shows / variety / fan engagement decide where the
> promotion weeks go — fan care stretches the popularity grace window.
> Stage names with suggestions, uniqueness, and the public/staff naming

> 0.2.1. Rode to main. Second group ships next as v0.2.2.

> The single-group vertical slice becomes an agency: `state.group` →

> a Studio group switcher, per-group results reports, and comeback
> directives that name their group and target whichever act has waited
> longest. Migration moves an existing save's group into the new shape

> releases and 2.0 groups per org, all 13 census bands alive.

> development, health, showcase, relationship, chemistry, friction,
> sit-down, release fallout, events, PR — routes through
> displayName/publicGiven; suite 011 sweeps 30 weeks of reports for

> Provisional groups: lock 1–3 members from the builder, optionally

> **v0.2.6 — the internet has decided** (owner: hype + solos, *"dude I
> want the hard version"*)
> Pre-debut hype as a decaying window: emergent events find magnetic
> trainees, the Desk grows a second clock, and past the threshold the
> CEO issues the hard directive — debut her in 20 weeks, group or solo,
> or eat −12 trust and watch her window collapse ("Remember that I
> remember"). Debuts cash hype into launch reception, founding fanbase,
> and the public's eye. Solo acts ship as one-member acts through the
> same machinery: her own nerve for chemistry, a charisma edge, ×1.4
> volatility, ×1.5 promo fatigue, nowhere to hide. Statistical suite

> Numbers: battery 14/14 (suite 014, green first run), soak clean with

> Every release enters the weekly scene chart (decay 0.88, honest

> posts, overshadow discourse, industry obituaries) plus ambient
> chatter, under the hard content law (snark at songs/styling/companies,
> never bodies; crushes wholesome) enforced as a negative-law scan in
> suite 020. Industry tab rebuilt as Scene/Chart/Feed. Whitecliff
> activated (3 starting rivals, each seeded with running acts — retires
> a §18 watch item). Migration 0.4.0 seeds the world into existing
> saves, narrated as the industry desk expanding. Two seed-snapshot
> assertions exposed by the new rng draws (suites 014, 018) were
> rewritten as mechanism-level invariants — the v0.3.0 lesson holding.
> Numbers: battery 20/20 (suites 019 industry, 020 feed), soak clean
> (24 bands: rival debuts 40/40, lifecycle 32/40, crowded releases

> **v0.4.1 — the five-band ladder** (owner: *"the rating system needs
> one more on between developing and strong. I'd call it capable…
> each would just occupy a 20 point range"*)
> BANDS is now Raw 1–20 / Developing 21–40 / Capable 41–60 / Strong
> 61–80 / Exceptional 81–100, exactly as specified (Law 1 amended).
> Blurb content rebalanced to match the words: lines that always read
> as does-the-job ("Capable when needed…", "Keeps up with the back
> line…", "Photographs fine…") moved from the old too-wide Developing

> Developing back up; charisma got an original Capable voice

> ("dependable is underrated — sign her for the room"). bandRank now
> derives from the table instead of a hardcoded list. Side effects
> owned in the Bible §5 note: Exceptional starts at 81 (rarer),
> Raw ends at 20 (kinder). No data migration (bands are read, never
> stored — Law 2), but the rubric change is narrated to existing saves
